chapters.r: Middle mediastinum, behind the sternum
chapters.b: Right & left coronary arteries (first branches of the aorta)
chapters.n: Cardiac plexus — vagus (slows) + sympathetic T1–T4 (speeds up)
chapters.bl: Two synchronized muscular pumps in one organ: four chambers, four one-way valves, coronary arteries, and the intrinsic SA-to-Purkinje electrical pacemaker.
chapters.sum: Roughly the size of a closed fist and beating about 100,000 times every day, the human heart is two synchronized muscular pumps sealed inside a single organ. The heart is a double pump. Its right side receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae and sends it to the lungs; its left side receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and ejects it into the aorta. The two sides never mix because of the interatrial and interventricular septa, and one-way valves keep blood moving forwards. Contraction is triggered by an electrical impulse that begins in the sinoatrial node and sweeps through the atria, the atrioventricular node, the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres. Within the human body, the heart (Cor) is situated in middle mediastinum, behind the sternum, receives arterial perfusion via right & left coronary arteries (first branches of the aorta), and is innervated by cardiac plexus — vagus (slows) + sympathetic T1–T4 (speeds up).

The superior vena cava (Vena cava superior) is the large vein draining the head, neck, upper limbs and thorax. It enters the upper part of the right atrium. Physiologically, the superior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from everything above the diaphragm. The inferior vena cava (Vena cava inferior) is the largest vein in the body. It collects blood from the abdomen, pelvis and lower limbs and enters the inferior part of the right atrium. Physiologically, the inferior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from below the diaphragm. The aorta is the largest artery in the body. It arises from the left ventricle, arches over the left main bronchus and descends through the thorax and abdomen. Physiologically, the aorta distributes oxygenated blood to the entire systemic circulation. The pulmonary trunk (Truncus pulmonalis) leaves the right ventricle and divides into right and left pulmonary arteries. Uniquely, it carries deoxygenated blood. Physiologically, the pulmonary trunk carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation. The pulmonary veins (Venae pulmonales) are four veins — two from each lung — that carry freshly oxygenated blood into the left atrium. Physiologically, the pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart. The myocardium is the thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of branching, interlinked cardiac muscle fibres joined by intercalated discs. Physiologically, the myocardium contracts to generate the pressure that ejects blood.

Clinically, regarding the superior vena cava, obstruction (SVC syndrome) causes facial and arm swelling with distended neck veins. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the inferior vena cava, compression in late pregnancy reduces venous return and can cause supine hypotension. In clinical pathology involving the aorta, a tear in the wall (aortic dissection) causes sudden tearing chest or back pain — a surgical emergency. Medical evaluation of the pulmonary trunk also notes that a clot lodging here (pulmonary embolism) causes breathlessness, pleuritic pain and hypoxia.

chapters.r: Pleural cavities of the thorax, either side of the mediastinum
chapters.b: Pulmonary arteries (gas exchange) + bronchial arteries (tissue supply)
chapters.n: Pulmonary plexus — vagus (bronchoconstriction) + sympathetic T2–T4
chapters.bl: Twenty-three generations of branching airways lead to hundreds of millions of elastic alveoli where inspired air meets pulmonary capillary blood across 0.5 µm.
chapters.sum: Beneath the ribcage, two spongy, elastic lungs branch through more than twenty generations of airways to bring fresh air within a fraction of a micron of blood. Air is conducted from the trachea through progressively dividing bronchi and bronchioles until it reaches the alveoli, where oxygen diffuses into pulmonary capillaries and carbon dioxide diffuses out. The right lung has three lobes separated by oblique and horizontal fissures; the left has two, with a cardiac notch and lingula to accommodate the heart. Each lung is wrapped in visceral pleura, opposed by parietal pleura across a thin fluid-filled cavity whose surface tension keeps the lung expanded. Within the human body, the lungs (Pulmones) is situated in pleural cavities of the thorax, either side of the mediastinum, receives arterial perfusion via pulmonary arteries (gas exchange) + bronchial arteries (tissue supply), and is innervated by pulmonary plexus — vagus (bronchoconstriction) + sympathetic T2–T4.

The trachea is a 10–12 cm tube held open by 16–20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, open posteriorly where the trachealis muscle lies. Lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Physiologically, the trachea conducts, warms, humidifies and filters inspired air. The main & lobar bronchi (Bronchi principales et lobares) is the trachea divides at the carina (T4/T5) into right and left main bronchi, which divide into lobar then segmental bronchi. Cartilage plates replace rings as the airways narrow. Physiologically, the main & lobar bronchi governs distribute air to each lobe and bronchopulmonary segment. Structurally, the bronchioles (Bronchioli) comprises airways under 1 mm with no cartilage and relatively more smooth muscle, ending in terminal then respiratory bronchioles. Physiologically, the bronchioles regulate airflow resistance and deliver air to the alveolar ducts. The right lung — three lobes (Pulmo dexter) are superior, middle and inferior lobes separated by the oblique and horizontal fissures. Shorter than the left because the liver sits below, but wider and heavier. Physiologically, the right lung — three lobes governs gas exchange across ~150 million alveoli. The left lung — two lobes (Pulmo sinister) are superior and inferior lobes separated by the oblique fissure only. Narrower than the right because the heart bulges to the left. Physiologically, the left lung — two lobes governs gas exchange; the lingula of the superior lobe is the equivalent of the right middle lobe. The fissures (Fissurae pulmonis) are deep invaginations of visceral pleura. The oblique fissure runs in both lungs (T4 posteriorly to the 6th rib anteriorly); the horizontal fissure is right-sided only. Physiologically, the fissures allow the lobes to slide against each other and define surgical planes.

Clinically, regarding the trachea, foreign bodies more often enter the right main bronchus because it is wider, shorter and more vertical. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the main & lobar bronchi, each segmental bronchus supplies a bronchopulmonary segment that can be surgically removed on its own. In clinical pathology involving the bronchioles, smooth-muscle spasm of the bronchioles is the main problem in asthma; smooth muscle is also the target of salbutamol. Medical evaluation of the right lung — three lobes also notes that the right middle lobe is prone to collapse (middle-lobe syndrome) because its bronchus is narrow and surrounded by nodes.

chapters.r: Cranial cavity, above the brainstem
chapters.b: Internal carotid + vertebral arteries → circle of Willis (15% of cardiac output)
chapters.n: Itself the source of cranial nerves I–XII
chapters.bl: Folded cerebral lobes, white-matter commissures, deep thalamic and basal nuclei, cerebellum, and brainstem circuits floating in protective cerebrospinal fluid.
chapters.sum: Weighing about 1.4 kilograms yet consuming nearly a fifth of the body's oxygen, the human brain weaves billions of neurons into folded cortex and deep relay nuclei. The brain integrates sensation, generates movement, and supports language, memory and consciousness. It uses about 20% of the body's oxygen and glucose despite being 2% of body weight, and it has almost no energy reserve — four minutes of ischaemia starts to kill neurons. The cerebral cortex is folded into gyri and sulci to pack ~0.15 m² of grey matter into the skull. Beneath it, white-matter tracts such as the corpus callosum connect the hemispheres, while the diencephalon and brainstem handle relay, arousal and the automatic control of breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. Within the human body, the brain (Encephalon) is situated in cranial cavity, above the brainstem, receives arterial perfusion via internal carotid + vertebral arteries → circle of Willis (15% of cardiac output), and serves directly as the origin of cranial nerves I–XII.

The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain: two hemispheres of folded cortex over deep white matter, basal ganglia and the lateral ventricles. Physiologically, the cerebrum governs voluntary movement, sensation, language, memory, personality and conscious thought. The frontal lobe (Lobus frontalis) is anterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. Contains the primary motor cortex, Broca's area (usually left) and the prefrontal cortex. Physiologically, the frontal lobe governs planning, judgement, personality, voluntary movement and expressive speech. Anatomically, the parietal lobe (Lobus parietalis) lies behind the central sulcus, above the temporal lobe. Houses the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus. Physiologically, the parietal lobe governs processing of touch, pain, temperature, position sense and spatial awareness. The occipital lobe (Lobus occipitalis) is the posterior pole, bounded medially by the parieto-occipital sulcus, containing the primary visual cortex on the banks of the calcarine sulcus. Physiologically, the occipital lobe governs vision — the retinal image is mapped point-for-point on the calcarine cortex. Anatomically, the temporal lobe (Lobus temporalis) lies below the lateral sulcus, including the hippocampal formation and primary auditory cortex on the superior temporal gyrus. Physiologically, the temporal lobe governs hearing, memory formation, language comprehension (Wernicke's area) and emotion. The corpus callosum is the great C-shaped commissure of ~200 million myelinated fibres: rostrum, genu, body and splenium. Physiologically, the corpus callosum connects matching regions of the two hemispheres so they work as one brain.

Clinically, regarding the cerebrum, its surface folding (gyri and sulci) triples cortical area; abnormal folding causes lissencephaly and epilepsy. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the frontal lobe, prefrontal damage (classically Phineas Gage) changes personality and impulse control while sparing memory and IQ. In clinical pathology involving the parietal lobe, right-sided lesions cause hemispatial neglect — the patient ignores the whole left side of space. Medical evaluation of the occipital lobe also notes that a posterior cerebral artery stroke causes a congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

chapters.r: Retroperitoneal, T12–L3 (left slightly higher)
chapters.b: Renal artery from the abdominal aorta — 20–25% of cardiac output
chapters.n: Renal plexus (sympathetic T10–L1) — mainly vasomotor
chapters.bl: Retroperitoneal filtration powerhouses: outer renal cortex, medullary pyramids, calyces, and a million nephrons that purify blood plasma and balance body water.
chapters.sum: Tucked behind the peritoneum on either side of the spine, the two bean-shaped kidneys filter the entire plasma volume dozens of times a day to keep body fluids balanced. Each kidney filters about 180 litres of plasma a day and returns all but 1–2 litres to the blood. Filtration happens in the renal corpuscle, where glomerular capillaries sit inside Bowman's capsule. The filtrate then passes through the proximal tubule (bulk reabsorption), the loop of Henle (concentration by countercurrent multiplication), the distal tubule (hormone-controlled fine tuning) and the collecting duct (final water handling under vasopressin). Nephrons drain via the papilla into minor and major calyces, the renal pelvis and the ureter. Within the human body, the kidney (Ren) is situated in retroperitoneal, T12–L3 (left slightly higher), receives arterial perfusion via renal artery from the abdominal aorta — 20–25% of cardiac output, and is innervated by renal plexus (sympathetic T10–L1) — mainly vasomotor.

The fibrous capsule (Capsula fibrosa) is a tough transparent layer of collagenous tissue directly on the kidney surface, surrounded by perinephric fat. Physiologically, the fibrous capsule protects the parenchyma and maintains its shape. The renal cortex (Cortex renalis) is the outer 1 cm, containing all the renal corpuscles, the proximal and distal convoluted tubules, and cortical tissue dipping between pyramids as the renal columns. Physiologically, the renal cortex governs site of blood filtration and most solute reabsorption. The renal pyramid (Pyramides renales) is 8–18 cone-shaped regions of medulla, striped by the straight loops of Henle, vasa recta and collecting ducts that run through them. Physiologically, the renal pyramid governs create and exploit the osmotic gradient that concentrates urine. The renal papilla (Papilla renalis) is the apex of each pyramid, pierced by dozens of duct openings (area cribrosa) that empty into a minor calyx. Physiologically, the renal papilla governs the final exit point for urine from the nephron system. Structurally, the minor & major calyces (Calices renales) comprises cup-like minor calyces (8–18) receive urine from papillae and join into 2–3 major calyces that funnel into the renal pelvis. Physiologically, the minor & major calyces collect urine and conduct it to the pelvis; their smooth muscle helps propel it. The renal pelvis (Pelvis renalis) is the funnel-shaped expansion of the upper ureter inside the hilum. Physiologically, the renal pelvis collects urine from the major calyces and channels it into the ureter.

Clinically, regarding the fibrous capsule, it does not stretch: swelling inside the capsule in acute inflammation causes the dull loin pain of pyelonephritis. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the renal cortex, thinning or scarring of the cortex on ultrasound indicates chronic kidney disease. In clinical pathology involving the renal pyramid, their striated appearance is lost in medullary cystic disease and in the scarring of chronic reflux nephropathy. Medical evaluation of the renal papilla also notes that analgesic abuse, diabetes and sickle-cell disease can cause papillary necrosis, with sloughed tissue in the urine.

chapters.r: Right hypochondrium & epigastrium, under the diaphragm
chapters.b: Dual: hepatic artery (25%) + hepatic portal vein (75%)
chapters.n: Hepatic plexus (vagus + sympathetic coeliac fibres)
chapters.bl: Fed by both the nutrient-rich portal vein and oxygen-rich hepatic artery, the liver's hexagonal lobules synthesize proteins, detoxify blood, and secrete bile.
chapters.sum: As the largest internal organ in the body, the liver sits beneath the right diaphragm and processes nearly every nutrient absorbed from the digestive tract. The liver receives blood twice over — oxygenated from the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich from the portal vein — and mixes them in the sinusoids between plates of hepatocytes. Each hepatocyte performs hundreds of jobs: making albumin and clotting factors, conjugating bilirubin, storing glycogen and vitamins, and detoxifying drugs through the cytochrome P450 system. Bile, made continuously, is concentrated in the gallbladder and released into the duodenum to emulsify fat. The liver is also the only visceral organ that can regenerate: removing 70% leaves a liver that regrows to full size. Within the human body, the liver (Hepar) is situated in right hypochondrium & epigastrium, under the diaphragm, receives arterial perfusion via dual: hepatic artery (25%) + hepatic portal vein (75%), and is innervated by hepatic plexus (vagus + sympathetic coeliac fibres).

The right lobe (Lobus dexter) is the larger lobe, four to six times the volume of the left, occupying the right hypochondrium. Its diaphragmatic surface is smooth and convex. Physiologically, the right lobe carries most of the hepatic mass and function. Structurally, the left lobe (Lobus sinister) comprises thinner and flatter, lying in the epigastrium and reaching across to the left. Separated from the right lobe on the diaphragmatic surface by the falciform ligament. Physiologically, the left lobe supplies the left half of the functional liver. The caudate lobe (Lobus caudatus) is a small lobe on the posterior surface between the IVC and the ligamentum venosum, draining directly into the IVC. Physiologically, the caudate lobe governs has independent vascular supply and biliary drainage. Anatomically, the quadrate lobe (Lobus quadratus) lies on the visceral surface between the gallbladder fossa and the fissure for the ligamentum teres. Physiologically, the quadrate lobe governs functionally part of the left hemiliver. The falciform ligament (Ligamentum falciforme) is a sickle-shaped fold of peritoneum attaching the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm; its free edge carries the ligamentum teres (obliterated umbilical vein). Physiologically, the falciform ligament anchors the liver and divides the anatomical lobes on the diaphragmatic surface. The gallbladder (Vesica biliaris) is a 7–10 cm pear-shaped sac on the visceral surface of the right lobe, with fundus, body and neck. Its wall concentrates bile up to tenfold. Physiologically, the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum when fat arrives (CCK-mediated).

Clinically, regarding the right lobe, its inferior edge is what you palpate below the costal margin in hepatomegaly. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the left lobe, in cirrhosis the left and caudate lobes often hypertrophy while the right lobe atrophies. In clinical pathology involving the caudate lobe, it hypertrophies in Budd–Chiari syndrome, and its size relative to the right lobe is a CT sign of cirrhosis. Medical evaluation of the quadrate lobe also notes that together with the caudate lobe it defines the surgical anatomy of the portohepatic segments.

chapters.r: Abdominal cavity, from diaphragm to pelvic floor
chapters.b: Coeliac trunk, superior & inferior mesenteric arteries
chapters.n: Vagus (parasympathetic) + thoracolumbar splanchnic (sympathetic)
chapters.bl: A continuous muscular digesting and absorbing tube from the acid-churning stomach through the villus-lined small intestine to the water-reclaiming colon.
chapters.sum: From the muscular churn of the stomach to the absorptive folds of the small intestine and water-reclaiming colon, the gastrointestinal tract is a dynamic muscular tube. Food is stored and acidified in the stomach, where pepsin begins protein digestion and the muscular wall churns it into chyme. The duodenum neutralises acid and receives bile and pancreatic juice; the jejunum and ileum absorb almost all nutrients across a surface amplified by circular folds, villi and microvilli to roughly 250 m². The colon then reclaims water and electrolytes and stores faeces. The gut also carries its own nervous system — the enteric plexuses — with more neurons than the spinal cord. Within the human body, the stomach & intestines (Gaster et intestina) is situated in abdominal cavity, from diaphragm to pelvic floor, receives arterial perfusion via coeliac trunk, superior & inferior mesenteric arteries, and is innervated by vagus (parasympathetic) + thoracolumbar splanchnic (sympathetic).

The oesophagus is a 25 cm muscular tube from pharynx to stomach, passing through the diaphragm at T10. Physiologically, the oesophagus propels the bolus by peristalsis; the lower sphincter prevents reflux. The fundus of stomach (Fundus ventriculi) is the dome above the oesophageal opening, usually filled with a gas bubble on erect films. Physiologically, the fundus of stomach stores swallowed air and gives the stomach its reservoir. The body of stomach (Corpus ventriculi) is the main reservoir between fundus and antrum, lined by acid- and pepsin-secreting mucosa with rugae. Physiologically, the body of stomach mixes food with acid and pepsin; intrinsic factor for B12 absorption is made here. The pyloric antrum & pylorus (Antrum pyloricum) is the distal funnel ending in the thick pyloric sphincter. Physiologically, the pyloric antrum & pylorus governs grinds food and meters chyme into the duodenum; G cells here secrete gastrin. Structurally, the rugae (Plicae gastricae) comprises longitudinal folds of gastric mucosa that flatten as the stomach distends. Physiologically, the rugae allow expansion and channel the flow of chyme. The duodenum is a C-shaped 25 cm first part of the small bowel wrapping the pancreatic head; the ampulla opens on its second part. Physiologically, the duodenum governs neutralises acid with bicarbonate and mixes chyme with bile and pancreatic enzymes.

Clinically, regarding the oesophagus, its lower third drains to the portal system via the left gastric vein — hence varices in portal hypertension. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the fundus of stomach, a fundal mass can be missed behind the gastric gas bubble on a plain radiograph. In clinical pathology involving the body of stomach, loss of parietal cells (autoimmune gastritis) causes pernicious anaemia through B12 malabsorption. Medical evaluation of the pyloric antrum & pylorus also notes that chronic antral gastritis from Helicobacter pylori is the main route to peptic ulcer and gastric cancer.

chapters.r: Orbit, protected by the bony orbital walls
chapters.b: Ophthalmic artery (central retinal + ciliary branches)
chapters.n: Optic (II) · motor III, IV, VI · autonomic for pupil
chapters.bl: A self-focusing optical globe: transparent cornea and crystalline lens bend light onto a ten-layered neural retina packed with rod and cone photoreceptors.
chapters.sum: Built like a self-focusing biological camera just 24 millimeters wide, the human eye bends incoming light across transparent media onto a neural carpet of photoreceptors. Light is refracted mostly at the cornea and finely focused by the lens, whose curvature is changed by the ciliary muscle for near vision. The iris adjusts pupil size to control light entry. The image lands on the retina, where rods (dim light, motion) and cones (colour, detail) convert photons into signals through bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons leave as the optic nerve. The fovea, a pit in the macula with cones only, gives sharp central vision. The retina is neural tissue: it is the only place in the body where the central nervous system can be seen directly. Within the human body, the eye (Oculus) is situated in orbit, protected by the bony orbital walls, receives arterial perfusion via ophthalmic artery (central retinal + ciliary branches), and is innervated by optic (II) · motor III, IV, VI · autonomic for pupil.

Structurally, the cornea comprises transparent, avascular, five-layered dome at the front of the eye. Provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power. Physiologically, the cornea bends and transmits light; its endothelium pumps water out to stay clear. The sclera is the tough white outer coat of collagen, continuous with the cornea anteriorly and the dural sheath of the optic nerve posteriorly. Physiologically, the sclera maintains the shape of the globe and anchors the extraocular muscles. The choroid (Choroidea) is the vascular middle layer between sclera and retina, densely packed with capillaries and melanin. Physiologically, the choroid feeds the outer retina and absorbs stray light to sharpen the image. The retina is ten-layered neural film: photoreceptors outermost (light must pass through the inner layers first), then bipolar and ganglion cells. Physiologically, the retina transduces light into nerve impulses. The macula & fovea (Macula lutea) is a 5.5 mm yellow-pigmented area at the posterior pole; its centre, the fovea, contains cones only and no vessels. Physiologically, the macula & fovea governs high-acuity central vision for reading and faces. Structurally, the optic disc (Discus opticus) comprises where ganglion axons and the central retinal vessels pierce the sclera. It has no photoreceptors. Physiologically, the optic disc governs exit point of the optic nerve and entry of the central retinal artery.

Clinically, regarding the cornea, endothelial failure causes oedema and cloudy vision; reshaping the cornea (LASIK) corrects refractive error. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the sclera, thins with age and in inflammation (scleritis, a painful red eye linked to autoimmune disease). In clinical pathology involving the choroid, its high blood flow makes it a common site for metastatic deposits and for uveitis. Medical evaluation of the retina also notes that retinal detachment is a surgical emergency — flashes, floaters and a curtain across the field.

chapters.r: Temporal bone: external, middle and inner ear
chapters.b: Labyrinthine artery (from basilar or AICA)
chapters.n: Vestibulocochlear (VIII)
chapters.bl: Three connected compartments in the temporal bone convert airborne pressure waves into cochlear nerve signals while tracking head rotation and gravity.
chapters.sum: Housed deep within the dense petrous temporal bone, the human ear pairs two remarkable sensory systems in one space: acoustic hearing and three-dimensional balance. Sound waves are funnelled by the auricle down the external canal to the tympanic membrane. The membrane vibrates the ossicular chain — malleus, incus and stapes, the three smallest bones in the body — which amplifies pressure about 22-fold as it transfers vibration from a large eardrum to the tiny oval window. In the fluid-filled cochlea, the travelling wave bends hair cells on the basilar membrane: high frequencies at the base, low at the apex. Beside it, the vestibule and three semicircular canals sense gravity and angular acceleration for balance. Within the human body, the ear (Auris) is situated in temporal bone: external, middle and inner ear, receives arterial perfusion via labyrinthine artery (from basilar or AICA), and is innervated by vestibulocochlear (VIII).

In the fluid-filled cochlea, the travelling wave bends hair cells on the basilar membrane: high frequencies at the base, low at the apex. Beside it, the vestibule and three semicircular canals sense gravity and angular acceleration for balance. Within the human body, the ear (Auris) is situated in temporal bone: external, middle and inner ear, receives arterial perfusion via labyrinthine artery (from basilar or AICA), and is innervated by vestibulocochlear (VIII).

The auricle (pinna) (Auricula) is a cartilaginous scoop: helix, antihelix, tragus, antitragus, concha and lobule. Physiologically, the auricle (pinna) collects sound and helps localise it, especially vertically. The external acoustic meatus (Meatus acusticus externus) is a 2.5 cm S-shaped canal, cartilaginous outer third and bony inner two-thirds, lined by skin with ceruminous glands. Physiologically, the external acoustic meatus conducts sound to the eardrum; cerumen traps dust and insects. The tympanic membrane (Membrana tympani) is a 9 × 10 mm cone of three layers, tilted so its umbo points medially; pars tensa below, pars flaccida above. Physiologically, the tympanic membrane converts sound pressure into mechanical vibration of the malleus. The malleus is the hammer: handle embedded in the eardrum, head articulating with the incus. Physiologically, the malleus governs first lever of the ossicular chain. The incus is the anvil, bridging malleus and stapes. Physiologically, the incus governs second lever; its long process is the most fragile part of the chain. The stapes are the stirrup: the smallest bone in the body (~3 mm), its footplate closing the oval window. Physiologically, the stapes delivers amplified vibration into the cochlear fluid.

Clinically, regarding the auricle (pinna), its skin is a classic site for gouty tophi and for sun-related skin cancer. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the external acoustic meatus, impacted wax and otitis externa (swimmer's ear) both cause conductive hearing loss and pain on pulling the pinna. In clinical pathology involving the tympanic membrane, a red bulging drum means otitis media; a pearly white mass behind it suggests cholesteatoma. Medical evaluation of the malleus also notes that its handle is what you see as the cone-of-light landmark on otoscopy.

chapters.r: Retroperitoneal, across L1–L2 behind the stomach
chapters.b: Splenic artery + pancreaticoduodenal arcades
chapters.n: Vagus + splanchnic via coeliac plexus
chapters.bl: A dual-function retroperitoneal gland: exocrine acini secrete bicarbonate and digestive enzymes into the duodenum while endocrine islets regulate blood glucose.
chapters.sum: Curled into the C-shaped loop of the duodenum behind the stomach, the pancreas works a double shift as both an enzyme factory for digestion and a hormone regulator. The pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine organ. Acinar cells package trypsinogen, lipase and amylase into zymogen granules and secrete them into the pancreatic duct, which joins the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla; bicarbonate-rich fluid from duct cells neutralises gastric acid. Scattered among the acini, the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin (beta cells), glucagon (alpha), somatostatin (delta) and pancreatic polypeptide directly into blood, minute-to-minute control of glucose. Within the human body, the pancreas (Pancreas) is situated in retroperitoneal, across L1–L2 behind the stomach, receives arterial perfusion via splenic artery + pancreaticoduodenal arcades, and is innervated by vagus + splanchnic via coeliac plexus.

The head (Caput pancreatis) is the broad end nestled in the C-loop of the duodenum, with the uncinate process hooking behind the superior mesenteric vessels. Physiologically, the head houses much of the exocrine tissue and the terminal duct. The neck (Collum pancreatis) is the short constriction in front of the portal vein's formation. Physiologically, the neck governs landmark separating head from body; the portal vein forms behind it. The body (Corpus pancreatis) is the middle third crossing the aorta and vertebral body, behind the stomach in the lesser sac. Physiologically, the body carries the duct and splenic vessels along its borders. The tail (Cauda pancreatis) is the narrow left end reaching the splenic hilum between the layers of the splenorenal ligament. Physiologically, the tail contains a high density of islets. The main pancreatic duct (Ductus pancreaticus) runs the length of the gland from tail to head, joining the common bile duct at the ampulla in the second part of duodenum. Physiologically, the main pancreatic duct delivers ~1.5 L of enzyme- and bicarbonate-rich juice daily. The accessory duct (of Santorini) (Ductus pancreaticus accessorius) is an inconstant second duct opening at the minor duodenal papilla above the main one. Physiologically, the accessory duct (of Santorini) provides alternative drainage, mainly of the head.

Clinically, regarding the head, a tumour here compresses the common bile duct, causing painless obstructive jaundice and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law). From a diagnostic standpoint, in the neck, it is the transection line in a Whipple procedure and in distal pancreatectomy. In clinical pathology involving the body, it lies against the splenic vein — thrombosis of that vein from pancreatitis causes isolated gastric varices. Medical evaluation of the tail also notes that it is easily injured during splenectomy, causing a postoperative pancreatic fistula.

chapters.r: Left hypochondrium, ribs 9–11, posterior to the stomach
chapters.b: Splenic artery (largest branch of the coeliac trunk)
chapters.n: Coeliac plexus (sympathetic) — mostly vasomotor
chapters.bl: Tucked beneath the left ribs, the spleen pairs immune white-pulp lymphoid follicles with filtering red-pulp cords that recycle aging red blood cells.
chapters.sum: Protected beneath ribs nine through eleven in the upper left abdomen, the spleen is the largest lymphoid organ in the body and a precision filter for circulating blood. Blood enters the spleen through the splenic artery and percolates through two compartments. White pulp — cuffs of lymphocytes around central arterioles — mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens, making IgM and opsonins. Red pulp is a mesh of sinusoids and cords where old, stiff or antibody-coated red cells are trapped and destroyed by macrophages, and where platelets are stored (a third of the body's pool). In fetal life the spleen makes red cells; after splenectomy the liver and marrow take over, but the loss of opsonisation leaves lifelong risk of encapsulated bacterial sepsis. Within the human body, the spleen (Lien (splen)) is situated in left hypochondrium, ribs 9–11, posterior to the stomach, receives arterial perfusion via splenic artery (largest branch of the coeliac trunk), and is innervated by coeliac plexus (sympathetic) — mostly vasomotor.

The capsule & trabeculae (Capsula lienis) is a fibroelastic capsule sending trabeculae into the pulp, carrying the vessels. Physiologically, the capsule & trabeculae governs structural framework and conduit for vessels. Structurally, the red pulp (Pulpa rubra) comprises splenic cords of Billroth and wide sinusoids lined by stave cells with slit-like gaps. Physiologically, the red pulp filters senescent and abnormal red cells; recycles iron; stores platelets and monocytes. Structurally, the white pulp (Pulpa alba) comprises periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (T cells), follicles (B cells) and a marginal zone rich in macrophages. Physiologically, the white pulp governs immune surveillance of blood: antibody and opsonin production, especially against capsules. Structurally, the splenic sinusoids (Sinus splenicus) comprises discontinuous, leaky channels whose endothelial slits force red cells to squeeze through. Physiologically, the splenic sinusoids governs the mechanical filter: healthy deformable cells pass; rigid ones are eaten. The hilum (Hilum lienis) is the notched medial border where splenic vessels enter and the tail of pancreas and stomach fundus relate. Physiologically, the hilum governs vascular gateway; also the site of accessory spleens in ~15% of people. The splenic artery (Arteria lienalis) is a tortuous branch of the coeliac trunk running along the upper border of the pancreas. Physiologically, the splenic artery supplies the spleen, pancreas (via branches) and part of the stomach.

Clinically, regarding the capsule & trabeculae, the capsule is thin and the pulp fragile — the spleen tears easily in blunt abdominal trauma and bleeds briskly. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the red pulp, in hereditary spherocytosis the rigid spheres are trapped here, causing haemolytic anaemia cured by splenectomy. In clinical pathology involving the white pulp, its loss explains why asplenic patients are vulnerable to pneumococcus, meningococcus and H. influenzae. Medical evaluation of the splenic sinusoids also notes that malaria parasites stiffen red cells, which is why the spleen enlarges in chronic infection.

chapters.r: Anterior neck, C5–T1, in front of trachea and larynx
chapters.b: Superior & inferior thyroid arteries (± thyroidea ima)
chapters.n: Sympathetic + parasympathetic (vasomotor only; secretion is TSH-driven)
chapters.bl: Wrapped like a butterfly around the upper trachea, thyroid follicles store iodinated thyroglobulin colloid to pace basal metabolism, with four parathyroids behind.
chapters.sum: Shaped like a butterfly wrapped around the upper windpipe, the thyroid gland stores its own hormone supply inside microscopic colloid spheres called follicles. The thyroid is built from follicles — spheres of cuboidal cells filled with colloid, a store of thyroglobulin. Iodide is trapped, oxidised and attached to tyrosine residues to make T3 and T4, released under control of pituitary TSH. These hormones raise basal metabolic rate, oxygen consumption and heat production, and are essential for growth and brain development. Parafollicular C cells secrete calcitonin. Embedded behind the gland, the four parathyroid glands sense calcium and release parathyroid hormone — the minute-to-minute controller of plasma calcium. Within the human body, the thyroid gland (Glandula thyroidea) is situated in anterior neck, C5–T1, in front of trachea and larynx, receives arterial perfusion via superior & inferior thyroid arteries (± thyroidea ima), and is innervated by sympathetic + parasympathetic (vasomotor only; secretion is TSH-driven).

The right lobe (Lobus dexter) is one of two lateral lobes, 5–8 cm long, lying against the trachea and oesophagus and covered by the pretracheal fascia. Physiologically, the right lobe secretes T3/T4 from its follicles. The left lobe (Lobus sinister) is the mirror-image lobe; asymmetry between lobes is common and usually benign. Physiologically, the left lobe secretes T3/T4. The isthmus is the bridge crossing the 2nd–4th tracheal rings, joining the two lobes. Physiologically, the isthmus connects the lobes into a single gland. The pyramidal lobe (Lobus pyramidalis) is a tongue of thyroid tissue ascending toward the hyoid in ~50% of people, a remnant of the thyroglossal duct. Physiologically, the pyramidal lobe governs functionally ordinary thyroid tissue. The trachea & larynx (Trachea et larynx) is the gland wraps the airway; the cricoid cartilage and thyroid cartilage lie above. Physiologically, the trachea & larynx governs anatomical landmark and the reason goitres cause compressive symptoms. The thyroid arteries (Arteriae thyroideae) are superior thyroid (from external carotid) and inferior thyroid (from thyrocervical trunk), with rich anastomoses. Physiologically, the thyroid arteries governs give the gland its extremely high blood flow per gram.

Clinically, regarding the right lobe, an enlarging lobe can compress the trachea (stridor) or the recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness). From a diagnostic standpoint, in the left lobe, a dominant nodule in one lobe is investigated with ultrasound and, if suspicious, fine-needle cytology. In clinical pathology involving the isthmus, it is the landmark for emergency tracheostomy and cricothyroidotomy is performed above it. Medical evaluation of the pyramidal lobe also notes that if left behind at thyroidectomy it can hypertrophy and mimic a recurrent goitre or a midline neck mass.

chapters.r: Pelvis, behind the pubic symphysis
chapters.b: Superior & inferior vesical arteries (internal iliac)
chapters.n: Parasympathetic S2–S4 (contracts) · sympathetic T11–L2 (stores)
chapters.bl: A compliant three-layered detrusor muscle reservoir lined by stretchable transitional urothelium, guarded by a smooth trigone and dual urethral sphincters.
chapters.sum: Resting on the pelvic floor just behind the pubic bones, the urinary bladder is a hollow muscular reservoir that expands smoothly as it fills and contracts on command. The bladder is a muscular sac lined by transitional (urothelial) epithelium that stretches from five cell layers down to two as it fills. The detrusor muscle contracts under parasympathetic control (S2–S4) while the internal sphincter (smooth muscle) and external sphincter (skeletal, pudendal nerve) keep urine in. The trigone — the triangle between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice — is smooth because it develops from the mesonephric duct, and its oblique ureteric tunnels act as flap valves preventing reflux. Micturition is a spinal reflex under voluntary control from the pons and cortex. Within the human body, the urinary bladder (Vesica urinaria) is situated in pelvis, behind the pubic symphysis, receives arterial perfusion via superior & inferior vesical arteries (internal iliac), and is innervated by parasympathetic S2–S4 (contracts) · sympathetic T11–L2 (stores).

The dome (apex) (Apex vesicae) is the superior part, pointing toward the pubic symphysis and connected to the urachus (median umbilical ligament). Physiologically, the dome (apex) expands upward into the abdomen as the bladder fills. The detrusor muscle (Musculus detrusor) is three layers of interlacing smooth muscle with the wall thickened into trabeculae when obstructed. Physiologically, the detrusor muscle governs contraction empties the bladder; relaxation allows storage at low pressure. The urothelium (Epithelium transitionale) is stratified transitional epithelium with umbrella cells whose plaques make it impermeable to urine. Physiologically, the urothelium governs a stretch-tolerant, urine-proof lining. The trigone (Trigonum vesicae) is the smooth triangle bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; mucosa firmly bound to muscle. Physiologically, the trigone governs funnel for emptying; its stretch receptors trigger the micturition reflex. Structurally, the ureteric orifices (Ostia ureterum) comprises slit-like openings of the ureters at the posterolateral corners of the trigone, with oblique intramural tunnels. Physiologically, the ureteric orifices governs one-way entry of urine; the tunnel acts as a flap valve. The internal urethral orifice (Ostium urethrae internum) is the inferior angle of the trigone where the bladder neck meets the urethra. Physiologically, the internal urethral orifice governs outlet guarded by the internal sphincter.

Clinically, regarding the dome (apex), a patent urachus can leak urine at the umbilicus in a newborn. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the detrusor muscle, chronic outlet obstruction (prostate) hypertrophies it into trabeculae and diverticula; overactivity causes urge incontinence. In clinical pathology involving the urothelium, its instability to carcinogens (smoking, aniline dyes) makes transitional-cell carcinoma the classic bladder cancer. Medical evaluation of the trigone also notes that the interureteric ridge between the orifices is the first landmark sought at cystoscopy.

chapters.r: Whole body surface — the largest organ
chapters.b: Dermal plexuses from segmental perforators
chapters.n: Somatic sensory (touch, pain, temperature) + sympathetic
chapters.bl: Our largest organ combines a self-renewing stratified epidermis with a collagen-rich dermis housing sweat glands, hair follicles, blood vessels, and touch nerves.
chapters.sum: Covering roughly two square meters in an average adult, the skin is our largest organ—acting simultaneously as a waterproof shield, radiator, and sensory surface. The epidermis is a keratinising stratified squamous epithelium renewed from the basal layer every ~4 weeks, with melanocytes, Langerhans cells and Merkel cells among the keratinocytes. Beneath it the dermis gives strength and elasticity (papillary loose, reticular dense connective tissue) and carries the vessels, nerves, hair follicles and glands. The hypodermis is fat that insulates and cushions. Skin makes vitamin D, senses the world, and regulates temperature by sweating and by shunting blood through arteriovenous anastomoses. Within the human body, the skin (Cutis) is situated in whole body surface — the largest organ, receives arterial perfusion via dermal plexuses from segmental perforators, and is innervated by somatic sensory (touch, pain, temperature) + sympathetic.
ov: Covering roughly two square meters in an average adult, the skin is our largest organ—acting simultaneously as a waterproof shield, radiator, and sensory surface. Within the human body, the skin (Cutis) is situated in whole body surface — the largest organ, receives arterial perfusion via dermal plexuses from segmental perforators, and is innervated by somatic sensory (touch, pain, temperature) + sympathetic.

Structurally, the stratum corneum comprises 15–20 layers of dead, flattened, keratin-filled corneocytes held by lipids — the "brick and mortar" barrier. Physiologically, the stratum corneum governs waterproofing and the main barrier to microbes and chemicals. The stratum basale & spinosum (Stratum basale) is the single basal row of dividing keratinocytes on the basement membrane, plus the prickle-cell layers above with desmosomes, melanocytes and Langerhans cells. Physiologically, the stratum basale & spinosum governs renews the epidermis; melanocytes transfer pigment; Langerhans cells present antigen. Structurally, the dermis (papillary & reticular) (Dermis) comprises papillary layer of loose connective tissue forming dermal papillae; reticular layer of dense irregular collagen and elastin. Physiologically, the dermis (papillary & reticular) governs strength, elasticity, sensation and the vascular supply of the epidermis. Structurally, the hypodermis (subcutis) (Tela subcutanea) comprises loose connective tissue and fat, with larger vessels and nerves and, in places, panniculus carnosus. Physiologically, the hypodermis (subcutis) governs insulation, energy store, shock absorption and skin mobility. The hair shaft & follicle (Folliculus pili) is a keratinised shaft growing from a follicle that dips into dermis or fat, with a bulb around a dermal papilla and a bulge of stem cells. Physiologically, the hair shaft & follicle governs protection, sensation and (in other mammals) insulation. The arrector pili muscle (Musculus arrector pili) is a band of smooth muscle from follicle to dermis, supplied by sympathetic fibres. Physiologically, the arrector pili muscle governs erects the hair (goose flesh) and helps express sebum.

Clinically, regarding the stratum corneum, its thickness defines palms and soles; loss in burns allows catastrophic fluid and heat loss. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the stratum basale & spinosum, basal cell carcinoma arises here at sun-exposed sites; melanoma from melanocytes. Clinically, the dermis (papillary & reticular) split-thickness grafts take from the dermal remnants left in the wound bed; keloids are dermal over-scarring. Medical evaluation of the hypodermis (subcutis) also notes that subcutaneous insulin absorption varies with site and temperature because of this layer's blood flow.

chapters.r: Vertebral canal, foramen magnum to L1/L2
chapters.b: Anterior spinal artery + two posterior, reinforced by radicular arteries
chapters.n: 31 pairs of spinal nerves; ascending & descending tracts
chapters.bl: Protected inside the vertebral canal, a butterfly core of gray-matter neuron horns is surrounded by ascending sensory and descending motor white-matter tracts.
chapters.sum: Running through the protective tunnel of the vertebral column, the spinal cord is a two-way superhighway linking the brain with every trunk and limb segment. In cross-section the cord shows an H- or butterfly-shaped core of grey matter — posterior (sensory) horns, lateral (autonomic) horns in thoracic segments and anterior (motor) horns — around the central canal. White matter surrounds it in funiculi carrying the dorsal column–medial lemniscus (fine touch, proprioception), the spinothalamic tracts (pain, temperature) and the corticospinal tracts (voluntary movement). Dorsal roots carry sensory fibres with their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion; ventral roots carry motor fibres. Three meninges and the denticulate ligaments suspend the cord in CSF. Within the human body, the spinal cord (Medulla spinalis) is situated in vertebral canal, foramen magnum to L1/L2, receives arterial perfusion via anterior spinal artery + two posterior, reinforced by radicular arteries, and is innervated by 31 pairs of spinal nerves; ascending & descending tracts.

White matter surrounds it in funiculi carrying the dorsal column–medial lemniscus (fine touch, proprioception), the spinothalamic tracts (pain, temperature) and the corticospinal tracts (voluntary movement). Dorsal roots carry sensory fibres with their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion; ventral roots carry motor fibres. Three meninges and the denticulate ligaments suspend the cord in CSF. The posterior (dorsal) horn (Cornu posterius) is the slender upper horns receiving sensory afferents; laminae I–VI including the substantia gelatinosa. Physiologically, the posterior (dorsal) horn governs first synapse for pain, temperature and touch; gate control of nociception happens here. The anterior (ventral) horn (Cornu anterius) is the broad lower horns containing the lower motor neuron cell bodies and Renshaw cells. Physiologically, the anterior (ventral) horn governs final common pathway: alpha motor neurons innervate skeletal muscle. Structurally, the lateral horn (Cornu laterale) comprises present only in T1–L2, holding preganglionic sympathetic neurons (and S2–S4 parasympathetic equivalents). Physiologically, the lateral horn governs origin of the sympathetic outflow. The central canal (Canalis centralis) is the ependyma-lined remnant of the neural tube lumen, continuous with the fourth ventricle. Physiologically, the central canal governs circulates a trickle of CSF within the cord. Structurally, the white funiculi & tracts (Funiculi) comprises dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis & cuneatus), lateral spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts. Physiologically, the white funiculi & tracts governs highways for sensation upward and motor commands downward. The dura mater is the tough outer sleeve, ending as the dural sac at S2 with the filum terminale beyond. Physiologically, the dura mater protects and forms the epidural and subarachnoid boundaries.

Clinically, regarding the posterior (dorsal) horn, loss of the spinothalamic decussation at a segment causes a segmental band of lost pain and temperature (syringomyelia). From a diagnostic standpoint, in the anterior (ventral) horn, poliovirus and ALS destroy these cells, giving flaccid paralysis, wasting and fasciculation. In clinical pathology involving the lateral horn, horner syndrome follows interruption of the T1 lateral horn or its pathway (e.g. Pancoast tumour). Medical evaluation of the central canal also notes that its dilatation defines syringomyelia, classically causing a cape-like loss of pain and temperature.

chapters.r: Pelvis, perineum and scrotum
chapters.b: Testicular arteries (abdominal aorta, L2)
chapters.n: Sympathetic T10–L2 (emission) · parasympathetic S2–S4 (erection)
chapters.bl: Temperature-regulated testes, coiled epididymal maturation ducts, muscular vas deferens, accessory glands, and the shared urogenital tract in complete context.
chapters.sum: The male reproductive system combines external temperature-regulated gonads with an internal network of muscular ducts and secretory glands built to mature and transport gametes. Spermatogenesis runs for ~74 days in the seminiferous tubules, where Sertoli cells nurse dividing germ cells behind the blood–testis barrier; Leydig cells between tubules make testosterone under LH. Sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis, then travel through the vas deferens, which joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct crossing the prostate. Seminal fluid from seminal vesicles (fructose), prostate (citrate, PSA) and bulbourethral glands makes up semen. The scrotum keeps the testis ~2 °C below core temperature. Within the human body, the male reproductive system (Organa genitalia masculina) is situated in pelvis, perineum and scrotum, receives arterial perfusion via testicular arteries (abdominal aorta, L2), and is innervated by sympathetic T10–L2 (emission) · parasympathetic S2–S4 (erection).

Sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis, then travel through the vas deferens, which joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct crossing the prostate. Seminal fluid from seminal vesicles (fructose), prostate (citrate, PSA) and bulbourethral glands makes up semen. The scrotum keeps the testis ~2 °C below core temperature. Within the human body, the male reproductive system (Organa genitalia masculina) is situated in pelvis, perineum and scrotum, receives arterial perfusion via testicular arteries (abdominal aorta, L2), and is innervated by sympathetic T10–L2 (emission) · parasympathetic S2–S4 (erection).

Structurally, the testis & seminiferous tubules (Testis) comprises 250–300 lobules of coiled seminiferous tubules (total ~250 m) with Sertoli cells and developing germ cells, wrapped in tunica albuginea. Physiologically, the testis & seminiferous tubules governs spermatogenesis and testosterone production. The epididymis is a 6 m coiled duct (head, body, tail) applied to the posterior border of the testis. Physiologically, the epididymis governs sperm maturation, motility acquisition and storage (up to weeks). The vas deferens (Ductus deferens) are a thick-walled 45 cm muscular duct from the epididymal tail, through the inguinal canal into the pelvis. Physiologically, the vas deferens propels sperm by powerful peristalsis at emission. The seminal vesicle (Vesicula seminalis) is a coiled sac behind the bladder whose duct joins the vas to form the ejaculatory duct. Physiologically, the seminal vesicle governs adds ~60% of semen volume: fructose, prostaglandins and clotting proteins. The prostate (Prostata) is a walnut-sized fibromuscular gland around the urethra below the bladder, with peripheral, central and transition zones. Physiologically, the prostate secretes citrate, zinc and PSA that liquefy the seminal coagulum. Structurally, the bulbourethral gland (Glandula bulbourethralis) comprises pea-sized glands (of Cowper) in the deep perineal pouch opening into the spongy urethra. Physiologically, the bulbourethral gland secrete pre-ejaculate mucus that lubricates and neutralises urethral acidity.

Clinically, regarding the testis & seminiferous tubules, undescended testis (cryptorchidism) raises infertility and germ-cell tumour risk; torsion is a 6-hour surgical emergency. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the epididymis, a common site of infection (epididymitis) and of obstruction after vasectomy or infection. In clinical pathology involving the vas deferens, vasectomy divides it for contraception; sperm granulomas may form at the cut ends. chapters.r: Pelvis: uterus, tubes, ovaries, vagina
chapters.b: Uterine + ovarian arteries (internal iliac & aorta)
chapters.n: Uterovaginal plexus (T12–L2 sympathetic, S2–S4 parasympathetic)
chapters.bl: Cyclic follicle maturation in the ovaries, ciliary transport along the uterine tubes, a hormonally dynamic uterus and cervix, vaginal canal, and external vulva.
chapters.sum: Spanning the true pelvis and perineum, the female reproductive system coordinates cyclic egg maturation, fertilization transport, pregnancy support, and childbirth. Each cycle, FSH recruits a follicle that secretes oestradiol and builds the endometrium; the LH surge triggers ovulation at a variable cycle day (often about 14 days before the next period), and the corpus luteum then secretes progesterone to make the endometrium secretory. If fertilisation does not occur the corpus luteum regresses, progesterone falls and menstruation follows. Fertilisation normally happens in the ampulla of the uterine tube, and the embryo reaches the uterus after 3–4 days. The cervix, with its mucus plug, and the vaginal microbiome form the defence against ascending infection. Within the human body, the female reproductive system (Organa genitalia feminina) is situated in pelvis: uterus, tubes, ovaries, vagina, receives arterial perfusion via uterine + ovarian arteries (internal iliac & aorta), and is innervated by uterovaginal plexus (T12–L2 sympathetic, S2–S4 parasympathetic).

The fundus & body (Fundus et corpus uteri) is the domed fundus above the tubal openings and the tapering body, of smooth muscle (myometrium) lined by endometrium. Physiologically, the fundus & body houses and nourishes a pregnancy; the myometrium generates labour. The endometrium is a functional layer of glands and stroma that proliferates under oestrogen and becomes secretory under progesterone, plus a permanent basal layer. Physiologically, the endometrium governs site of implantation; sheds each cycle if no embryo implants. The cervix (Cervix uteri) is the fibrous neck projecting into the vagina, with an endocervical canal of mucus-secreting columnar epithelium and a squamous ectocervix. Physiologically, the cervix keeps pregnancy in and microbes out; dilates 10 cm in labour. The vagina is a fibromuscular canal lined by glycogen-rich stratified squamous epithelium, angled back over the levator plate. Physiologically, the vagina governs birth canal, menstrual outlet and copulatory organ; lactobacilli keep pH ~4. The uterine tube (Tuba uterina) is a 10 cm ciliated duct with interstitial, isthmic, ampullary and infundibular parts. Physiologically, the uterine tube governs captures the oocyte, is the site of fertilisation (ampulla) and transports the embryo by ciliary beat and peristalsis. Structurally, the fimbriae (Fimbriae tubae) comprises finger-like projections around the tubal opening, one (fimbria ovarica) attached to the ovary. Physiologically, the fimbriae governs sweep the oocyte into the tube at ovulation.

Clinically, regarding the fundus & body, fibroids (leiomyomas) arise in the myometrium and cause heavy bleeding and pressure symptoms. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the endometrium, ectopic endometrium (endometriosis) causes cyclical pain and infertility; unopposed oestrogen drives hyperplasia and carcinoma. In clinical pathology involving the cervix, the squamocolumnar junction is where cervical cancer begins — the target of smear tests and HPV vaccination. Medical evaluation of the vagina also notes that the acidic pH protects against infection; antibiotics and oestrogen loss can allow candidiasis.

chapters.r: Whole body: central + peripheral
chapters.b: Internal carotid + vertebral arteries
chapters.n: Itself — plus autonomic control of every organ
chapters.bl: One integrated signaling web: the central brain and spinal cord compute while 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves link every tissue.
chapters.sum: Stretching from the folded cerebral cortex down to the finest digital nerve endings in the fingertips, the nervous system coordinates thought, sensation, and motion in milliseconds. The master page of control. Follow the cord down, watch plexuses redistribute fibres to limbs, and see where the autonomic chain hugs the spine. Within the human body, the nervous system — overview (Systema nervosum) is situated in whole body: central + peripheral, receives arterial perfusion via internal carotid + vertebral arteries, and is innervated by itself — plus autonomic control of every organ.

Structurally, the brain (Encephalon) comprises cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem inside the cranial vault. Physiologically, the brain governs integration, consciousness, motor planning and autonomic control. Structurally, the cerebellum comprises hindbrain structure behind the brainstem. Physiologically, the cerebellum governs coordination, balance and motor learning. Structurally, the brainstem (Truncus encephali) comprises midbrain, pons and medulla connecting cord to brain. Physiologically, the brainstem governs vital centres: respiration, heart rate, consciousness. Structurally, the spinal cord (Medulla spinalis) comprises 31-segment cord from foramen magnum to L1–L2. Physiologically, the spinal cord governs two-way tracts plus segmental reflex circuits. Structurally, the cervical plexus (Plexus cervicalis (C1–C4)) comprises nerve network in the posterior triangle of the neck. Physiologically, the cervical plexus governs neck muscles and skin; phrenic nerve to diaphragm. Structurally, the brachial plexus (Plexus brachialis (C5–T1)) comprises roots-trunks-divisions-cords-branches behind the clavicle. Physiologically, the brachial plexus governs all motor and sensory supply of the upper limb.

Clinically, regarding the brain, head injury scales from concussion to diffuse axonal injury. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the cerebellum, lesion → intention tremor and ataxia on the same side. In clinical pathology involving the brainstem, brainstem death is legal death in most jurisdictions. Medical evaluation of the spinal cord also notes that cord transection level predicts deficit pattern precisely.

chapters.r: Head & neck
chapters.b: Carotid + vertebrobasilar
chapters.n: The nerves themselves
chapters.bl: Twelve paired nerves (CN I–XII) emerge directly from the forebrain and brainstem, passing through skull-base foramina to serve special senses, face, and viscera.
chapters.sum: Emerging in twelve paired sets directly from the brain and brainstem, the cranial nerves govern vision, hearing, balance, facial expression, swallowing, and vagal organ control. Deep dive: each nerve with its nucleus, route and lesion. Mnemonics live in the clinical notes. Within the human body, the cranial nerves (Nervi craniales I–XII) is situated in head & neck, receives arterial perfusion via carotid + vertebrobasilar, and is innervated by the nerves themselves.

Structurally, the i · Olfactory nerve (N. olfactorius) comprises sensory filaments from nasal epithelium to bulb. Physiologically, the i · Olfactory nerve governs smell. Structurally, the II · Optic nerve (N. opticus) comprises retinal ganglion axons to the chiasm. Physiologically, the II · Optic nerve governs vision. Structurally, the III · Oculomotor nerve (N. oculomotorius) comprises midbrain nerve to four eye muscles + lid + pupil. Physiologically, the III · Oculomotor nerve governs eye elevation/adduction, lid lift, pupil constriction. Structurally, the IV · Trochlear nerve (N. trochlearis) comprises thinnest cranial nerve; exits dorsally. Physiologically, the IV · Trochlear nerve governs superior oblique — looks down and in. The v · Trigeminal nerve (N. trigeminus) is three divisions: ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular. Physiologically, the v · Trigeminal nerve governs face sensation + muscles of mastication. The VI · Abducens nerve (N. abducens) is long intracranial course to lateral rectus. Physiologically, the VI · Abducens nerve governs eye abduction.

Clinically, regarding the i · Olfactory nerve, lesion: anosmia — test each nostril with coffee. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the II · Optic nerve, papilloedema signals raised intracranial pressure. In clinical pathology involving the III · Oculomotor nerve, first sign of uncal herniation: a blown pupil. Medical evaluation of the IV · Trochlear nerve also notes that palsy: double vision on stairs.

chapters.r: Viscera + vertebral column
chapters.b: Visceral vessels
chapters.n: Intrinsic — autonomic
chapters.bl: The involuntary balance between thoracolumbar sympathetic fight-or-flight chains, craniosacral vagal and pelvic parasympathetic rest-and-digest outflow, and gut plexuses.
chapters.sum: Operating beneath conscious awareness every second of life, the autonomic nervous system balances heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, and pupil size through two complementary divisions. Deep dive into ganglia and plexuses: where fibres relay, which organs they reach, and what happens when the balance breaks. Within the human body, the autonomic nervous system (Systema nervosum autonomicum) is situated in viscera + vertebral column, receives arterial perfusion via visceral vessels, and is innervated by intrinsic — autonomic.

The sympathetic trunk (Truncus sympathicus) is paired chain from neck to sacrum beside vertebrae. Physiologically, the sympathetic trunk governs mass fight-or-flight discharge. Structurally, the chain ganglion (Ganglion trunci) comprises relay station on the trunk. Physiologically, the chain ganglion governs synapse for pre→postganglionic fibres. Structurally, the coeliac ganglion & plexus (Ganglion coeliacum) comprises largest prevertebral relay at T12/L1, around coeliac trunk. Physiologically, the coeliac ganglion & plexus governs foregut sympathetic supply. Structurally, the superior mesenteric ganglion (Ganglion mesentericum superius) comprises relay at the SMA origin. Physiologically, the superior mesenteric ganglion governs midgut sympathetic supply. Structurally, the inferior mesenteric ganglion (Ganglion mesentericum inferius) comprises relay at IMA origin. Physiologically, the inferior mesenteric ganglion governs hindgut and pelvic sympathetic supply. Structurally, the vagus parasympathetic (N. vagus (parasymp.)) comprises cranial parasympathetic to thorax and fore/midgut. Physiologically, the vagus parasympathetic governs rest-digest: slow heart, stimulate gut.

Clinically, regarding the sympathetic trunk, chronic overdrive: hypertension, anxiety physiology. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the chain ganglion, stellate ganglion block treats refractory angina pain. In clinical pathology involving the coeliac ganglion & plexus, coeliac plexus block for pancreatic cancer pain. Medical evaluation of the superior mesenteric ganglion also notes that mesenteric ischaemia pain is carried with these fibres.

chapters.r: Pectoral region, T2–T6 ribs
chapters.b: Internal thoracic + lateral thoracic arteries
chapters.n: Intercostal nerves T2–T6 + lactiferous reflex
chapters.bl: Mammary glandular lobules and converging lactiferous ducts supported by fibrous Cooper ligaments over the pectoral fascia, with key axillary lymphatic drainage.
chapters.sum: Positioned over the pectoralis major muscle inside the superficial fascia of the chest wall, the breast combines specialized glandular lobules with fibrous suspensory support. Female breast in cut-away with every ductal and structural part; the male breast is the same blueprint, undeveloped. Within the human body, the breast (Mamma / Glandula mammaria) is situated in pectoral region, T2–T6 ribs, receives arterial perfusion via internal thoracic + lateral thoracic arteries, and is innervated by intercostal nerves T2–T6 + lactiferous reflex.

The lactiferous ducts (Ductus lactiferi) are 15–20 branching channels to the nipple. Physiologically, the lactiferous ducts transport milk. The subareolar lactiferous ducts (Ductus lactiferi) are branching ducts converge near the nipple; classic large lactiferous sinuses are not consistently seen on ultrasound. Physiologically, the subareolar lactiferous ducts carry milk from alveoli and lobules toward nipple openings, rather than acting as a major storage reservoir. Structurally, the nipple (Papilla mammaria) comprises pigmented projection with 15–20 duct openings. Physiologically, the nipple governs milk delivery; erotic sensation. Structurally, the areola (Areola mammae) comprises pigmented ring with sebaceous Montgomery tubercles. Physiologically, the areola governs lubrication and latch cue. Structurally, the adipose tissue (Corpus adiposum) comprises fat between glandular compartments. Physiologically, the adipose tissue governs size and contour.

Clinically, regarding the lobules (glandular), most breast cancers start in lobules or ducts. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the lactiferous ducts, ductal carcinoma in situ stays inside this lining. In clinical pathology involving the subareolar lactiferous ducts, a blocked duct may cause a localized tender area; ultrasound revised the older “sinus reservoir” model. Medical evaluation of the nipple also notes that paget's disease: eczema-like nipple change = cancer until proven otherwise.

chapters.bl: Over 300 named skeletal muscle records and 32 tendon pathways across 13 body regions, showing origins, insertions, nerve supply, and sliding-filament action.
chapters.sum: More than six hundred named skeletal muscles wrap the human frame, converting chemical energy into mechanical pull across joints so we can breathe, stand, speak, and sprint. Surface-to-deep anterior musculature: origin-insertion logic and the clinical test for each. Within the human body, the muscular system (Systema musculare) is situated in ≈ 600 skeletal muscles, receives arterial perfusion via segmental + named arteries, and is innervated by somatic motor nerves.

Structurally, the trapezius (M. trapezius) comprises occiput to scapular spine. Physiologically, the trapezius governs shrug and scapular rotation. Structurally, the deltoid (M. deltoideus) comprises clavicle/scapula to humeral shaft. Physiologically, the deltoid governs arm abduction beyond 15°. Structurally, the pectoralis major (M. pectoralis major) comprises clavicle/sternum to humerus. Physiologically, the pectoralis major governs arm adduction and push power. The forearm flexors (Mm. flexores antebrachii) are medial epicondyle group. Physiologically, the forearm flexors governs wrist and finger flexion.

Clinically, regarding the sternocleidomastoid, torticollis; landmark for carotid pulse. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the trapezius, accessory nerve palsy → shrug weakness. In clinical pathology involving the deltoid, IM injection site — axillary nerve beneath. Medical evaluation of the pectoralis major also notes that torn in bench-press injuries.

chapters.r: Whole body
chapters.b: Returns via subclavian veins
chapters.n: Autonomic on vessels
chapters.bl: One-way lymphatic capillaries, filtering cervical, axillary, and inguinal node chains, the thoracic duct, thymus, and spleen working together for fluid and immunity.
chapters.sum: Every day, several liters of fluid filter out of blood capillaries into body tissues; the lymphatic system collects that fluid, screens it through immune nodes, and returns it to veins. Node groups, trunks and the organs of immunity — with the clinical rule that nodes enlarge downstream of infection and cancer. Within the human body, the lymphatic system (Systema lymphoideum) is situated in whole body, receives arterial perfusion via returns via subclavian veins, and is innervated by autonomic on vessels.

Structurally, the cervical nodes (Ll. cervicales) comprises chains along jugular and spine. Physiologically, the cervical nodes drain head and neck. Structurally, the thoracic duct (Ductus thoracicus) comprises largest lymph channel, cisterna chyli to left venous angle. Physiologically, the thoracic duct returns 3/4 of body lymph. Structurally, the thymus comprises bilobed school for T cells, behind sternum. Physiologically, the thymus governs t-cell maturation in childhood. Structurally, the spleen (Splen / Lien) comprises largest lymphoid organ, left upper quadrant. Physiologically, the spleen filters blood; recycles iron; antibodies.

Clinically, regarding the cervical nodes, rubbery vs hard-fixed distinguishes infection from malignancy. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the axillary nodes, sentinel node first receives breast cancer cells. In clinical pathology involving the inguinal nodes, enlarge in leg infections and STIs. Medical evaluation of the thoracic duct also notes that chylothorax if torn in chest surgery.

chapters.r: Whole body
chapters.b: The heart
chapters.n: Autonomic vasomotor

The arterial and venous maps a surgeon names daily, from carotids to saphenous. Within the human body, the vascular system (Systema cardiovasculare) is situated in whole body, receives arterial perfusion via the heart, and is innervated by autonomic vasomotor.

The brachial artery (A. brachialis) is upper-arm continuation. Physiologically, the brachial artery governs arm and forearm supply; BP cuff site. Structurally, the descending aorta (Aorta descendens) comprises thoracic then abdominal aorta. Physiologically, the descending aorta governs segmental branches to wall and viscera. Structurally, the coeliac trunk (Truncus coeliacus) comprises t12 branch: left gastric, splenic, hepatic. Physiologically, the coeliac trunk governs foregut supply.

Clinically, regarding the aortic arch, coarctation: hypertension above, weak femorals below. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the common carotid artery, carotid bruit = stroke risk; press on the sinus to slow the heart. In clinical pathology involving the subclavian artery, subclavian steal reverses vertebral flow on exertion. Medical evaluation of the brachial artery also notes that intra-arterial cannulation risk at elbow.

chapters.r: Whole body — ductless glands
chapters.b: Rich arterial supply to each gland
chapters.n: Autonomic + trophic hormones
chapters.bl: Hormone-secreting glands—hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreas, and gonads—communicating through bloodstream feedback loops.
chapters.sum: Unlike exocrine glands that empty into ducts, endocrine glands release chemical messengers directly into surrounding capillaries to coordinate metabolism, growth, and stress responses. Every ductless gland on one figure — including the ones you never see: pineal, parathyroids, adrenals and the islets. Within the human body, the endocrine system (Systema endocrinum) is situated in whole body — ductless glands, receives arterial perfusion via rich arterial supply to each gland, and is innervated by autonomic + trophic hormones.

Physiologically, the parathyroid glands governs PTH — raises plasma calcium. Structurally, the adrenal glands (Gll. suprarenales) comprises caps on each kidney: cortex + medulla. Physiologically, the pancreatic islets governs insulin (β) and glucagon (α) — glucose control.

Clinically, regarding the pituitary gland, pituitary adenoma → visual field loss (optic chiasm above). From a diagnostic standpoint, in the pineal gland, calcifies with age; useful midline marker on CT. In clinical pathology involving the thyroid gland, goitre and thyrotoxicosis are common presentations. Medical evaluation of the parathyroid glands also notes that accidental removal in thyroidectomy → tetany.

chapters.r: Knee model + whole-body ligaments
chapters.b: Genicular arteries
chapters.n: Articular branches
chapters.bl: How fibrous sutures, cartilaginous symphyses, and fluid-lubricated synovial capsules balance smooth anatomical motion with ligamentous joint stability.
chapters.sum: Where two rigid bones meet, specialized joints and tough collagenous ligaments balance two competing biomechanical demands: smooth freedom of motion and structural stability. Open the knee to see cruciates, collaterals and menisci; the part list then tours the other major ligaments of the body. Within the human body, the joints & ligaments (Articulationes et ligamenta) is situated in knee model + whole-body ligaments, receives arterial perfusion via genicular arteries, and is innervated by articular branches.

Physiologically, the anterior cruciate ligament governs blocks anterior tibial translation; pivots in rotation. The posterior cruciate ligament (Lig. cruciatum posterius) is medial femoral condyle to posterior tibia. Physiologically, the posterior cruciate ligament governs blocks posterior tibial slide (dashboard injury). Structurally, the medial collateral ligament (Lig. collaterale tibiale) comprises femoral epicondyle to tibial shaft, fused with meniscus. Physiologically, the medial collateral ligament governs resists valgus stress. Structurally, the lateral collateral ligament (Lig. collaterale fibulare) comprises femoral epicondyle to fibular head. Physiologically, the lateral collateral ligament governs resists varus stress. Structurally, the menisci (medial & lateral) (Menisci) comprises fibrocartilage crescents on the tibial plateau. Physiologically, the menisci (medial & lateral) governs load sharing, shock absorption, joint lubrication. Structurally, the patellar ligament (Lig. patellae) comprises patella to tibial tuberosity (quadriceps continuation). Physiologically, the patellar ligament transmits quadriceps force to the tibia.

Clinically, regarding the anterior cruciate ligament, ACL tear: pop + giving way; reconstructed with graft. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the posterior cruciate ligament, PCL injuries need far greater force than ACL. In clinical pathology involving the medial collateral ligament, valgus blow + medial pain = MCL; meniscus often torn with it. Medical evaluation of the lateral collateral ligament also notes that varus injuries are rarer and often hit the peroneal nerve too.

chapters.r: Glenohumeral joint
chapters.b: Anterior & posterior circumflex humeral
chapters.n: Axillary nerve
chapters.bl: Why the shallow ball-and-socket glenohumeral joint achieves 360-degree reach, stabilized by the fibrocartilaginous labrum and four SITS rotator cuff tendons.
chapters.sum: Shaped like a golf ball resting on a shallow tee, the glenohumeral shoulder joint trades bony depth for unmatched mobility—relying on a muscular cuff to stay centered. Cut-away view of the cuff, labrum, capsule and biceps tendon — the structures behind most shoulder clinics. Within the human body, the shoulder joint (Articulatio humeri) is situated in glenohumeral joint, receives arterial perfusion via anterior & posterior circumflex humeral, and is innervated by axillary nerve.

Within the human body, the shoulder joint (Articulatio humeri) is situated in glenohumeral joint, receives arterial perfusion via anterior & posterior circumflex humeral, and is innervated by axillary nerve.

Anatomically, the supraspinatus tendon (Tendo m. supraspinati) lies over the top of the humeral head. Physiologically, the supraspinatus tendon initiates abduction (first 15°). Anatomically, the teres minor tendon (Tendo m. teretis minoris) lies below infraspinatus. Physiologically, the teres minor tendon governs external rotation + capsule tension. Structurally, the subscapularis tendon (Tendo m. subscapularis) comprises front of the head from the scapular fossa. Physiologically, the subscapularis tendon governs internal rotation; anterior stability. Structurally, the glenoid labrum (Labrum glenoidale) comprises fibrocartilage rim deepening the socket. Physiologically, the glenoid labrum governs adds ~50% of glenoid depth. Structurally, the glenohumeral capsule & ligaments (Capsula articularis) comprises loose sleeve with three glenohumeral ligaments. Physiologically, the glenohumeral capsule & ligaments governs permits huge range; limits extremes.

Clinically, regarding the supraspinatus tendon, most torn cuff tendon — painful arc 60–120°. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the infraspinatus tendon, tear → weak external rotation. In clinical pathology involving the teres minor tendon, part of cuff tears in overhead athletes. Medical evaluation of the subscapularis tendon also notes that lift-off test detects its tear.

chapters.r: Nose to trachea
chapters.b: Branches of external & internal carotid
chapters.n: Vagus (IX/X for pharynx)
chapters.bl: Warming nasal conchae, the three-part pharynx, and the nine cartilages of the larynx that protect the lower airway during swallowing and vibrate vocal folds.
chapters.sum: At the crossroads of breathing and swallowing, the upper airway warms and filters inspired air while the cartilaginous larynx guards the lungs and generates the human voice. Midsagittal cut from nasal conchae to tracheal rings — including the parts you cannot see from outside: sinuses, adenoid, vocal folds. Within the human body, the upper airway (Via aerea superior) is situated in nose to trachea, receives arterial perfusion via branches of external & internal carotid, and is innervated by vagus (IX/X for pharynx).
