Physiologically, the nasopharynx & adenoid governs air passage; immune sampling in childhood. Anatomically, the oropharynx lies behind the mouth, tonsils at its sides. Physiologically, the oropharynx governs shared food–air corridor; speech resonance. The epiglottis is elastic leaf above the larynx. Physiologically, the epiglottis governs flips to cover the larynx during swallowing. Structurally, the larynx comprises thyroid + cricoid cartilages housing the folds. Physiologically, the larynx governs voice production and airway protection.

Clinically, regarding the nasal cavity & conchae, deviated septum + turbinate hypertrophy = blocked nose. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the paranasal sinuses, sinusitis pain follows the sinus walls — maxillary = cheekache. In clinical pathology involving the nasopharynx & adenoid, adenoid hypertrophy causes snoring and glue ear in kids. Medical evaluation of the oropharynx also notes that OSA collapse happens here during sleep.

chapters.r: Inside every bone
chapters.b: Nutrient + metaphyseal arteries
chapters.n: Autonomic fibres
chapters.bl: Inside spongy trabecular bone, pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells generate millions of oxygen-carrying red cells, immune leukocytes, and platelets every second.
chapters.sum: Hidden inside the honeycomb cavities of the axial skeleton, red bone marrow manufactures hundreds of billions of fresh red cells, leukocytes, and platelets every single day. Cut long bone plus a cellular inset — the organs no eye ever sees without a microscope, highlighted here. Within the human body, the bone marrow & blood (Medulla ossium) is situated in inside every bone, receives arterial perfusion via nutrient + metaphyseal arteries, and is innervated by autonomic fibres.

Physiologically, the compact bone (cortex) governs bending and torsional strength; calcium bank. Structurally, the endosteum & osteoblasts (Endosteum) comprises cellular lining of all internal bone surfaces. Physiologically, the endosteum & osteoblasts governs remodelling: osteoblasts build, osteoclasts eat. Structurally, the haematopoietic stem cells (Cellulae stirpes) comprises pluripotent marrow stem cells. Physiologically, the haematopoietic stem cells governs give rise to myeloid and lymphoid lines.

Clinically, regarding the red marrow, marrow failure = aplastic anaemia; infiltration = leukaemia. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the yellow marrow, reconverts in chronic anaemia or severe bleeding. In clinical pathology involving the trabecular (spongy) bone, osteoporosis thins trabeculae first — vertebral fractures. Medical evaluation of the compact bone (cortex) also notes that cortical thickening responds to load (Wolff's law).

chapters.r: Pelvic sagittal section
chapters.b: Internal iliac branches
chapters.n: Pudendal + pelvic splanchnics
chapters.bl: Sagittal and perineal views of the male pelvis: bladder neck, walnut-sized prostate, rectum, levator ani muscular sling, and pudendal neurovascular canals.
chapters.sum: Within the bony ring of the male pelvis, the urinary bladder, prostate, and rectum share a compact muscular floor that supports abdominal viscera and controls continence. Deep regional anatomy — the pouches, sphincters and nerves examined in every pelvic module. Within the human body, the male pelvis & perineum (Pelvis masculina) is situated in pelvic sagittal section, receives arterial perfusion via internal iliac branches, and is innervated by pudendal + pelvic splanchnics.

Structurally, the prostatic & membranous urethra (Urethra masculina) comprises urethra traversing prostate and perineum. Physiologically, the prostatic & membranous urethra governs conduit for urine and semen; sphincters here. Structurally, the ejaculatory ducts (Ductus ejaculatorii) comprises vas + seminal vesicle ducts through prostate. Physiologically, the ejaculatory ducts deliver sperm into prostatic urethra. Structurally, the rectum comprises terminal 12–15 cm with three valves. Physiologically, the rectum stores stool before defecation. Structurally, the anal canal & sphincters (Canalis analis) comprises internal (smooth) + external (striated) sphincters. Physiologically, the anal canal & sphincters governs continence control.

Clinically, regarding the urinary bladder, outlet obstruction in men is usually prostatic. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the prostate gland, BPH compresses the urethra — hesitancy and nocturia. In clinical pathology involving the prostatic & membranous urethra, catheterisation respects the puboprostatic curve. Medical evaluation of the ejaculatory ducts also notes that obstruction → low-volume ejaculate.

chapters.r: Pelvic sagittal section
chapters.b: Internal iliac branches
chapters.n: Pudendal + pelvic splanchnics
chapters.bl: Sagittal and perineal views of the female pelvis: bladder, anteverted uterus, vesicouterine and rectouterine pouches, levator ani floor, and perineal body.
chapters.sum: The female pelvis is wider and more circular than the male pelvis, cradling the bladder, uterus, and rectum above a dynamic muscular sling built for both support and childbirth. Deep regional anatomy of the female pelvis: pouches, cardinal ligaments, pelvic floor and perineum. Within the human body, the female pelvis & perineum (Pelvis femina) is situated in pelvic sagittal section, receives arterial perfusion via internal iliac branches, and is innervated by pudendal + pelvic splanchnics.

Physiologically, the uterus & cervix (relations) governs gestation and menstruation. Structurally, the vesico- & recto-uterine pouches (Excavationes) comprises peritoneal recesses front and back of uterus. Physiologically, the vesico- & recto-uterine pouches allow organ movement; collect free fluid. Structurally, the rectum comprises terminal bowel behind the vagina. Physiologically, the rectum governs stool storage.

Clinically, regarding the urinary bladder, stress incontinence follows pelvic-floor weakness. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the female urethra, short length explains higher UTI rates in women. In clinical pathology involving the vagina, anteverted uterus rests on its anterior wall; pessaries sit here. Medical evaluation of the uterus & cervix (relations) also notes that retroversion is a normal variant in ~20%.

chapters.r: Midline pelvis between bladder and rectum
chapters.b: Uterine artery (internal iliac), anastomoses with ovarian artery
chapters.n: Uterovaginal plexus; pelvic visceral afferents
chapters.bl: From the dome-like fundus to the internal os: how the cyclic endometrium, thick smooth-muscle myometrium, and spiral arteries remodel across life stages.
chapters.sum: Hollow, pear-shaped, and lined by a hormonally responsive mucosa, the uterus is engineered to renew its inner lining each cycle and expand dramatically during pregnancy. Read the uterus from outside inward, then trace the menstrual endometrium and the lower segment relevant to obstetric and surgical anatomy. Within the human body, the uterus — layers & cavity (Uterus) is situated in midline pelvis between bladder and rectum, receives arterial perfusion via uterine artery (internal iliac), anastomoses with ovarian artery, and is innervated by uterovaginal plexus; pelvic visceral afferents.

Structurally, the uterine cavity (Cavitas uteri) comprises triangular cavity between the anterior and posterior endometrium. Physiologically, the uterine cavity receives embryo; menstrual efflux passes to cervical canal. The endometrium — functionalis (Stratum functionale) is superficial cyclic glandular layer; sheds with menses. Physiologically, the endometrium — functionalis governs proliferates under estrogen and becomes secretory under progesterone. The endometrium — basalis (Stratum basale) is deep regenerative endometrial layer next to myometrium. Physiologically, the endometrium — basalis governs regrows the functionalis after menstruation.

Clinically, regarding the fundus, fundal height is a rough gestational growth marker. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the uterine body, fibroids often arise here and may distort the cavity. In clinical pathology involving the uterine cornua, interstitial ectopic pregnancy arises near the cornu. Medical evaluation of the uterine cavity also notes that polyps or submucosal fibroids deform the cavity.

chapters.r: Uterine neck projecting into vaginal fornices
chapters.b: Descending uterine + vaginal branches
chapters.n: Uterovaginal plexus; pelvic visceral afferents
chapters.bl: The collagen-dense lower neck of the uterus, where mucus-secreting columnar endocervical epithelium meets squamous ectocervix at the transformation zone.
chapters.sum: Acting as the structural gatekeeper between the vaginal canal and uterine cavity, the cervix combines a collagen-dense wall with a dynamic epithelial junction. Learn which epithelium lines each surface and why the transformation zone matters for cervical cytology and colposcopy — without turning anatomy into a screening guideline. Within the human body, the cervix — transformation zone (Cervix uteri) is situated in uterine neck projecting into vaginal fornices, receives arterial perfusion via descending uterine + vaginal branches, and is innervated by uterovaginal plexus; pelvic visceral afferents.

Physiologically, the ectocervix governs covered by nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. Structurally, the endocervical canal (Canalis cervicis uteri) comprises canal linking internal to external os. Physiologically, the endocervical canal conducts sperm and menstrual flow; glandular mucus changes cyclically. Structurally, the endocervical columnar epithelium (Epithelium columnare) comprises mucus-secreting simple columnar lining of the canal. Physiologically, the endocervical columnar epithelium produces cervical mucus under hormonal regulation. Structurally, the ectocervical squamous epithelium (Epithelium squamosum) comprises nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium continuous with vaginal mucosa. Physiologically, the ectocervical squamous epithelium protects exposed cervical surface. Structurally, the squamocolumnar junction (Junctio squamocolumnaris) comprises border where glandular and squamous epithelia meet. Physiologically, the squamocolumnar junction governs migrates with age, hormones and pregnancy. Physiologically, the transformation zone governs physiologic remodeling of exposed columnar epithelium.

Clinically, regarding the ectocervix, visual examination and directed biopsy sample this surface. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the endocervical canal, stenosis may obstruct sampling or menstrual outflow. In clinical pathology involving the endocervical columnar epithelium, glandular lesions need distinct cytologic evaluation. Medical evaluation of the ectocervical squamous epithelium also notes that squamous metaplasia alters the visible junction.

chapters.r: Lateral pelvis / broad ligament
chapters.b: Ovarian artery from aorta + tubal branches of uterine artery
chapters.n: Ovarian and uterovaginal autonomic plexuses
chapters.bl: Follicular waves and corpus luteum formation in the ovarian cortex paired with the fimbriae, wide ampulla, and ciliated mucosa of the fallopian tube.
chapters.sum: Paired on either side of the uterus, the ovaries and feather-tipped uterine tubes work in concert yet are not fused—requiring sweeping fimbriae to catch each ovulated egg. Follow the oocyte from dominant follicle across a peritoneal gap to the fimbriae and ampulla, then trace the tube to the uterine cornu. Within the human body, the ovary & uterine tube (Ovarium et tuba uterina) is situated in lateral pelvis / broad ligament, receives arterial perfusion via ovarian artery from aorta + tubal branches of uterine artery, and is innervated by ovarian and uterovaginal autonomic plexuses.

The ovarian medulla (Medulla ovarii) is central vascular stromal zone. Physiologically, the ovarian medulla supports vessels, nerves and the hilum. The primordial follicles (Folliculi primordiales) are small oocyte with flat granulosa cells in outer cortex. Physiologically, the primordial follicles governs dormant ovarian reserve pool. Structurally, the growing follicles (Folliculi crescentes) comprises developing granulosa and theca layers, then antrum. Physiologically, the growing follicles governs estrogen synthesis and oocyte maturation. The dominant antral follicle (Folliculus maturus) is large fluid-filled preovulatory follicle. Physiologically, the dominant antral follicle releases a secondary oocyte after the LH surge. Structurally, the corpus luteum comprises yellow luteinized structure after ovulation. Physiologically, the corpus luteum produces progesterone during luteal phase.

Clinically, regarding the ovarian cortex, cortical tissue is considered in fertility-preserving surgery. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the ovarian medulla, ovarian pedicle bleeding arises at the hilum. In clinical pathology involving the primordial follicles, reserve declines with age and treatment exposure. Medical evaluation of the growing follicles also notes that follicle tracking uses size, not a diagnosis of oocyte quality.

chapters.r: Pelvic canal between bladder/urethra and rectum
chapters.b: Vaginal + uterine artery branches; internal pudendal distally
chapters.n: Uterovaginal plexus above, pudendal nerve below
chapters.bl: A distensible fibromuscular canal lined by glycogen-rich stratified squamous epithelium, recessed around the cervix into anterior, lateral, and posterior fornices.
chapters.sum: Extending from the vestibule of the vulva to the uterine cervix, the vaginal canal is a fibromuscular tube whose upper vault wraps around the cervix to form recessed fornices. The sagittal cut clarifies relationships used in speculum examination, pelvic surgery and posterior fornix assessment. Within the human body, the vagina — walls & fornices (Vagina) is situated in pelvic canal between bladder/urethra and rectum, receives arterial perfusion via vaginal + uterine artery branches; internal pudendal distally, and is innervated by uterovaginal plexus above, pudendal nerve below.

Structurally, the vaginal lumen (Lumen vaginae) comprises potential space whose walls normally lie against one another. Physiologically, the vaginal lumen governs passage for menstrual flow, intercourse and birth. Structurally, the anterior vaginal wall (Paries anterior vaginae) comprises shorter wall adjoining bladder base and urethra. Physiologically, the anterior vaginal wall provides anterior pelvic support. Structurally, the posterior vaginal wall (Paries posterior vaginae) comprises wall lying anterior to rectum, longer near posterior fornix. Physiologically, the posterior vaginal wall supports the posterior compartment. Structurally, the vaginal mucosa & rugae (Tunica mucosa vaginae) comprises nonkeratinizing squamous mucosa with transverse folds. Physiologically, the vaginal mucosa & rugae governs distends and responds to estrogen; no intrinsic mucosal glands. Structurally, the vaginal muscularis (Tunica muscularis vaginae) comprises circular and longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles. Physiologically, the vaginal muscularis allows distension and elastic return. The adventitia & paravaginal fascia (Tunica adventitia) is outer connective tissue joining vaginal walls to pelvic sidewall. Physiologically, the adventitia & paravaginal fascia contains neurovascular routes and supports the canal.

Clinically, regarding the vaginal lumen, distensibility varies; do not interpret the lumen as a permanently open tube. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the anterior vaginal wall, anterior compartment weakness may be associated with cystocele. In clinical pathology involving the posterior vaginal wall, posterior wall defects may accompany rectocele. Medical evaluation of the vaginal mucosa & rugae also notes that atrophy can cause fragility; moisture derives mainly from transudate and cervical secretions.

chapters.r: External genital region / urogenital triangle
chapters.b: Internal & external pudendal arteries
chapters.n: Pudendal (S2–S4), ilioinguinal & genitofemoral branches
chapters.bl: Honest surface anatomy of the external female genital region—mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoral glans, and separate urethral and vaginal openings.
chapters.sum: In anatomical terminology, the vulva refers specifically to the external genital structures visible on the perineal surface—distinct from the internal vaginal canal. The vulva is the external genital region, not the internal vaginal canal. This cleaned surface teaching illustration shows the mons, labia, clitoral glans, vestibule and separate urethral and vaginal openings. Deeper glands, nerves and clitoral erectile tissue are described without a misleading surface pointer. Within the human body, the vulva — external genital anatomy (Vulva) is situated in external genital region / urogenital triangle, receives arterial perfusion via internal & external pudendal arteries, and is innervated by pudendal (S2–S4), ilioinguinal & genitofemoral branches.

Structurally, the mons pubis comprises fatty pad over pubic symphysis. Physiologically, the mons pubis cushions pubic bone. The labia majora (Labia majora pudendi) is outer skin folds containing fat and connective tissue. Physiologically, the labia majora protect the vestibule and inner folds. The labia minora (Labia minora pudendi) is inner hairless folds, highly variable in size and pigmentation. Physiologically, the labia minora governs border the vestibule and contribute to clitoral hood. Structurally, the clitoral glans & hood (Glans et preputium clitoridis) comprises glans at the anterior meeting of labia minora, under prepuce. Physiologically, the clitoral glans & hood governs highly innervated erectile tissue. Structurally, the vulvar vestibule (Vestibulum vaginae) comprises space between labia minora containing urethral and vaginal openings. Physiologically, the vulvar vestibule governs shared surface region for urinary and genital outlets. Structurally, the external urethral meatus (Ostium urethrae externum) comprises urinary opening anterior to vaginal introitus. Physiologically, the external urethral meatus governs urine exits here, not through the vagina.

Clinically, regarding the mons pubis, normal hair pattern and contour vary widely. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the labia majora, vulvar lymph largely drains to superficial inguinal nodes. In clinical pathology involving the labia minora, normal asymmetry is common and not pathological. Medical evaluation of the clitoral glans & hood also notes that clitoral neurovascular supply should be respected in vulvar surgery.

chapters.r: Uterus, sidewall and pelvic floor
chapters.b: Uterine / ovarian / vaginal / internal pudendal vessels
chapters.n: Inferior hypogastric plexus + pudendal nerve
chapters.bl: How the tonic levator ani muscular dome, cardinal and uterosacral ligaments, and endopelvic fascial planes suspend pelvic organs above the urogenital hiatus.
chapters.sum: Pelvic organs stay suspended over the urogenital opening thanks to a two-part engineering system: a tonic muscular trampoline below and fibrous fascial tethers above. Study true support separately from peritoneal reflections. This realistic pelvis plate shows why the ureter and arteries demand a careful surgical plane. Within the human body, the pelvic support & surgical planes (Fascia et ligamenta pelvis feminae) is situated in uterus, sidewall and pelvic floor, receives arterial perfusion via uterine / ovarian / vaginal / internal pudendal vessels, and is innervated by inferior hypogastric plexus + pudendal nerve.

The broad ligament (Ligamentum latum uteri) is double peritoneal sheet draped over uterus, tubes and associated structures. Physiologically, the broad ligament supports relationships but is not the main mechanical uterine support. Structurally, the mesometrium comprises largest sheet of broad ligament lateral to uterus. Physiologically, the mesometrium governs conveys uterine vessels and connective tissue in base. The mesosalpinx is broad ligament portion related to uterine tube. Physiologically, the mesosalpinx supports tube and its vessels. The mesovarium is short fold suspending ovarian hilum from posterior broad ligament. Physiologically, the mesovarium transmits vessels to ovary. Structurally, the round ligament (Ligamentum teres uteri) comprises band from uterine cornu through inguinal canal to labium majus. Physiologically, the round ligament helps maintain anteversion; not principal apical support. Structurally, the ovarian ligament (Ligamentum ovarii proprium) comprises cornu-to-ovary band medial to ovarian hilum. Physiologically, the ovarian ligament anchors ovary toward uterus.

Clinically, regarding the broad ligament, ureter and uterine vessels course at its base. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the mesometrium, surgical dissection exposes adjacent ureter. In clinical pathology involving the mesosalpinx, tubal surgery separates this vascular fold. Medical evaluation of the mesovarium also notes that distinct from the suspensory ovarian ligament.

chapters.r: Scrotum and spermatic cord
chapters.b: Testicular artery from aorta; pampiniform plexus
chapters.n: Testicular plexus (visceral); scrotal somatic innervation
chapters.bl: Inside the fibrous tunica albuginea: 250 testicular lobules, coiled seminiferous tubules, Sertoli blood-testis barrier, rete testis, and epididymal maturation.
chapters.sum: Inside each oval testis, roughly two hundred fifty wedge-shaped lobules pack tightly coiled seminiferous tubules that would stretch hundreds of meters if unrolled. A realistic cut section maps the invisible seminiferous loops, blood–testis barrier and sperm outflow route. Within the human body, the testis & epididymis — microanatomy (Testis et epididymis) is situated in scrotum and spermatic cord, receives arterial perfusion via testicular artery from aorta; pampiniform plexus, and is innervated by testicular plexus (visceral); scrotal somatic innervation.

A realistic cut section maps the invisible seminiferous loops, blood–testis barrier and sperm outflow route. The tunica vaginalis (Tunica vaginalis testis) is serous covering with visceral and parietal layers. Physiologically, the tunica vaginalis allows mobile testis within scrotum. The tunica albuginea (Tunica albuginea testis) is dense white capsule under tunica vaginalis. Physiologically, the tunica albuginea governs partitions testis into lobules via septa. The mediastinum testis is posterior thickening of albuginea containing rete testis. Physiologically, the mediastinum testis governs organizes lobules and duct outflow. Structurally, the testicular lobules (Lobuli testis) comprises septa divide testis into lobules containing seminiferous tubules. Physiologically, the testicular lobules governs compartmentalize sperm production. The seminiferous tubules (Tubuli seminiferi) are coiled tubules lined by developing germ cells and Sertoli cells. Physiologically, the seminiferous tubules governs spermatogenesis. Structurally, the Sertoli cells / blood–testis barrier (Cellulae sustentaculares) comprises supportive epithelium joined by tight junctions. Physiologically, the Sertoli cells / blood–testis barrier governs nurse developing germ cells; secrete inhibin B.

Clinically, regarding the tunica vaginalis, fluid accumulation in the cavity forms a hydrocele. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the tunica albuginea, traumatic rupture may require urgent evaluation. In clinical pathology involving the mediastinum testis, important landmark in testicular ultrasound. Medical evaluation of the testicular lobules also notes that germ-cell tumors often distort intratesticular architecture.

chapters.r: Bladder neck, pelvic floor and perineum
chapters.b: Inferior vesical / internal pudendal branches
chapters.n: Inferior hypogastric plexus + pudendal somatic branches
chapters.bl: McNeal's peripheral, central, and transition zones of the prostate surrounding the prostatic urethra where seminal vesicle and vas deferens ducts converge.
chapters.sum: Sitting immediately beneath the neck of the urinary bladder, the walnut-sized prostate surrounds the upper urethra at the exact junction where urinary and reproductive paths merge. A sagittal regional cut clarifies zones, bladder neck, ejaculatory duct entry and the urethral path through prostate and penis. Within the human body, the prostate, ducts & penis (Prostata et penis) is situated in bladder neck, pelvic floor and perineum, receives arterial perfusion via inferior vesical / internal pudendal branches, and is innervated by inferior hypogastric plexus + pudendal somatic branches.

Structurally, the bladder neck / internal sphincter (Collum vesicae) comprises smooth-muscle outlet superior to prostate. Physiologically, the bladder neck / internal sphincter closes during emission to limit retrograde ejaculation. Structurally, the prostatic transition zone (Zona transitionis) comprises zone surrounding proximal prostatic urethra. Physiologically, the prostatic transition zone contains glandular ducts and fibromuscular tissue. The prostatic peripheral zone (Zona peripherica) is posterior-lateral zone palpable through rectum. Physiologically, the prostatic peripheral zone produces prostatic secretions. Structurally, the prostatic central zone (Zona centralis) comprises tissue surrounding ejaculatory ducts. Physiologically, the prostatic central zone governs secretory prostatic gland region. Structurally, the prostatic urethra (Pars prostatica urethrae) comprises urethra through prostate from bladder neck to membrane. Physiologically, the prostatic urethra conducts urine and semen in separate phases. Structurally, the seminal colliculus (verumontanum) (Colliculus seminalis) comprises ridge in posterior prostatic urethra with duct openings. Physiologically, the seminal colliculus (verumontanum) governs landmark for ejaculatory duct openings.

Clinically, regarding the bladder neck / internal sphincter, bladder-neck dysfunction may affect voiding. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the prostatic transition zone, common origin of benign prostatic enlargement. In clinical pathology involving the prostatic peripheral zone, most prostatic cancers arise in this zone. Medical evaluation of the prostatic central zone also notes that less frequently a primary site of carcinoma.

chapters.l: Clitoris · corpora cavernosa et bulbi vestibuli
chapters.r: Anterior perineum; deep to vulvar surface and along ischiopubic rami
chapters.b: Internal pudendal → deep and dorsal clitoral arteries; posterior labial branches
chapters.n: Dorsal nerve of clitoris (pudendal S2–S4); cavernous autonomic fibers via pelvic plexus
chapters.bl: Beyond the visible glans: the internal clitoral body, paired diverging crura anchored to the ischiopubic rami, vestibular bulbs, and dorsal sensory nerves.
chapters.sum: Only the small glans of the clitoris is visible externally; the majority of the clitoral complex arches internally beneath the pubic bones as paired crura and vestibular bulbs. The visible glans is not the whole clitoris. Two corpora cavernosa join into a body, while proximal crura anchor to the ischiopubic rami. The glans is particularly sensory and is not simply another corpus cavernosum. Paired vestibular bulbs are neighboring erectile tissue flanking the vestibule, anatomically distinguished from the corpora. Arterial inflow, smooth-muscle relaxation and venous outflow restriction contribute to engorgement; somatic sensation travels largely in the dorsal clitoral nerve. Within the human body, the clitoral erectile complex (Clitoris · corpora cavernosa et bulbi vestibuli) is situated in anterior perineum; deep to vulvar surface and along ischiopubic rami, receives arterial perfusion via internal pudendal → deep and dorsal clitoral arteries; posterior labial branches, and is innervated by dorsal nerve of clitoris (pudendal S2–S4); cavernous autonomic fibers via pelvic plexus.

Structurally, the clitoral glans (Glans clitoridis) comprises external distal part beneath or exposed by the hood; dense sensory innervation and distinct histology from cavernous bodies. Physiologically, the clitoral glans governs conveys fine sensation. Structurally, the clitoral prepuce (Preputium clitoridis) comprises fold of skin derived from the anterior labia minora covering part of the glans. Physiologically, the clitoral prepuce protects and permits mobility of glans. Structurally, the clitoral body (Corpus clitoridis) comprises midline body formed by apposition of the paired corpora cavernosa, deep to the external glans. Physiologically, the clitoral body governs engorges via cavernous vascular spaces. The right corpus cavernosum (Corpus cavernosum dextrum) is one of the paired erectile cylinders of the clitoral body, enclosed by tunica albuginea. Physiologically, the right corpus cavernosum governs fills with blood during arousal. Structurally, the left corpus cavernosum (Corpus cavernosum sinistrum) comprises contralateral cavernous cylinder joining the body along the midline. Physiologically, the left corpus cavernosum governs contributes to body rigidity and expansion. The crura of clitoris (Crura clitoridis) is two proximal cavernous limbs fixed to the inferior pubic and ischial rami. Physiologically, the crura of clitoris anchor the erectile body to pelvic bone.

Clinically, regarding the clitoral glans, do not describe the glans as a paired cavernous body. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the clitoral prepuce, its form and degree of coverage vary normally. In clinical pathology involving the clitoral body, the externally visible part understates total size. Medical evaluation of the right corpus cavernosum also notes that separate it anatomically from the vestibular bulb.

chapters.r: Root, shaft and glans of penis; superficial perineal pouch to external genitalia
chapters.b: Internal pudendal → deep, dorsal and bulbourethral/urethral arteries
chapters.n: Dorsal penile nerve (pudendal S2–S4); cavernous nerves from pelvic plexus
chapters.bl: Three cylindrical vascular columns—paired dorsal corpora cavernosa and the ventral urethra-bearing corpus spongiosum—wrapped in tough tunica albuginea and Buck fascia.
chapters.sum: In cross-section, the shaft of the penis is built around three cylindrical columns of vascular sinusoidal tissue wrapped in tough collagenous sleeves. The paired corpora cavernosa are enveloped by strong tunica albuginea and form the main rigid erectile compartment; the ventral corpus spongiosum surrounds the penile urethra and expands distally as the glans. Deep penile arteries feed cavernous spaces. Parasympathetic-associated cavernous neural signaling relaxes smooth muscle, increasing arterial inflow and restricting subtunical venous outflow. The spongiosum remains comparatively compliant to protect urethral patency. Within the human body, the penile erectile tissue (Corpora cavernosa · corpus spongiosum) is situated in root, shaft and glans of penis; superficial perineal pouch to external genitalia, receives arterial perfusion via internal pudendal → deep, dorsal and bulbourethral/urethral arteries, and is innervated by dorsal penile nerve (pudendal S2–S4); cavernous nerves from pelvic plexus.

The paired corpora cavernosa (Corpora cavernosa penis) is two dorsal longitudinal erectile cylinders that unite in shaft and separate proximally as crura. Physiologically, the paired corpora cavernosa governs primary rigid erectile compartment. The corpus spongiosum (Corpus spongiosum penis) is single ventral erectile column surrounding spongy urethra. Physiologically, the corpus spongiosum governs engorges without compressing urethral lumen closed. Structurally, the tunica albuginea comprises strong fibrous sheath encasing cavernosa, with distinct collagen layers. Physiologically, the tunica albuginea governs resists expansion and aids venous occlusion. Structurally, the cavernosal trabeculae (Trabeculae corporum cavernosorum) comprises smooth-muscle and connective-tissue struts bordering interconnected blood sinusoids. Physiologically, the cavernosal trabeculae governs relaxation permits filling of cavernous lacunae. Structurally, the deep penile arteries (Arteriae profundae penis) comprises internal pudendal branches traveling within each corpus cavernosum. Physiologically, the deep penile arteries governs feed cavernosal tissue. The helicine arteries (Arteriae helicinae) are small coiled branches entering cavernous sinusoidal spaces. Physiologically, the helicine arteries governs dilate as smooth muscle relaxes, increasing inflow.

Clinically, regarding the paired corpora cavernosa, fibrous tunica helps compress emissary venous outflow. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the corpus spongiosum, its distal expansion is the glans penis. In clinical pathology involving the tunica albuginea, disruption during trauma can constitute penile fracture. Medical evaluation of the cavernosal trabeculae also notes that vascular dysfunction can impair rigidity.

chapters.r: Whole-body integument; thick glabrous skin of palms/soles differs from thin hairy skin
chapters.b: Dermal superficial and deep vascular plexuses; epidermis is avascular
chapters.n: Cutaneous sensory afferents and sympathetic sudomotor/vasomotor fibers
chapters.bl: Five epidermal keratinocyte strata, interlocking dermal papillae, reticular collagen bundles, eccrine and sebaceous glands, and specialized touch corpuscles.
chapters.sum: Zooming in on a few millimeters of human skin reveals a continuously renewing brick-and-mortar epithelium anchored to a vascular dermal web of collagen and nerve endings. Epidermis is a stratified keratinizing epithelium nourished by diffusion from vascular dermis. From deep to superficial: basale, spinosum, granulosum, optional lucidum (most evident in thick skin), and corneum. Basement membrane joins epidermis to papillary dermis; reticular dermis provides strength. The hypodermis is adipose-rich subcutis beneath the dermis. Hair, sebaceous glands and most sweat glands are skin appendages; cutaneous receptors relay varied forms of mechanical and thermal input. Within the human body, the skin layers & appendages (Epidermis · dermis · tela subcutanea) is situated in whole-body integument; thick glabrous skin of palms/soles differs from thin hairy skin, receives arterial perfusion via dermal superficial and deep vascular plexuses; epidermis is avascular, and is innervated by cutaneous sensory afferents and sympathetic sudomotor/vasomotor fibers.

The stratum basale is deep single proliferative keratinocyte layer adjoining basement membrane. Physiologically, the stratum basale governs renews overlying epidermis. Structurally, the stratum spinosum comprises several layers of keratinocytes strongly joined by desmosomes. Physiologically, the stratum spinosum provides mechanical cohesion. Structurally, the stratum granulosum comprises flattened keratinocytes with keratohyalin granules and lipid-releasing lamellar bodies. Physiologically, the stratum granulosum governs builds the water-permeability barrier. The stratum lucidum is thin translucent transition zone most apparent in glabrous palms and soles. Physiologically, the stratum lucidum governs adds specialized layer in thick skin. Structurally, the stratum corneum comprises anucleate flattened corneocytes surrounded by intercellular lipid lamellae. Physiologically, the stratum corneum governs principal external permeability barrier. Structurally, the basement membrane zone (Junctio dermoepidermalis) comprises anchoring complex joining epidermis to dermis with hemidesmosomes and matrix. Physiologically, the basement membrane zone governs resists separation and supports renewal.

Clinically, regarding the stratum basale, basal-cell carcinoma derives from basal-type cells. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the stratum spinosum, desmosomal disruption causes epidermal blistering. In clinical pathology involving the stratum granulosum, barrier injury increases transepidermal water loss. Medical evaluation of the stratum lucidum also notes that do not expect a distinct lucidum in ordinary thin hairy skin.

chapters.r: Pons → internal acoustic meatus → facial canal → stylomastoid foramen → parotid plexus
chapters.b: AICA/labyrinthine and petrosal branches intracranially; stylomastoid artery distally
chapters.n: CN VII motor, parasympathetic and taste fibers; cutaneous face sensation mainly CN V
chapters.bl: Tracing Cranial Nerve VII from the pons through the temporal bone canal and parotid gland to its five facial expression branches, chorda tympani taste, and tear fibers.
chapters.sum: Every smile, blink, and raised eyebrow depends on the seventh cranial nerve—a complex mixed nerve that threads through the temporal bone before fanning across the face. CN VII contains motor fibers to muscles of facial expression, taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue (via chorda tympani), and parasympathetic pathways for lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands. It enters the internal acoustic meatus, bends at geniculate ganglion, traverses the facial canal and exits at stylomastoid foramen. Within the parotid it forms a motor plexus giving temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches; it passes through the gland but does not provide its secretomotor supply. Within the human body, the facial nerve · cn vii (Nervus facialis) is situated in pons → internal acoustic meatus → facial canal → stylomastoid foramen → parotid plexus, receives arterial perfusion via AICA/labyrinthine and petrosal branches intracranially; stylomastoid artery distally, and is innervated by CN VII motor, parasympathetic and taste fibers; cutaneous face sensation mainly CN V.

Structurally, the facial motor nucleus (Nucleus nervi facialis) comprises motor cell bodies in pons send axons looping around abducens nucleus before exit. Physiologically, the facial motor nucleus controls muscles of facial expression. Structurally, the nervus intermedius comprises sensory and parasympathetic root accompanying the motor root. Physiologically, the nervus intermedius carries taste and secretomotor pathways. Structurally, the internal acoustic meatus (Meatus acusticus internus) comprises temporal-bone canal shared by CN VII, CN VIII and labyrinthine artery. Physiologically, the internal acoustic meatus governs conveys nerve toward facial canal. Structurally, the geniculate ganglion (Ganglion geniculi) comprises sensory ganglion at first sharp bend of facial canal; greater petrosal branch arises nearby. Physiologically, the geniculate ganglion houses sensory neuron cell bodies. The greater petrosal nerve (Nervus petrosus major) carries preganglionic fibers toward pterygopalatine ganglion. Physiologically, the greater petrosal nerve supports lacrimal and nasal/palatine gland secretion. Structurally, the nerve to stapedius (Nervus stapedius) comprises branch in facial canal to stapedius muscle of middle ear. Physiologically, the nerve to stapedius governs dampens stapes movement.

Clinically, regarding the facial motor nucleus, upper face often retains bilateral cortical input in supranuclear lesions. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the nervus intermedius, explains why CN VII is not solely motor. In clinical pathology involving the internal acoustic meatus, lesions here may affect facial movement and hearing/balance. Medical evaluation of the geniculate ganglion also notes that herpes zoster may affect geniculate region.

chapters.r: Pons → trigeminal ganglion → orbit, midface and mandible
chapters.b: Brainstem branches and regional meningeal/orbital arterial branches
chapters.n: Main somatic sensory supply of face; V3 also innervates muscles of mastication
chapters.bl: Tracing Cranial Nerve V from the trigeminal ganglion into ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) sensory territories plus the muscles of chewing.
chapters.sum: Named for its 'three twins,' the trigeminal nerve is the largest cranial nerve, mapping touch, temperature, and pain across the face, corneas, sinuses, and teeth. Most facial skin sensation travels by CN V. Ophthalmic V1 supplies forehead and cornea; maxillary V2 supplies the cheek, upper lip and upper teeth; mandibular V3 supplies lower jaw, lower teeth and general anterior tongue sensation and carries motor fibers to mastication muscles. Taste from anterior tongue is carried by facial chorda tympani joining lingual V3, not by trigeminal sensory neurons. Corneal reflex enters by V1 and blink exits by VII. Within the human body, the trigeminal nerve · cn v (Nervus trigeminus) is situated in pons → trigeminal ganglion → orbit, midface and mandible, receives arterial perfusion via brainstem branches and regional meningeal/orbital arterial branches, and is innervated by main somatic sensory supply of face; V3 also innervates muscles of mastication.

The trigeminal sensory root (Radix sensoria nervi trigemini) is large sensory root emerges from lateral pons into trigeminal cistern. Physiologically, the trigeminal sensory root governs conveys facial somatic sensation centrally. Structurally, the trigeminal ganglion (Ganglion trigeminale) comprises sensory neuron cell bodies in Meckel cave; divides into V1, V2 and V3. Physiologically, the trigeminal ganglion governs first-order facial sensory neurons. The ophthalmic V1 (Nervus ophthalmicus) passes superior orbital fissure into orbit; gives frontal, lacrimal and nasociliary branches. Physiologically, the ophthalmic V1 governs sensation from forehead, upper lid and cornea. The frontal nerve (Nervus frontalis) is superior orbital branch dividing into supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves. Physiologically, the frontal nerve governs sensation over forehead and anterior scalp. Structurally, the nasociliary nerve (Nervus nasociliaris) comprises orbital V1 branch giving long ciliary, ethmoidal and infratrochlear fibers. Physiologically, the nasociliary nerve carries corneal sensation through long ciliary nerves. The maxillary V2 (Nervus maxillaris) leaves cranial cavity via foramen rotundum to pterygopalatine fossa. Physiologically, the maxillary V2 governs sensation to midface, upper teeth and palate.

Clinically, regarding the trigeminal sensory root, brainstem lesions can combine facial and body sensory findings. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the trigeminal ganglion, classic site involved in trigeminal neuralgia pathways. In clinical pathology involving the ophthalmic V1, afferent limb of corneal reflex. Medical evaluation of the frontal nerve also notes that forehead sensory loss suggests V1 pathway involvement.

chapters.r: Orbit; anterior refractive media to posterior neural retina and optic nerve
chapters.b: Ophthalmic artery: central retinal and posterior ciliary branches; aqueous is avascular
chapters.n: II vision; III/IV/VI eye movement; V1 corneal sensation; III parasympathetic pupil/contraction
chapters.bl: Microscopic architecture of the three ocular coats: five-layered cornea, aqueous humor flow from ciliary processes to Schlemm's canal, and zonular lens suspension.
chapters.sum: At the tissue scale, the wall of the eye is organized into three concentric tunics—a tough outer sclera-cornea coat, a vascular uveal middle layer, and the inner retina. The globe has an outer fibrous tunic (cornea and sclera), vascular uvea (iris, ciliary body and choroid) and inner neural tunic (retina). Aqueous from ciliary processes flows posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork/Schlemm canal or uveoscleral routes. Corneal epithelium, Bowman layer, stroma, Descemet membrane and endothelium are the classical five-layer teaching scheme; some texts describe an additional pre-Descemet layer. Retina transforms light to neural signals; the optic disc lacks photoreceptors. Within the human body, the eye · microscopic layers (Bulbus oculi · tunicae oculi) is situated in orbit; anterior refractive media to posterior neural retina and optic nerve, receives arterial perfusion via ophthalmic artery: central retinal and posterior ciliary branches; aqueous is avascular, and is innervated by II vision; III/IV/VI eye movement; V1 corneal sensation; III parasympathetic pupil/contraction.

Structurally, the corneal epithelium (Epithelium anterius corneae) comprises surface stratified nonkeratinizing epithelial layer. Physiologically, the corneal epithelium governs barrier and smooth refractive surface. Structurally, the Bowman layer (Lamina limitans anterior) comprises acellular anterior limiting layer beneath epithelium. Physiologically, the Bowman layer governs adds anterior structural support. Structurally, the corneal stroma (Substantia propria corneae) comprises organized collagen lamellae form most of corneal thickness. Physiologically, the corneal stroma governs precise collagen arrangement maintains transparency. Structurally, the descemet membrane (Lamina limitans posterior) comprises basement membrane of corneal endothelium. Physiologically, the descemet membrane supports endothelial monolayer. The corneal endothelium (Endothelium posterius corneae) is single posterior cell layer lining anterior chamber. Physiologically, the corneal endothelium pumps fluid from stroma to maintain optical clarity. Structurally, the sclera comprises opaque collagenous external coat continuous with cornea at limbus. Physiologically, the sclera protects and preserves globe contour.

Clinically, regarding the corneal epithelium, abrasion causes pain because the cornea is richly innervated. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the Bowman layer, damage may scar rather than regenerate as normal layer. In clinical pathology involving the corneal stroma, edema disrupts transparency. Clinically, the descemet membrane can develop folds with corneal edema.

chapters.r: Inner posterior globe; photoreceptors interface with pigment epithelium and choroid
chapters.b: Inner retina: central retinal artery; outer retina: choriocapillaris
chapters.n: Ganglion cell axons → optic nerve II; autonomic supply regulates ocular vessels
chapters.bl: How light traverses ten transparent neural layers to trigger rod and cone phototransduction, bipolar-to-ganglion processing, and high-acuity foveal vision.
chapters.sum: The human retina is an outpost of the central nervous system where incoming photons pass through transparent interneurons before striking rods and cones at the back. Light traverses inner retinal layers before reaching rods and cones against retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Neural signaling runs the opposite direction: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells → optic nerve. Horizontal and amacrine cells modify lateral signaling. The foveal center has dense cones and displaced inner layers for acuity, while the optic disc has no photoreceptors. Inner retina is supported mainly by central retinal circulation; photoreceptors and RPE depend strongly on the choriocapillaris. Within the human body, the retina · neural microanatomy (Retina neurosensorialis · epithelium pigmentosum) is situated in inner posterior globe; photoreceptors interface with pigment epithelium and choroid, receives arterial perfusion via inner retina: central retinal artery; outer retina: choriocapillaris, and is innervated by ganglion cell axons → optic nerve II; autonomic supply regulates ocular vessels.

Structurally, the internal limiting membrane (Membrana limitans interna) comprises müller-cell endfeet make retinal inner boundary against vitreous. Physiologically, the internal limiting membrane supports vitreoretinal interface. Structurally, the nerve fiber layer (Stratum neurofibrarum) comprises unmyelinated ganglion axons converge toward optic disc. Physiologically, the nerve fiber layer conducts output to optic nerve. Structurally, the ganglion cell layer (Stratum ganglionare) comprises retinal ganglion somata whose axons become optic nerve. Physiologically, the ganglion cell layer governs final retinal output neurons. Structurally, the inner plexiform layer (Stratum plexiforme internum) comprises synapses among bipolar, amacrine and ganglion processes. Physiologically, the inner plexiform layer processes contrast and temporal information. Structurally, the inner nuclear layer (Stratum nucleare internum) comprises bipolar, horizontal, amacrine and Müller cell bodies. Physiologically, the inner nuclear layer relays and modulates photoreceptor signals. Structurally, the outer plexiform layer (Stratum plexiforme externum) comprises photoreceptor terminals synapse with bipolar and horizontal cells. Physiologically, the outer plexiform layer governs first central synaptic relay for light signals.

Clinically, regarding the internal limiting membrane, epiretinal traction can distort macula. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the nerve fiber layer, glaucoma thins nerve fiber layer. In clinical pathology involving the ganglion cell layer, ganglion-cell loss contributes to glaucomatous vision loss. Medical evaluation of the inner plexiform layer also notes that layer distortion can accompany retinal edema.

chapters.r: Renal cortex (corpuscle and convoluted tubules) → medulla (loop and collecting system)
chapters.b: Afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries/vasa recta
chapters.n: Renal sympathetic fibers reach vasculature, juxtaglomerular cells and tubules
chapters.bl: From the fenestrated glomerulus and podocyte filtration slits through the proximal tubule, countercurrent loop of Henle, macula densa, and collecting duct.
chapters.sum: Each kidney contains roughly one million microscopic nephrons—tiny biological purifying plants that filter blood plasma under pressure and selectively reclaim vital solutes. Each nephron begins with a glomerular capillary tuft inside Bowman capsule; the filtration barrier includes fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms. Filtrate enters proximal tubule, descends and ascends in the loop of Henle, then passes distal tubule into a collecting duct. Collecting ducts arise from a different embryologic lineage than nephron tubules. Peritubular capillaries and vasa recta reclaim water and solutes; juxtaglomerular apparatus links distal salt sensing to renin secretion. Within the human body, the nephron · kidney microanatomy (Nephron · corpusculum renale) is situated in renal cortex (corpuscle and convoluted tubules) → medulla (loop and collecting system), receives arterial perfusion via afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries/vasa recta, and is innervated by renal sympathetic fibers reach vasculature, juxtaglomerular cells and tubules.

Structurally, the afferent arteriole (Arteriola afferens) comprises brings arterial blood into glomerular capillary tuft. Physiologically, the afferent arteriole regulates incoming glomerular pressure. Structurally, the glomerular capillaries (Glomerulus) comprises fenestrated capillary loops between afferent and efferent arterioles. Physiologically, the glomerular capillaries pass plasma water and small solutes toward Bowman space. Structurally, the efferent arteriole (Arteriola efferens) comprises vessel leaves glomerulus and feeds downstream capillary network. Physiologically, the efferent arteriole maintains filtration pressure and supplies cortical/medullary beds. Structurally, the Bowman capsule (Capsula glomeruli) comprises parietal squamous layer and visceral podocyte layer enclosing Bowman space. Physiologically, the Bowman capsule collects primary filtrate from glomerulus. The filtration basement membrane (Membrana basalis glomerularis) is specialized basement membrane shared by capillary endothelium and podocytes. Physiologically, the filtration basement membrane governs contributes size/charge selectivity. Structurally, the podocyte foot processes (Pedicelli podocytorum) comprises interdigitating podocyte extensions with slit diaphragms over glomerular capillaries. Physiologically, the podocyte foot processes governs final cellular component of filtration barrier.

Clinically, regarding the afferent arteriole, diameter influences filtration rate. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the glomerular capillaries, damage may permit albumin or red cells into urine. In clinical pathology involving the efferent arteriole, unique arteriole between two capillary beds. Medical evaluation of the Bowman capsule also notes that filtrate flows from urinary pole to proximal tubule.

chapters.r: C5–T1 ventral rami between scalene muscles → behind clavicle → axilla and upper limb
chapters.b: Cords surround axillary artery; regional supply from subclavian/axillary branches
chapters.n: Ventral rami C5–T1, with frequent prefixed/postfixed variation
chapters.bl: How spinal nerve roots C5–T1 braid into trunks, divisions, and cords to form the musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, and ulnar nerves of the upper limb.
chapters.sum: Crossing from the lateral neck through the axilla into the upper limb, the brachial plexus braids five spinal nerve roots into the motor and sensory cables of the arm and hand. The brachial plexus usually arises from ventral rami C5–T1. C5–6 form upper trunk, C7 middle trunk and C8–T1 lower trunk. Each trunk divides anteriorly and posteriorly; anterior divisions of upper/middle form lateral cord, lower forms medial cord, all posterior divisions form posterior cord. Cords are named relative to the axillary artery. Musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves reach the limb; several important scapular and pectoral branches leave the plexus before these endpoints. Within the human body, the brachial plexus · arm nerves (Plexus brachialis) is situated in c5–T1 ventral rami between scalene muscles → behind clavicle → axilla and upper limb, receives arterial perfusion via cords surround axillary artery; regional supply from subclavian/axillary branches, and is innervated by ventral rami C5–T1, with frequent prefixed/postfixed variation.

Physiologically, the c5–T1 ventral rami provide segmental motor and sensory fibers to upper limb. Structurally, the interscalene passage (Spatium interscalenum) comprises roots and trunks pass between anterior and middle scalene muscles. Physiologically, the interscalene passage governs conveys plexus out of neck. Structurally, the upper trunk (Truncus superior) comprises formed by union of C5 and C6 ventral rami. Physiologically, the upper trunk governs redistributes upper-root fibers into divisions. Structurally, the middle trunk (Truncus medius) comprises continuation of C7 ventral ramus. Physiologically, the middle trunk feeds anterior and posterior divisions. Structurally, the lower trunk (Truncus inferior) comprises formed by C8 and T1 ventral rami. Physiologically, the lower trunk carries lower-root fibers toward hand pathways. The anterior divisions (Divisiones anteriores) are one anterior division from each trunk, usually destined for limb flexor compartments. Physiologically, the anterior divisions governs create lateral and medial cords.

Clinically, regarding the c5–T1 ventral rami, anatomy can be prefixed C4–C8 or postfixed C6–T2. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the interscalene passage, site of interscalene regional anesthesia. In clinical pathology involving the upper trunk, upper-trunk traction can weaken shoulder abduction and elbow flexion. Medical evaluation of the middle trunk also notes that c7 contribution enters multiple terminal nerves.

chapters.l: Cortex cerebri · substantia alba · nuclei basales
chapters.r: Cerebral hemispheres: cortical ribbon, deep white matter, ventricles and diencephalon
chapters.b: Anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arterial territories; perforators supply deep nuclei
chapters.n: Corticospinal, thalamocortical, commissural and association pathways
chapters.bl: Coronal deep-brain architecture: six-layered neocortex, corpus callosum, internal capsule projection highway, caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, and thalamus.
chapters.sum: Beneath the folded gray mantle of the cerebral cortex lies an intricate three-dimensional architecture of white matter highways and deep subcortical nuclei. Most cerebral neocortex has six microscopic layers, but cortical areas and older hippocampal cortex differ. Beneath cortical gray matter, association fibers link areas within a hemisphere, commissural fibers cross hemispheres and projection fibers connect cortex with deeper structures. The internal capsule carries densely packed motor and sensory pathways between thalamus/basal nuclei. The caudate and putamen form dorsal striatum; globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra participate in motor circuits. The thalamus relays and modulates most sensory streams and important motor signals. Within the human body, the cerebrum · cortex & deep pathways (Cortex cerebri · substantia alba · nuclei basales) is situated in cerebral hemispheres: cortical ribbon, deep white matter, ventricles and diencephalon, receives arterial perfusion via anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arterial territories; perforators supply deep nuclei, and is innervated by corticospinal, thalamocortical, commissural and association pathways.

Structurally, the cortical gray matter (Substantia grisea corticalis) comprises neuronal cell-body sheet folded into gyri and sulci. Physiologically, the cortical gray matter integrates sensory, motor and association information. The layer I · molecular (Lamina molecularis) is superficial neuropil-rich layer below pia, with relatively few neuronal somata. Physiologically, the layer I · molecular supports horizontal intracortical connections. The layer II · external granular (Lamina granularis externa) is small pyramidal and granule-cell zone. Physiologically, the layer II · external granular governs contributes intracortical signaling. Structurally, the layer III · external pyramidal (Lamina pyramidalis externa) comprises pyramidal neurons send many corticocortical and callosal projections. Physiologically, the layer III · external pyramidal links cortical regions and hemispheres. Structurally, the layer IV · internal granular (Lamina granularis interna) comprises prominent thalamic input layer, particularly in primary sensory cortex. Physiologically, the layer IV · internal granular receives major thalamocortical afferents. The layer V · internal pyramidal (Lamina pyramidalis interna) is large pyramidal cells project to brainstem and spinal cord; Betz cells are an example. Physiologically, the layer V · internal pyramidal provides major descending cortical output.

Clinically, regarding the cortical gray matter, regional cortical lesions give different deficits. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the layer I · molecular, six-layer plan is a template, not identical in every area. In clinical pathology involving the layer II · external granular, cell density varies across sensory and motor cortex. Medical evaluation of the layer III · external pyramidal also notes that white-matter injury can disconnect otherwise intact cortex.

chapters.l: Meninges · liquor cerebrospinalis · sinus durae matris
chapters.r: Skull and spinal canal: layered coverings, ventricular cavities and dural venous channels
chapters.b: Middle meningeal artery supplies dura; venous sinuses drain cerebral veins to jugular system
chapters.n: Trigeminal and upper cervical sensory innervation to cranial dura; brain parenchyma itself lacks pain receptors
chapters.bl: Three protective meningeal membranes (dura, arachnoid, pia), buoyancy-providing cerebrospinal fluid from choroid plexuses, and dural venous sinus drainage.
chapters.sum: Suspended in crystal-clear cerebrospinal fluid and wrapped in three protective membranes, the living brain floats inside the skull so its own weight does not crush its base. Cranial dura has periosteal and meningeal layers that separate at dural venous sinuses and create falx/tentorium folds. The arachnoid bridges across sulci; CSF occupies the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia, which closely follows brain contours. Choroid plexus secretes much CSF into ventricles: lateral → interventricular foramina → third → cerebral aqueduct → fourth → median/lateral apertures → subarachnoid cisterns. Arachnoid granulations drain much of it to dural sinuses, alongside other clearance routes. The subdural space is a potential pathologic space, not the normal CSF compartment. Within the human body, the meninges, csf & venous sinuses (Meninges · liquor cerebrospinalis · sinus durae matris) is situated in skull and spinal canal: layered coverings, ventricular cavities and dural venous channels, receives arterial perfusion via middle meningeal artery supplies dura; venous sinuses drain cerebral veins to jugular system, and is innervated by trigeminal and upper cervical sensory innervation to cranial dura; brain parenchyma itself lacks pain receptors.

The periosteal cranial dura (Stratum periostale durae) is outer cranial dural layer adherent to inner skull. Physiologically, the periosteal cranial dura forms tough outer covering and part of sinus walls. The meningeal cranial dura (Stratum meningeale durae) is inner tough dural layer reflecting as falx and tentorium. Physiologically, the meningeal cranial dura governs partitions cranial cavity and surrounds sinuses. Structurally, the falx cerebri comprises vertical sickle-shaped dural sheet between hemispheres. Physiologically, the falx cerebri supports superior and inferior sagittal sinuses. Structurally, the tentorium cerebelli comprises dural roof over cerebellum with tentorial notch around midbrain. Physiologically, the tentorium cerebelli governs partitions supratentorial and infratentorial spaces. Structurally, the superior sagittal sinus (Sinus sagittalis superior) comprises midline dural channel at upper attached edge of falx. Physiologically, the superior sagittal sinus receives superficial cerebral veins and arachnoid granulation drainage. Structurally, the straight sinus (Sinus rectus) comprises sinus at falx–tentorium junction receiving inferior sagittal and great cerebral venous drainage. Physiologically, the straight sinus governs transfers deep cerebral venous return posteriorly.

Clinically, regarding the periosteal cranial dura, spinal epidural space differs from cranial periosteal interface. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the meningeal cranial dura, dural folds constrain mass displacement. In clinical pathology involving the falx cerebri, bridging veins cross toward its superior sinus. Medical evaluation of the tentorium cerebelli also notes that herniation at notch threatens brainstem.

chapters.r: Midbrain → pons → medulla; cerebellum dorsal to pons/medulla
chapters.b: Vertebrobasilar branches, PICA, AICA and superior cerebellar artery territories
chapters.n: Brainstem cranial nerve nuclei, ascending/descending tracts and cerebellar peduncles
chapters.bl: Midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata nuclei, corticospinal pyramidal decussation, and the three peduncles linking the brainstem to the cerebellar cortex.
chapters.sum: Every nerve signal traveling between the cerebral hemispheres and spinal cord must pass through the brainstem, while the cerebellum behind it fine-tunes every movement. Midbrain, pons and medulla form the brainstem, carrying ascending sensation and descending motor commands while housing many cranial nerve nuclei and arousal/autonomic networks. Dorsal to pons and medulla, cerebellum compares intended and actual movement through cortex and deep nuclei. Inferior, middle and superior cerebellar peduncles connect it to medulla, pons and midbrain respectively; traffic direction is not identical in each peduncle. Purkinje cells inhibit deep nuclei; cerebellar dysfunction causes coordination deficits rather than classic isolated paralysis. Within the human body, the brainstem & cerebellar circuitry (Truncus encephali · cerebellum) is situated in midbrain → pons → medulla; cerebellum dorsal to pons/medulla, receives arterial perfusion via vertebrobasilar branches, PICA, AICA and superior cerebellar artery territories, and is innervated by brainstem cranial nerve nuclei, ascending/descending tracts and cerebellar peduncles.

Structurally, the midbrain (Mesencephalon) comprises rostral brainstem around cerebral aqueduct between diencephalon and pons. Physiologically, the midbrain governs hosts III/IV-related nuclei and visual/auditory orienting circuits. Structurally, the superior colliculus (Colliculus superior) comprises dorsal midbrain paired structure. Physiologically, the superior colliculus coordinates orienting eye/head movements to visual stimuli. Structurally, the inferior colliculus (Colliculus inferior) comprises dorsal caudal midbrain auditory relay structure. In clinical pathology involving the inferior colliculus, auditory pathways are largely bilateral centrally. Medical evaluation of the substantia nigra also notes that degeneration of pars compacta occurs in Parkinson disease.

chapters.r: Distal to a terminal bronchiole within secondary pulmonary lobules
chapters.b: Pulmonary arterioles → alveolar capillaries → pulmonary venules; bronchial arteries supply conducting tissue
chapters.n: Autonomic fibers to airways/vessels; alveolar wall is not a skeletal-muscle structure
chapters.bl: Inside the terminal respiratory unit: flat Type I pneumocytes, surfactant-secreting Type II cells, alveolar macrophages, and the 0.5-micron blood-air barrier.
chapters.sum: At the terminal tips of the bronchial tree, roughly 300 to 500 million microscopic air sacs create a gas-exchange surface area nearly the size of a tennis court. A terminal bronchiole is the last purely conducting airway. Its distal respiratory bronchioles bear occasional alveoli and lead to alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli. Thin type I pneumocytes cover most air-exchange surface; type II cells secrete surfactant and can contribute to epithelial repair. The air–blood barrier includes alveolar epithelium, thin interstitium/fused basement membranes and capillary endothelium. Alveolar macrophages provide immune surveillance; capillary red cells pass closely alongside exchange surfaces. Physiologically, the terminal bronchiole delivers air to downstream acinus. Physiologically, the respiratory bronchiole governs combines air conduction and some gas exchange. Structurally, the alveolar duct (Ductus alveolaris) comprises distal passage whose walls are largely alveolar openings. Physiologically, the alveolar duct distributes air to multiple alveolar sacs. Structurally, the alveolar sac (Sacculus alveolaris) comprises common terminal chamber opening into a cluster of alveoli. Physiologically, the alveolar sac governs shares airflow among terminal alveoli. The alveolus (Alveolus pulmonis) is tiny airspace lined by specialized epithelium and surrounded by capillaries. Physiologically, the alveolus provides extensive diffusion surface. Structurally, the type I pneumocyte (Pneumocytus typus I) comprises very thin squamous alveolar epithelial cell covering most alveolar surface. Physiologically, the type I pneumocyte governs minimizes gas diffusion distance.

Clinically, the terminal bronchiole contains no cartilage plates or submucosal glands. Clinically, the respiratory bronchiole marks proximal boundary of acinus. In clinical pathology involving the alveolar duct, more extensively alveolated than respiratory bronchiole. Medical evaluation of the alveolar sac also notes that not synonymous with a single alveolus.

chapters.r: Liver parenchyma: portal tracts at lobule periphery and central venule inside
chapters.b: Portal venules and hepatic arterioles → sinusoids → central vein → hepatic veins
chapters.n: Autonomic fibers accompany portal vessels and biliary tree; hepatocyte plates are not motor nerves
chapters.bl: Hexagonal liver micro-units where portal vein and hepatic artery blood flows inward across fenestrated sinusoids to the central vein while bile flows outward.
chapters.sum: Under the microscope, the liver is organized into hexagonal lobules where nutrient-rich portal blood and oxygenated arterial blood mix and flow past hepatocyte plates. The classical hepatic lobule places a central vein in the middle and portal tracts at its margins. Portal venous and hepatic arterial blood mix in sinusoids and travel toward the central vein, while hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi that drain outward toward portal bile ducts. Fenestrated sinusoidal endothelium borders the space of Disse; Kupffer macrophages reside in/along sinusoids and stellate cells in the perisinusoidal space. The hepatic acinus maps perfusion zones: zone 1 periportal receives blood first; zone 3 near terminal hepatic venules is relatively most hypoxia-vulnerable. Physiologically, the interlobular bile duct receives bile from canalicular/ductular route. Physiologically, the portal tract governs organizes inflow and bile outflow at lobular margin. Structurally, the central vein (Vena centralis) comprises terminal hepatic venule at center of classical lobule. Physiologically, the central vein collects sinusoidal blood toward hepatic veins. Structurally, the hepatic sinusoid (Sinusoideum hepaticum) comprises wide, discontinuous capillary channel between plates of hepatocytes. Physiologically, the hepatic sinusoid allows blood–hepatocyte exchange en route to central vein.

Clinically, regarding the portal venule, portal obstruction can raise portal pressure. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the hepatic arteriole, not the same as portal venous inflow. In clinical pathology involving the interlobular bile duct, duct injury causes cholestatic patterns. Medical evaluation of the portal tract also notes that triad diagrams omit additional vessels/lymphatics.

chapters.r: Small bowel from luminal epithelium through mucosa, submucosa, muscularis and serosa
chapters.b: Mesenteric arterial branches → villus capillaries; lacteals carry dietary lipids
chapters.n: Myenteric and submucosal enteric plexuses modulated by vagal/sympathetic input
chapters.bl: Four gastrointestinal wall tunics, absorptive villi with central lacteals, stem-cell crypts of Lieberkühn, and the submucosal and myenteric enteric nerve plexuses.
chapters.sum: Three nested levels of folding—circular folds, finger-like villi, and microscopic brush-border microvilli—turn the inner lining of the small intestine into a vast absorptive surface. The small-intestinal wall has mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis externa (inner circular and outer longitudinal layers) and serosa/adventitia depending on site. Villi expand surface area and crypts house renewing stem cells, antimicrobial Paneth cells and secretory lineages. Enterocytes absorb nutrients; goblet cells secrete mucus; enteroendocrine cells release signals. The submucosal plexus regulates local secretion/flow, while the myenteric plexus between muscle layers coordinates motility. These locations are different from the intestinal lumen. Within the human body, the small intestine · wall & enteric plexuses (Tunicae intestini tenuis · plexus enterici) is situated in small bowel from luminal epithelium through mucosa, submucosa, muscularis and serosa, receives arterial perfusion via mesenteric arterial branches → villus capillaries; lacteals carry dietary lipids, and is innervated by myenteric and submucosal enteric plexuses modulated by vagal/sympathetic input.

Structurally, the villus (Villus intestinalis) comprises fingerlike projection of small-intestinal mucosa with epithelial cover and lamina propria core. Physiologically, the villus expands absorptive surface. Structurally, the crypt of Lieberkühn (Glandula intestinalis) comprises epithelial invagination between villus bases toward muscularis mucosae. Physiologically, the crypt of Lieberkühn houses stem and secretory cell niches. Structurally, the enterocyte (Enterocytus) comprises absorptive columnar epithelial cell with apical microvilli. Physiologically, the enterocyte governs takes up digested nutrients. The brush border (Limbus striatus) is dense apical microvilli on enterocytes, not the large villi themselves. Physiologically, the brush border governs increases membrane area and supports digestive enzymes. Structurally, the goblet cell (Cellula caliciformis) comprises mucin-producing epithelial cell scattered among enterocytes. Physiologically, the goblet cell lubricates and helps protect mucosal surface. Structurally, the paneth cell (Cellula Paneth) comprises granule-rich cell near base of small-intestinal crypt. Physiologically, the paneth cell produces antimicrobial molecules supporting stem-cell niche.

Clinically, regarding the villus, typical colon lacks villi. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the crypt of Lieberkühn, crypt loss can impair epithelial renewal. In clinical pathology involving the enterocyte, loss of brush-border surface impairs absorption. Medical evaluation of the brush border also notes that villus and microvillus are different scales.

chapters.r: Head: 8 cranial bones around the brain and 14 facial bones supporting jaws, orbits and nose
chapters.b: External carotid branches supply much of face; internal carotid/ophthalmic contributions supply orbit and forehead
chapters.n: CN V carries most facial skin sensation; CN VII moves expression muscles; CN V3 moves major chewing muscles
chapters.bl: Complete osteology of all 22 adult skull bones—8 cranial vault bones and 14 facial bones—paired with anterior surface and medial sagittal cutaway views.
chapters.sum: Built from twenty-two interlocking bones joined primarily by immovable sutures, the adult human skull forms both an armored vault for the brain and a frame for the face. An adult skull has 22 bones: 14 facial (six paired types and the unpaired vomer and mandible) and 8 cranial. The maxillae anchor upper teeth, the mandible is the mobile lower jaw, and the palatine bones lie deep at the back of the hard palate. Ethmoid contributes to the upper bony nasal septum but is counted as a cranial bone; the inferior nasal conchae are separate paired facial bones. A front view cannot reliably identify every deep or posterior bone; those entries use an unpinned sectional reference. The hyoid and the six ear ossicles belong in the wider 206-bone adult skeleton count but not the 22 skull bones. Structurally, the right maxilla (Maxilla dextra) comprises right upper jaw below the orbit, housing upper-tooth sockets and much of the maxillary sinus. Physiologically, the right maxilla forms upper jaw, orbit floor and anterior hard palate. Structurally, the left maxilla (Maxilla sinistra) comprises left upper jaw below the orbit; meets the opposite maxilla at the anterior midline. Physiologically, the left maxilla holds upper teeth and forms the left anterior hard palate. Structurally, the right zygomatic bone (Os zygomaticum dextrum) comprises right cheekbone forming the lateral rim and part of the floor of the orbit. Physiologically, the right zygomatic bone supports cheek contour and the bony orbit. Structurally, the left zygomatic bone (Os zygomaticum sinistrum) comprises left cheekbone forming the outer orbital rim and meeting the temporal bone at the arch. Physiologically, the left zygomatic bone protects the outer orbit and supports facial shape. The right nasal bone (Os nasale dextrum) is small right bone at the bony bridge of the nose, above the nasal opening. Physiologically, the right nasal bone forms the upper nasal bridge, not the flexible nose tip.

Clinically, regarding the frontal bone, the frontal sinus lies within the bone; fracture patterns can involve the anterior cranial floor. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the right maxilla, the infraorbital nerve (CN V2) exits through its infraorbital foramen. In clinical pathology involving the left maxilla, dental roots and maxillary sinus lie close together. Medical evaluation of the right zygomatic bone also notes that zygomatic fractures may affect the orbital rim and cheek projection.

chapters.r: Alveolar sockets of upper maxillae and lower mandible, within the oral cavity
chapters.b: Superior and inferior alveolar arterial branches serve tooth pulps and supporting tissues
chapters.n: CN V2 superior alveolar branches: upper teeth; CN V3 inferior alveolar branches: lower teeth
chapters.bl: Interactive Universal (#1–32 / A–T) and FDI two-digit dental charts, four tooth classes, enamel-dentin-pulp layers, periodontal ligaments, and V2/V3 nerves.
chapters.sum: Every human tooth is a living organ anchored in jawbone by a shock-absorbing periodontal ligament, crowned with the hardest mineralized tissue in the body: dental enamel. Dental anatomy links each named tooth position to a tooth class and a representative cross-section. The crown bears enamel over dentin; roots bear cementum and anchor in the jaw through the periodontal ligament. Pulp contains nerves and vessels that communicate through root canals and apical foramina. Incisors cut, canines grip, premolars crush, and molars grind, although roots and cusps vary. A full permanent arch has 32 positions including third molars; primary dentition has 20, without premolars. This chart uses Universal and FDI numbering while explicitly distinguishing patient right from viewer left. Upper dental sensation primarily follows maxillary CN V2 superior alveolar branches, and lower dental sensation mandibular CN V3 inferior alveolar branches; facial nerve CN VII moves expression muscles but does not supply pulp sensation. Physiologically, the anatomical crown governs offers a cutting or grinding surface depending on tooth class. Structurally, the enamel (Enamelum) comprises highly mineralized outer cover of the crown, shown white above the gum; enamel does not normally cover the root. Physiologically, the enamel protects deeper dentin from wear and acid, though it can demineralize. Structurally, the dentin (Dentinum) comprises yellowish tissue beneath crown enamel and root cementum; surrounds pulp throughout the tooth. Physiologically, the dentin supports the crown and houses dentinal tubules. The pulp chamber (Cavitas pulpae) is central space in the crown holding vascular, neural and connective dental pulp; its roof lies under occlusal dentin. Physiologically, the pulp chamber supports tooth vitality, defense and dentin formation. Structurally, the tooth root (Radix dentis) comprises portion anchored below the crown in an alveolar socket; molar roots may be multiple but number and canal shape vary. Physiologically, the tooth root anchors the tooth through periodontal ligament and cementum. The root canal (Canalis radicis dentis) is narrow continuation of the pulp space inside each root, opening toward its apex. Physiologically, the root canal governs conveys pulpal nerve and blood supply through the root.

Clinically, regarding the anatomical crown, do not confuse anatomical crown with clinical crown. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the enamel, once mature enamel is lost, it does not regrow as an intact enamel layer. In clinical pathology involving the dentin, exposed dentin can be sensitive and is more vulnerable than enamel. Medical evaluation of the pulp chamber also notes that deep caries can inflame pulp; a digital cutaway cannot diagnose pulp disease.

chapters.r: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
