parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Right and left in medical terminology always refer to the patient’s own right and left sides, never the observer’s perspective. When viewing an anterior anatomical illustration or a standard frontal chest radiograph, the patient’s right side appears on the viewer’s left and the patient’s left side appears on the viewer’s right.
parts.f: Prevents laterality reversals when documenting physical exam findings, interpreting diagnostic scans, or planning surgical approaches across paired organs and limbs.
parts.c: Strict adherence to patient-centered right and left is the foundation of surgical site verification protocols and standard radiological viewing conventions (where axial CT and MRI slices are viewed as if looking upward from the patient’s feet).

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Vertical longitudinal plane passing directly through the anatomical midline of the head, neck, and trunk—intersecting the sagittal suture, nasal septum, sternum, umbilicus, and vertebral spinous processes—to divide the body into symmetrical right and left halves.
parts.f: Defines the central longitudinal axis of bilateral symmetry and serves as the zero-reference line for measuring medial and lateral relationships.
parts.c: Midline sagittal MRI sequences are the gold standard for evaluating the corpus callosum, pituitary sella, brainstem, fourth ventricle, and cervical-to-lumbar intervertebral discs.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Any vertical longitudinal plane oriented parallel to the median sagittal plane but offset to the right or left of the midline, dividing the body into unequal right and left portions (such as the midclavicular sagittal plane passing through the midpoint of the clavicle).
parts.f: Allows clinicians and radiologists to trace off-center longitudinal structures such as the kidneys, paraspinous muscles, carotid sheaths, and shoulder or knee joints.
parts.c: On sagittal MRI or ultrasound of the abdomen and spine, parasagittal slices sequentially step laterally from the midline to evaluate neural foramina, pedicles, and paired retroperitoneal viscera.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Vertical plane oriented perpendicular to the median sagittal plane (paralleling the coronal suture of the skull) that divides the body or an organ into anterior (ventral) and posterior (dorsal) portions.
parts.f: Organizes front-to-back anatomical depth and defines the plane in which limb abduction, adduction, and lateral trunk flexion occur.
parts.c: Coronal CT and MRI reconstructions simultaneously display bilateral structures—such as both lungs, both kidneys, the paranasal sinuses, and the hip joints—on a single comparative slice.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Horizontal plane oriented perpendicular to the long vertical axis of the upright human body, dividing the trunk, head, or limbs into superior (cranial) and inferior (caudal) cross-sectional segments.
parts.f: Provides the cross-sectional geometry fundamental to axial computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and transverse anatomical compartmentalization.
parts.c: Clinical axial CT and MRI slices are conventionally displayed in inferior-to-superior perspective (as if standing at the foot of the bed), placing the patient’s right on the viewer’s left and the anterior body wall at the top of the image.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Sectional plane oriented at an angle that is not parallel to the standard sagittal, coronal, or transverse cardinal planes, tailored to match the natural diagonal axis of an internal organ or vessel.
parts.f: Follows structures whose long axes run diagonally through the body—such as the left-anterior-inferolateral axis of the heart, the ribs, the optic nerve, or the inguinal canal.
parts.c: Echocardiography and cardiac MRI routinely use specialized oblique views (four-chamber, short-axis, and left ventricular outflow tract planes) because the heart sits obliquely within the middle mediastinum.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Anterior (ventral) denotes a position nearer the front surface of the body in standard anatomical position, whereas posterior (dorsal) denotes a position nearer the back surface along the front-to-back coronal axis.
parts.f: Establishes depth relationships between serial structures—for example, the sternum lies anterior to the heart, the heart lies anterior to the esophagus, and the esophagus lies anterior to the thoracic vertebrae.
parts.c: In clinical neurology and embryology, ventral is often used synonymously with anterior in the trunk (e.g., ventral motor horn of the spinal cord) and dorsal with posterior (e.g., dorsal sensory root ganglion).

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Superior (cranial or cephalic) indicates a position closer to the vertex of the head, whereas inferior (caudal) indicates a position closer to the soles of the feet along the vertical longitudinal axis of the body.
parts.f: Orders axial structures from head to toe—for example, the thoracic diaphragm lies inferior to the lungs and heart but superior to the liver, stomach, and spleen.
parts.c: During embryological development and trunk anatomy, cranial and caudal (toward the coccygeal tail) provide posture-independent equivalents to superior and inferior along the neural axis.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Medial describes a structure situated closer to the median sagittal plane of the body, whereas lateral describes a structure situated farther away from the midline toward the right or left side.
parts.f: Differentiates paired structures, ligaments, and neurovascular bundles across the transverse width of the trunk and limbs.
parts.c: Because the forearm is supinated in anatomical position, the ulna and little finger (5th digit) are always medial, whereas the radius and thumb (1st digit) are always lateral— making the medial collateral ligament of the knee tibial and the lateral collateral ligament fibular.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Proximal designates a location closer to the attachment root of a limb on the trunk (or closer to the origin of a branching tubular structure), whereas distal designates a location farther away along the limb or branch.
parts.f: Provides unambiguous longitudinal orientation along the upper and lower extremities and along branching vascular, bronchial, and intestinal trees.
parts.c: A proximal humeral fracture involves the surgical or anatomical neck near the glenohumeral shoulder joint, whereas a distal radial fracture (such as a Colles fracture) occurs just proximal to the radiocarpal wrist joint.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Superficial (external) refers to a layer or structure positioned closer to the outer cutaneous surface of the body, whereas deep (internal) refers to a structure positioned farther inward toward the core axis.
parts.f: Stratifies body-wall and extremity anatomy from epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tela (superficial fascia) down through investing deep fascia, skeletal muscle compartments, periosteum, and visceral cavities.
parts.c: Distinguishing superficial from deep venous systems is vital in vascular medicine: deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in the femoral or popliteal veins carries a high risk of pulmonary embolism, unlike superficial thrombophlebitis of the great saphenous vein.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Ipsilateral indicates two structures, pathways, or clinical signs located on the same side of the median sagittal plane, whereas contralateral indicates structures or signs located on opposite sides of the midline.
parts.f: Traces decussating (crossing) versus non-decussating neuroanatomical tracts and paired vascular supply routes.
parts.c: Because the corticospinal motor tract decussates in the caudal medulla, an ischemic stroke in the left cerebral hemisphere produces contralateral right-sided hemiparesis, whereas a cerebellar hemisphere lesion produces ipsilateral limb ataxia.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Sagittal-plane angular movements around a transverse joint axis: flexion generally decreases the angle between articulating bones (bringing ventral surfaces closer in the trunk, shoulder, hip, and elbow), whereas extension increases the angle back to or beyond anatomical position.
parts.f: Powers forward locomotion, reaching, lifting, and postural uprightness across hinge, condyloid, and ball-and-socket synovial joints.
parts.c: Because the lower limb rotates 180 degrees medially during embryonic development, flexion at the knee and toes bends the distal segment posteriorly, whereas flexion at the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hip moves the segment anteriorly.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Frontal-plane angular movements around an anteroposterior joint axis: abduction moves a limb or digit laterally away from the median plane (or midline of the hand/foot), whereas adduction draws it medially back toward the midline.
parts.f: Controls lateral limb elevation at the glenohumeral shoulder joint, pelvic stabilization via hip abductors during single-leg stance, and finger/toe spreading.
parts.c: In the hand, abduction and adduction are referenced to the axial line of the middle (3rd) finger (mediated by dorsal and palmar interossei), whereas in the foot they are referenced to the second toe.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Torsional movement in the transverse plane around the longitudinal axis of a long bone: medial (internal) rotation turns the anterior surface of the humerus or femur toward the median plane, whereas lateral (external) rotation turns the anterior surface away from the midline.
parts.f: Positions the hand and foot in space through coordinated action of the glenohumeral rotator cuff (subscapularis vs infraspinatus/teres minor) and deep gluteal rotators of the hip.
parts.c: Clinical testing of internal and external rotation at 0 and 90 degrees of abduction isolates individual rotator cuff tendons and detects femoroacetabular impingement at the hip.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Sequential compound movement combining flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction so that the proximal joint end remains at a fixed pivot while the distal limb extremity sweeps out a conical trajectory in space.
parts.f: Maximizes three-dimensional workspace at multiaxial ball-and-socket (glenohumeral, coxofemoral) and biaxial condyloid or saddle (radiocarpal, first carpometacarpal) joints.
parts.c: Smooth circumduction requires intact capsuloligamentous restraints and sequential co-activation of antagonistic muscle groups around the joint perimeter.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Specialized rotational movements at the proximal and distal radioulnar pivot joints: in pronation, the radial head spins within the annular ligament and the distal radius crosses anteriorly over the ulna to turn the palm posteriorly; supination uncrosses the bones to return the palm anteriorly.
parts.f: Rotates the hand through nearly 180 degrees for tool use, turning doorknobs, and feeding without requiring shoulder displacement.
parts.c: Biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator of the flexed forearm (assisted by the deep supinator muscle), whereas pronator teres and pronator quadratus (innervated by the median nerve) drive pronation.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Sagittal-plane hinge movements at the talocrural (tibiotalar) ankle mortise joint: dorsiflexion lifts the dorsum of the foot superiorly toward the anterior tibia, whereas plantarflexion depresses the sole inferiorly toward the ground.
parts.f: Dorsiflexion clears the toes during the swing phase of gait, while powerful plantarflexion by the gastrocnemius-soleus complex via the Achilles tendon propels push-off.
parts.c: Injury to the common fibular (peroneal) nerve at the fibular neck paralyzes the anterior crural dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior), resulting in clinical foot-drop and a high-stepping gait.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Frontal-plane movements occurring primarily at the subtalar (talocalcaneal) and transverse tarsal (calcaneocuboid and talonavicular) joints: inversion tilts the plantar sole medially toward the midline, whereas eversion tilts the sole laterally outward.
parts.f: Allows the foot to adapt dynamically to uneven terrain while maintaining upright balance during stance and running.
parts.c: Forced inversion of a plantarflexed ankle is the most common mechanism of lateral ankle sprain, stretching or tearing the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL).

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Composite movement at the first carpometacarpal (trapeziometacarpal) saddle joint combining abduction, flexion, and medial axial rotation of the first metacarpal so the fleshy pad of the thumb contacts the palmar pads of digits 2–5; reposition returns the thumb to anatomical position.
parts.f: Forms the biomechanical basis of human precision pinch (tip-to-tip and pad-to-pad) and cylindrical power grip.
parts.c: Opponens pollicis in the thenar eminence is innervated by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve; severe carpal tunnel syndrome or palmar laceration causes thenar wasting (ape-hand deformity) and loss of opposition.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Consistent, externally visible or palpable bony prominences and soft-tissue contours—such as the jugular (suprasternal) notch, sternal angle of Louis (2nd costal cartilage / T4–T5 disc), xiphoid process, anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), and C7 vertebra prominens.
parts.f: Bridges external physical inspection, palpation, auscultation, and procedural needle placement with deep internal visceral and neurovascular topography.
parts.c: The sternal angle marks the level of the second rib for accurate intercostal space counting, the tracheal bifurcation (carina), and the junction of the ascending aorta with the aortic arch.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: A cross-sectional modality (CT, MRI, ultrasound, or anatomical cryosection) displays a discrete two-dimensional tissue slice of defined thickness, whereas a conventional radiographic projection (plain X-ray) superimposes all three-dimensional structures traversed by the X-ray beam onto a single flat detector plane.
parts.f: Explains why overlapping bones and soft tissues obscure depth on plain radiographs but are cleanly resolved into distinct anterior-to-posterior and medial-to-lateral coordinates on cross-sectional slices.
parts.c: Interpreting chest radiographs requires two orthogonal projections (posteroanterior and lateral) to localize a pulmonary nodule in three dimensions, whereas a single axial CT stack provides exact volumetric coordinates.

parts.reg: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Naturally occurring, non-pathological differences in organ size, lobation, vascular branching, accessory ducts, or nerve courses among healthy individuals (such as a retrocecal appendix, bovine aortic arch branching, or an absent palmaris longus tendon).
parts.f: Reminds clinicians and surgeons that textbook plates depict the statistically most common morphological pattern (~65–80% of individuals) rather than an invariant rule.
parts.c: Recognizing common arterial and biliary variations—such as a replaced right hepatic artery arising from the superior mesenteric artery during cholecystectomy—is essential to prevent intraoperative hemorrhage or ductal injury.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Posterior continuous axial compartment enclosed by bone and lined by the three meninges (dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater), subdivided into the superior cranial cavity and the inferior vertebral (spinal) canal.
parts.f: Encases, cushions, and mechanically shields the delicate central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) within a buoyant bath of cerebrospinal fluid.
parts.c: Because the subarachnoid space is continuous between the cranial and vertebral subdivisions, lumbar puncture at L3–L4 or L4–L5 samples cerebrospinal fluid and measures pressure across the entire dorsal neuraxis.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Intracranial vault formed by the eight fused neurocranial bones (frontal, paired parietals, paired temporals, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid), housing the cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem, cranial nerves, dural venous sinuses, and cerebral vasculature.
parts.f: Provides a rigid protective helmet around the brain and partitions the intracranial space via dural reflections (falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli).
parts.c: Because the adult cranial vault is rigid and non-expansile (Monro-Kellie doctrine), an expanding intracranial hematoma, tumor, or cerebral edema rapidly elevates intracranial pressure and risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Tubular bony canal formed by the stacked vertebral foramina of the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral vertebrae, bounded anteriorly by vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs and posteriorly by laminae and ligamenta flava.
parts.f: Protects the spinal cord, cauda equina, spinal meninges, and internal vertebral venous plexus while allowing segmental spinal nerves to exit through intervertebral foramina.
parts.c: The adult spinal cord terminates at the conus medullaris near the L1–L2 intervertebral disc; degenerative disc herniation or spinal stenosis below this level compresses the cauda equina within the lumbar vertebral canal.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Large anterior coelomic compartment of the trunk bounded by the thoracic cage and abdominopelvic musculature, partitioned into the superior thoracic cavity and inferior abdominopelvic cavity by the muscular dome of the diaphragm.
parts.f: Houses the respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive, urinary, and internal reproductive viscera within mobile serous-lined compartments that accommodate volume changes during breathing, cardiac filling, and peristalsis.
parts.c: Embryologically derived from the intraembryonic coelom, the ventral cavity is lined by mesothelium-derived serous membranes (pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum) that secrete lubricating fluid to prevent visceral adhesions.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Superior subdivision of the ventral body cavity enclosed by the sternum, twelve pairs of ribs, costal cartilages, intercostal muscles, and thoracic vertebrae, extending from the superior thoracic aperture (thoracic inlet) down to the diaphragm.
parts.f: Contains the right and left lateral pleural cavities (housing the lungs) and the central mediastinum (housing the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus) while generating negative intrathoracic pressure for ventilation.
parts.c: Penetrating chest trauma or rib fractures can breach the thoracic wall, equalizing intrathoracic pressure with atmospheric air and causing pneumothorax or hemothorax.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Paired, anatomically separate right and left serous potential spaces situated between the visceral pleura adherent to each lung surface and the parietal pleura lining the rib cage, diaphragm, and mediastinum.
parts.f: Contains a thin capillary film of pleural fluid (5–15 mL) that creates surface tension coupling the lungs to the expanding chest wall while eliminating friction during respiration.
parts.c: Accumulation of air (pneumothorax), blood (hemothorax), or transudative/exudative fluid (pleural effusion) converts the potential pleural space into a real space that compresses the ipsilateral lung.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Central interpleural compartment of the thoracic cavity spanning from the sternum anteriorly to the thoracic vertebral column posteriorly and from the thoracic inlet superiorly to the diaphragm inferiorly; divided at the sternal angle (T4–T5) into superior and inferior (anterior, middle, posterior) subdivisions.
parts.f: Serves as the central thoracic conduit and housing for the heart and pericardium (middle), thymus (anterior), aortic arch and great vessels (superior), and esophagus, thoracic duct, vagus nerves, and descending aorta (posterior).
parts.c: Mediastinal widening on a chest radiograph is a critical red flag for thoracic aortic dissection, lymphoma, thymoma, or esophageal perforation (mediastinitis).

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Closed serous potential space enclosed within the middle mediastinum between the visceral serous pericardium (epicardium) covering the myocardium and the parietal serous pericardium fused to the tough outer fibrous pericardial sac.
parts.f: Holds 15–50 mL of serous pericardial fluid that lubricates the heart surfaces during every systolic contraction and diastolic relaxation cycle.
parts.c: Rapid accumulation of blood or fluid within the non-compliant fibrous pericardium produces cardiac tamponade, compressing the right atrium and ventricle and critically impairing diastolic ventricular filling.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Dome-shaped musculotendinous septum separating the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity, arising from the xiphoid process, lower six ribs/costal cartilages, and lumbar vertebrae (right and left crura) to converge on a central tendon; pierced by the caval (T8), esophageal (T10), and aortic (T12) hiatuses.
parts.f: Acts as the primary muscle of inspiration: contraction flattens its domes inferiorly, increasing vertical thoracic volume and drawing air into the lungs while aiding venous return.
parts.c: Innervated by the paired phrenic nerves (C3–C5); irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura or peritoneum refers sharp pain to the ipsilateral shoulder tip via the supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4).

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Superior major portion of the abdominopelvic cavity extending from the inferior surface of the thoracic diaphragm down to the pelvic inlet (linea terminalis), bounded by the anterolateral abdominal wall musculature and posterior lumbar spine.
parts.f: Contains the liver, gallbladder, stomach, spleen, pancreas, small intestine, and most of the large intestine, along with the retroperitoneal kidneys, adrenal glands, abdominal aorta, and inferior vena cava.
parts.c: Blunt or penetrating abdominal trauma requires rapid evaluation (such as FAST ultrasound of Morison’s hepatorenal pouch and the splenorenal recess) to detect free intraperitoneal blood.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Funnel-shaped inferior portion of the abdominopelvic cavity cradled within the true (lesser) bony pelvis below the pelvic inlet and bounded inferiorly by the muscular pelvic diaphragm (levator ani and coccygeus muscles).
parts.f: Houses and supports the urinary bladder, terminal ureters, rectum, anal canal, and internal reproductive organs (uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, and vagina in females; prostate, seminal vesicles, and pelvic vas deferens in males).
parts.c: In the upright or supine position, the rectouterine pouch of Douglas (in females) and rectovesical pouch (in males) form the most dependent gravity-draining points of the abdominopelvic peritoneal cavity.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Largest serous membrane in the body: parietal peritoneum lines the internal surface of the abdominopelvic wall, while visceral peritoneum invests intraperitoneal organs, forming double-layered mesenteries, omenta, and peritoneal ligaments that suspend viscera and transmit neurovascular bundles.
parts.f: Secretes lubricating peritoneal fluid for frictionless intestinal peristalsis, stores fat within the greater omentum, and walls off localized intra-abdominal infection.
parts.c: Parietal peritoneum receives somatic innervation from intercostal and phrenic nerves (producing sharp, well-localized pain and rebound tenderness in peritonitis), whereas visceral peritoneum receives autonomic innervation (producing dull, poorly localized midline pain).

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Anatomical space situated posterior to the parietal peritoneum and anterior to the transversalis fascia of the posterior abdominal wall, containing primary retroperitoneal organs (kidneys, adrenal glands, ureters, aorta, IVC) and secondary retroperitoneal organs (duodenum C2–C4, pancreas head/body, ascending and descending colon).
parts.f: Anchors major vascular trunks and urinary/digestive organs firmly against the posterior body wall outside the mobile peritoneal sac.
parts.c: Retroperitoneal hemorrhage or duodenal/pancreatic perforation is clinically occult on anterior abdominal palpation because blood and enzymes are sequestered behind the parietal peritoneum, often presenting with flank ecchymosis (Grey Turner sign) or back pain.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Superior right quarter of the abdomen formed by intersecting the median sagittal plane with the transverse umbilical plane through L3–L4; overlies the right lobe of the liver, gallbladder, biliary tree, pylorus, duodenum (C1–C3), head of the pancreas, right kidney, and hepatic flexure of the colon.
parts.f: Serves as the primary bedside examination zone for hepatobiliary, duodenal, and right renal assessment.
parts.c: Acute RUQ pain and inspiratory arrest during deep subcostal palpation (positive Murphy sign) are classic clinical hallmarks of acute calculous cholecystitis.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Superior left quarter of the abdomen above the umbilical plane and left of the midline; overlies the spleen, stomach fundus and body, left lobe of the liver, body and tail of the pancreas, left kidney and adrenal gland, and splenic flexure of the colon.
parts.f: Guides palpation and percussion of the spleen and gastric contour below the left costal margin.
parts.c: Blunt trauma to the left lower rib cage (ribs 9–11) frequently lacerates the spleen in the LUQ, producing left upper quadrant tenderness and referred left shoulder pain (Kehr sign) from diaphragmatic irritation.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Inferior right quarter of the abdomen below the transverse umbilical plane and right of the midline; overlies the cecum, vermiform appendix, terminal ileum, ascending colon origin, right ureter, and (in females) the right ovary and fallopian tube or (in males) the right spermatic cord.
parts.f: Provides the classic clinical localization zone for ileocecal, appendiceal, and right adnexal evaluation.
parts.c: Focal tenderness at McBurney’s point (one-third of the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus) is the hallmark sign of acute appendicitis once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Inferior left quarter of the abdomen below the umbilical plane and left of the midline; overlies the descending colon, sigmoid colon, left ureter, and (in females) the left ovary and fallopian tube or (in males) the left spermatic cord.
parts.f: Directs clinical palpation and imaging of the distal colonic tract and left pelvic adnexa.
parts.c: In adults, acute LLQ pain accompanied by fever and leukocytosis most commonly reflects acute sigmoid diverticulitis, whereas in reproductive-age females left ovarian torsion or ectopic pregnancy must also be ruled out.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Superior-right compartment of the nine-region abdominal grid, bounded medially by the right midclavicular line and inferiorly by the subcostal (or transpyloric) plane beneath the right costal cartilages.
parts.f: Houses the bulk of the right hepatic lobe, gallbladder fundus, biliary ducts, and upper pole of the right kidney under the protective lower rib cage.
parts.c: Deep palpation beneath the right costal margin during inspiration brings the descending liver edge and gallbladder fundus into contact with the examiner’s fingers.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Superior-central compartment of the nine-region abdominal grid situated between the right and left midclavicular lines, inferior to the xiphoid process and superior to the transpyloric/subcostal plane.
parts.f: Overlies the lesser curvature and pylorus of the stomach, gastroesophageal junction, head and body of the pancreas, duodenum, left hepatic lobe, abdominal aorta, and celiac trunk.
parts.c: Foregut structures innervated by the greater splanchnic nerves (T5–T9)—including the stomach, duodenum, pancreas, and gallbladder—refer visceral pain to the epigastric region; inferior myocardial infarction can also mimic acute epigastric indigestion.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Superior-left compartment of the nine-region grid situated lateral to the left midclavicular line and superior to the subcostal plane, sheltered beneath the left lower ribs.
parts.f: Contains the spleen, gastric fundus and greater curvature, tail of the pancreas, splenic flexure of the colon, and superior pole of the left kidney.
parts.c: Normally, a healthy spleen lies entirely under the protection of ribs 9–11 in the left hypochondrium and only becomes palpable below the costal margin when enlarged to at least two to three times its normal volume (splenomegaly).

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Middle-right lateral compartment (right flank) bounded superiorly by the subcostal plane, inferiorly by the intertubercular (transtubercular) plane, and medially by the right midclavicular line.
parts.f: Overlies the ascending colon, right kidney, right ureter, and lateral loops of the small intestine.
parts.c: Bimanual ballottement in the right lumbar region evaluates right renal enlargement, while costovertebral angle (CVA) percussion posteriorly detects pyelonephritis or obstructive nephrolithiasis.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Central compartment of the nine-region grid surrounding the umbilicus (navel), bounded laterally by the right and left midclavicular lines between the subcostal and intertubercular planes.
parts.f: Contains the transverse colon, jejunum and ileum loops, third and fourth parts of the duodenum, greater omentum, abdominal aorta bifurcation (at L4), and inferior vena cava.
parts.c: Midgut derivatives (distal duodenum through the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, including the appendix) refer early visceral pain via the lesser splanchnic nerves (T10–T11) to the periumbilical T10 dermatome.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Middle-left lateral compartment (left flank) situated lateral to the left midclavicular line between the subcostal and intertubercular planes.
parts.f: Contains the descending colon, lower pole of the left kidney, left ureter, and jejunal coils.
parts.c: Colicky pain radiating from the left lumbar flank downward into the left groin and labium or scrotum is characteristic of a calculus migrating down the left ureter.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Inferior-right compartment of the nine-region grid situated lateral to the right midclavicular line and inferior to the intertubercular plane, overlying the right iliac fossa and inguinal ligament.
parts.f: Houses the cecum, vermiform appendix, terminal ileum, and deep/superficial inguinal rings.
parts.c: Direct and indirect inguinal hernias protrude near the medial half of the inguinal ligament in this region, alongside appendiceal and right adnexal pathology.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Inferior-central compartment (suprapubic region) located between the right and left midclavicular lines below the intertubercular plane and immediately superior to the pubic symphysis.
parts.f: Overlies the urinary bladder (especially when distended), sigmoid colon, rectum, small intestinal loops, and pregnant or enlarged uterus.
parts.c: Hindgut structures and pelvic viscera (distended urinary bladder, uterus, and sigmoid colon) refer visceral pain to the suprapubic hypogastric region; suprapubic catheterization is performed in the midline just above the pubic symphysis when the bladder is full.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Inferior-left compartment of the nine-region grid located lateral to the left midclavicular line and inferior to the intertubercular plane in the left iliac fossa.
parts.f: Contains the junction of the descending colon with the S-shaped sigmoid colon, left inguinal canal, and (in females) the left ovary and uterine tube.
parts.c: Palpation of a tender, rope-like mass in the left iliac fossa is a frequent physical finding in acute sigmoid diverticulitis or fecal impaction.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Flat, elongated anterior midline bone of the thoracic cage consisting of the superior manubrium, central body (gladiolus), and inferior cartilaginous/bony xiphoid process, directly subcutaneous along the anterior chest wall.
parts.f: Articulates with the clavicles and first seven costal cartilages to complete the anterior rib cage and protect the heart and great vessels in the mediastinum.
parts.c: The lower half of the sternal body is the anatomical site for external chest compressions during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and median sternotomy through the sternum provides standard surgical access to the heart.

parts.reg: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Curved, thickened superior border of the wing (ala) of the ilium extending from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) anteriorly to the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) posteriorly along the lateral waist margin.
parts.f: Serves as a major attachment rim for the external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, quadratus lumborum, latissimus dorsi, and gluteal muscles.
parts.c: A horizontal supracristal (intercristal) line drawn across the highest points of both iliac crests passes through the L4 spinous process, providing the standard bedside landmark for safe lumbar puncture at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Fundamental living structural and functional unit of the human body, bounded by a selectively permeable plasma membrane and containing a nucleus (in most mature cell types), cytosol, cytoskeleton, and membrane-bound organelles.
parts.f: Executes cellular metabolism, protein synthesis, energy transduction, excitability, and mitotic or meiotic division to sustain all tissues and organs.
parts.c: Over 200 specialized cell phenotypes—ranging from 7.5-micrometer biconcave erythrocytes to meter-long motor neurons—arise from a single fertilized zygote through differential gene expression.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Fluid-mosaic amphipathic phospholipid bilayer (~7.5–10 nm thick) stabilized by cholesterol and studded with integral ion channels, carrier proteins, G-protein-coupled receptors, and an external carbohydrate glycocalyx.
parts.f: Maintains electrochemical gradients (such as the Na+/K+-ATPase resting potential), mediates selective transport and endocytosis/exocytosis, and transduces extracellular hormone and neurotransmitter signals.
parts.c: Mutations in plasma-membrane transport proteins cause major clinical channelopathies—for example, defective CFTR chloride channels in cystic fibrosis impair epithelial mucus hydration in the lungs and pancreas.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: All intracellular contents located between the plasma membrane and the nuclear envelope: the cytosol is the aqueous, gel-like intracellular fluid rich in enzymes, ions, and metabolites, while the cytoplasm encompasses both the cytosol and suspended organelles plus cytoskeletal filaments.
parts.f: Serves as the biochemical reaction medium for glycolysis, signal transduction cascades, ribosomal translation, and vesicular trafficking along microtubule and actin tracks.
parts.c: High intracellular potassium (~140 mEq/L) and low free intracellular calcium (~100 nM) within the cytosol are tightly regulated; cytosolic enzyme release into plasma (such as ALT from hepatocytes or troponin from cardiomyocytes) is a key diagnostic marker of cell necrosis.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Largest membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells, enclosed by a double-membrane nuclear envelope perforated by nuclear pore complexes, housing chromosomal DNA wound around histone octamers (chromatin) and a dense nucleolus where ribosomal RNA is transcribed.
parts.f: Stores the diploid human genome (46 chromosomes), regulates transcriptional gene expression, and coordinates DNA replication prior to mitosis.
parts.c: While most cells have a single nucleus, mature mammalian erythrocytes extrude their nuclei to maximize hemoglobin space, whereas skeletal myofibers and osteoclasts are multinucleated syncytia.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Double-membrane organelles featuring a smooth outer membrane and a deeply folded inner membrane (cristae) enclosing the mitochondrial matrix; uniquely possess their own circular maternal DNA (mtDNA) and 70S-like ribosomes.
parts.f: Generate the vast majority of cellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) via the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, beta-oxidation of fatty acids, and the electron transport chain (oxidative phosphorylation), while also regulating intrinsic apoptosis via cytochrome c.
parts.c: High-energy tissues—cardiomyocytes, renal proximal tubule cells, neurons, and oxidative skeletal myofibers—are densely packed with mitochondria and are the first to fail in hypoxia, cyanide poisoning, or maternally inherited mitochondrial myopathies.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Ribonucleoprotein complexes (80S in eukaryotic cytoplasm, composed of 60S and 40S subunits) that exist either free in the cytosol or docked onto the cytosolic face of flattened interconnected membrane cisternae forming the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER).
parts.f: Free ribosomes synthesize cytosolic, nuclear, and mitochondrial proteins, whereas RER-bound ribosomes co-translationally translocate secretory proteins, lysosomal enzymes, and integral membrane proteins into the ER lumen for folding and N-linked glycosylation.
parts.c: Cells specialized for heavy protein secretion—such as antibody-secreting plasma cells, pancreatic acinar cells, and Nissl-rich motor neurons—exhibit abundant basophilic rough endoplasmic reticulum.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Polarized stack of flattened, membrane-bound cisternae organized from a cis-receiving face (adjacent to the rough ER) through medial compartments to a trans-Golgi network (TGN) that buds off clathrin- and coat-protein-vesicles.
parts.f: Performs post-translational O-linked glycosylation, sulfation, proteolytic cleavage, and mannose-6-phosphate tagging to sort proteins toward constitutive secretion, regulated secretory granules, the plasma membrane, or lysosomes.
parts.c: Defective phosphorylation of mannose residues in the cis-Golgi prevents lysosomal enzyme targeting, causing inclusion-cell (I-cell) disease, a severe lysosomal storage disorder.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Complex non-cellular macromolecular scaffold secreted by resident cells, composed of hydrated ground substance (glycosaminoglycans such as hyaluronan, proteoglycans, and multiadhesive glycoproteins like fibronectin and laminin) reinforced by collagen, reticular, and elastic fibers.
parts.f: Provides compressive resilience, tensile strength, biochemical growth-factor reservoirs, and mechanical anchoring cues (mechanotransduction via integrins) that govern cell migration and tissue repair.
parts.c: Pathological excess of extracellular matrix deposition driven by TGF-beta leads to organ fibrosis (hepatic cirrhosis, pulmonary fibrosis), whereas enzymatic matrix degradation by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) facilitates tumor invasion.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Avacular, densely packed cellular sheets united by junctional complexes (tight junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions) that cover external body surfaces, line internal luminal cavities and vessels, and invaginate to form exocrine and endocrine glands.
parts.f: Forms selective physical and chemical barriers, performs transcellular absorption and ion secretion, and provides mucociliary or sensory surface specializations.
parts.c: Because epithelial cells undergo continuous mitotic turnover and are directly exposed to environmental mutagens, over 80–90% of adult human malignancies arise from epithelial tissue (carcinomas and adenocarcinomas).

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Strict structural and functional asymmetry of epithelial cells in which the apical domain faces the external environment or internal lumen—often bearing actin-cored microvilli (brush border), stereocilia, or motile 9+2 axonemal cilia—while the basolateral domain contacts adjacent cells and the basal lamina.
parts.f: Segregates distinct ion transporters, enzymes, and receptors between apical and basolateral membranes to drive unidirectional transepithelial absorption (e.g., glucose and sodium in the gut and nephron) and secretion.
parts.c: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) composed of claudin and occludin proteins seal the subapical perimeter, preventing paracellular back-leak and maintaining strict membrane polarity.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Specialized acellular sheet (~40–120 nm thick) at the base of all epithelia, composed of a self-assembling meshwork of Type IV collagen, laminin, nidogen (entactin), and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (perlecan), anchored to underlying Type III reticular fibers to form the light-microscopic basement membrane.
parts.f: Mechanically tethers avascular epithelium to the underlying connective tissue via hemidesmosomes, filters macromolecules (as in the glomerular filtration barrier), and guides epithelial regeneration after injury.
parts.c: In oncological pathology, the basement membrane is the definitive boundary between pre-invasive carcinoma in situ and invasive carcinoma capable of accessing stromal lymphatics and blood vessels.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Morphological classification based on cell layer count and cell shape (squamous, cuboidal, columnar): simple epithelia consist of a single cell layer where every cell contacts the basal lamina and reaches the lumen, whereas stratified epithelia stack two or more layers above the basal germinative layer.
parts.f: Simple epithelia minimize diffusion distance for gas exchange (alveoli), filtration (Bowman capsule), and absorption (intestine), whereas stratified squamous epithelia (epidermis, esophagus, vagina) withstand severe mechanical abrasion.
parts.c: Chronic irritation can induce adaptive epithelial metaplasia—such as Barrett esophagus, where acid reflux converts stratified squamous epithelium into simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, or smoking-induced squamous metaplasia of respiratory pseudostratified ciliated epithelium.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Most abundant and widely distributed tissue family, derived from embryonic mesenchyme and characterized by relatively sparse cells embedded within an abundant extracellular matrix; encompasses connective tissue proper (loose areolar, dense regular/irregular, adipose, reticular), cartilage, bone, and blood.
parts.f: Forms the structural framework of every organ, binds epithelia to muscle, stores energy and minerals, transports blood-borne gases and immune cells, and orchestrates wound healing.
parts.c: Genetic defects in connective-tissue matrix proteins produce systemic disorders such as Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 elastic microfibril mutation risking aortic root aneurysm) and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (collagen synthesis/processing defects).

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Principal resident spindle-shaped mesenchymal cell of connective tissue proper, possessing an euchromatic oval nucleus, branched cytoplasmic processes, and abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi membranes when actively synthesizing matrix (quiescent mature cells are termed fibrocytes).
parts.f: Synthesizes and secretes procollagen, tropoelastin, reticular fibers, glycosaminoglycans, and proteoglycans to build and continually remodel the extracellular stroma.
parts.c: Following tissue laceration or infarction, local fibroblasts proliferate and differentiate into alpha-smooth-muscle-actin-expressing myofibroblasts that contract wound margins and deposit dense collagenous scar tissue.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Inelastic, high-tensile-strength extracellular protein bundles assembled from triple-helical tropocollagen molecules (rich in glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline) that display a characteristic 67-nm cross-banding periodicity under electron microscopy.
parts.f: Imparts immense resistance to pulling and tearing forces: Type I collagen dominates bone, dermis, tendons, and ligaments; Type II forms hyaline cartilage; Type III forms delicate reticular networks in liver, spleen, and lymph nodes; Type IV forms basal laminae.
parts.c: Post-translational hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues requires Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as a cofactor; Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, marked by fragile capillaries, bleeding gums, and poor wound healing.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Thin-walled microvessel (5–10 micrometers in diameter) lined by a single layer of simple squamous endothelial cells and sparse pericytes within the loose areolar lamina propria immediately beneath the epithelial basement membrane.
parts.f: Delivers oxygen, glucose, amino acids, and leukocytes to the subepithelial stroma so nutrients can diffuse across the basal lamina into the completely avascular overlying epithelium.
parts.c: During acute inflammation, histamine and bradykinin cause post-capillary venular endothelial cells in the loose connective tissue to contract, increasing microvascular permeability and producing localized tissue edema.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Excitable, contractile mesodermal tissue composed of elongated cells (myofibers or myocytes) packed with actin thin filaments and myosin II thick filaments that slide past one another via ATP-dependent cross-bridge cycling triggered by cytosolic calcium influx.
parts.f: Generates mechanical force for voluntary locomotion and posture (skeletal muscle), rhythmic circulatory pumping (cardiac muscle), and involuntary visceral peristalsis and vascular tone (smooth muscle).
parts.c: Because skeletal and cardiac muscle account for roughly 40–50% of total body mass, muscle tissue is also the body’s primary metabolic sink for insulin-mediated glucose uptake and thermogenesis.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Long, cylindrical, unbranched multinucleated syncytial cell (10–100 micrometers in diameter and up to several centimeters long) formed by the embryonic fusion of myoblasts, exhibiting prominent transverse A- and I-band striations and flattened nuclei pushed to the periphery beneath the sarcolemma.
parts.f: Contracts rapidly and forcefully under voluntary somatic motor control from alpha motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction (motor end plate) via nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and T-tubule/sarcoplasmic-reticulum excitation-contraction coupling.
parts.c: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, absence of the subsarcolemmal linker protein dystrophin causes mechanical tearing of the sarcolemma during contraction, leading to progressive myofiber necrosis and fibrofatty replacement.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Delicate sheath of reticular fibers (Type III collagen), basal lamina, and tortuous continuous capillaries that wraps each individual skeletal muscle fiber within a fascicle, continuous externally with the perimysium and epimysium.
parts.f: Electrically insulates individual myofibers, houses satellite stem cells for muscle regeneration, and transmits lateral contractile tension through the perimysium and epimysium to the tendon and bone periosteum.
parts.c: Satellite cells residing between the sarcolemma and the endomysial basal lamina proliferate after exercise-induced microtrauma to repair and hypertrophy damaged skeletal myofibers.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Branched, cross-striated cardiomyocytes containing one (occasionally two) centrally located oval nuclei, abundant large mitochondria (~35–40% of cell volume), and specialized step-like intercellular junctions called intercalated discs.
parts.f: Intercalated discs combine fascia adherens and desmosomes (for mechanical tension transfer) with large gap junctions (connexin-43) that allow action potentials to spread rapidly from cell to cell, enabling the myocardium to contract as a functional electrical syncytium.
parts.c: Adult cardiomyocytes have negligible regenerative capacity; ischemic necrosis from coronary artery occlusion (myocardial infarction) replaces functional cardiac muscle with non-contractile collagenous scar tissue.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Fusiform (spindle-shaped), non-striated contractile cells containing a single central corkscrew-like nucleus, dense bodies (analogous to Z-discs) anchored to intermediate filaments, and caveolae in place of T-tubules.
parts.f: Produces slow, sustained, energy-efficient involuntary contractions regulated by the autonomic nervous system, hormones, and local stretch via calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK).
parts.c: Forms the tunica media of blood vessels (regulating systemic blood pressure and peripheral vascular resistance) and the muscularis externa of the gastrointestinal, urinary, respiratory, and reproductive tracts.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Ectodermally derived communication network (originating from the embryonic neural tube and neural crest) composed of electrically excitable neurons and a tenfold-larger population of non-excitable supporting neuroglial cells, organized into the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and peripheral nervous system.
parts.f: Transduces internal and external sensory stimuli, integrates information across billions of chemical and electrical synapses, and issues rapid motor and neuroendocrine commands.
parts.c: Although comprising only ~2% of body weight, central nervous tissue consumes ~20% of total body oxygen and glucose continuously and suffers irreversible ischemic injury within 4–6 minutes of circulatory arrest.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: The neuronal soma (perikaryon) contains a large euchromatic nucleus with a prominent nucleolus and abundant rough ER (Nissl substance), giving rise to multiple tapering, branched dendritic trees studded with dendritic spines that receive excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs.
parts.f: Summates graded postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs and IPSPs) across its dendritic arbor and soma, initiating an all-or-none action potential at the voltage-gated sodium-channel-rich axon hillock (initial segment) when threshold is reached.
parts.c: Because mature neurons are post-mitotic (G0 phase), neurodegenerative disorders that destroy neuronal somata—such as dopaminergic loss in the substantia nigra in Parkinson disease or motor neuron loss in ALS—produce permanent neurological deficits.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Single, uniform-diameter cylindrical cytoplasmic process arising from the axon hillock and extending up to a meter to terminate at presynaptic boutons (axon terminals) containing neurotransmitter synaptic vesicles; lacks rough ER and relies on kinesin-mediated anterograde and dynein-mediated retrograde axonal transport along microtubules.
parts.f: Propagates regenerative action potentials away from the cell body toward target neurons, skeletal myofibers, or glandular cells to trigger calcium-dependent exocytosis of neurotransmitters across the synaptic cleft.
parts.c: Transection of a peripheral axon triggers Wallerian degeneration of the distal stump; in the peripheral nervous system, intact Schwann-cell basalamina tubes guide axonal regeneration at ~1–3 mm per day, whereas CNS axons fail to regenerate due to glial scar and myelin inhibitory proteins.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Multilayered, lipid-rich concentric membrane wrapping (~75–80% lipid, 20–25% protein) around axons formed by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system (each myelinating multiple axons) and by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system (each myelinating a single internode), interrupted every 1–2 mm by bare axonal gaps called nodes of Ranvier.
parts.f: Electrically insulates the internodal axolemma (increasing membrane resistance and decreasing capacitance) so action potentials leap rapidly from node to node (saltatory conduction) at speeds up to 70–120 m/s while conserving metabolic ATP.
parts.c: Autoimmune demyelination of CNS oligodendrocytes causes multiple sclerosis (presenting with optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and motor/sensory plaques), whereas autoimmune demyelination of PNS Schwann cells causes Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute ascending paralysis).

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Specialized non-neuronal cells of the nervous system: in the CNS, astrocytes (maintain the blood-brain barrier and potassium/glutamate homeostasis), oligodendrocytes (myelinate CNS axons), microglia (resident yolk-sac-derived phagocytic macrophages), and ependymal cells (line ventricles and secrete/circulate CSF); in the PNS, Schwann cells and ganglionic satellite cells.
parts.f: Provide structural scaffolding, metabolic lactate shuttle support, neurotransmitter reuptake, electrical insulation, and immune surveillance for neurons.
parts.c: Unlike post-mitotic neurons, glial cells retain the ability to divide; consequently, the vast majority of primary adult brain tumors (gliomas, including astrocytomas, glioblastomas, and oligodendrogliomas) originate from glial precursors.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Every human organ is assembled from four primary histogenesis families: epithelial tissue (covering/lining and glandular parenchyma), connective tissue (structural stroma, bone, cartilage, and blood), muscle tissue (contractile force generation), and nervous tissue (electrical signaling and control).
parts.f: Integrates barrier transport, mechanical strength, motility, and neural regulation into composite organ walls—such as the small intestine, which layers mucosal epithelium, lamina propria/submucosal connective tissue, muscularis externa smooth muscle, and enteric nervous plexuses.
parts.c: Understanding how the four tissue types interact in any organ allows students and clinicians to predict both normal physiological function and the specific histopathological patterns of inflammation, repair, and neoplasia.

parts.reg: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
parts.bld: Regional systemic and microvascular perfusion across body compartments
parts.nrv: Somatic and autonomic innervation organized by segmental and regional pathways
parts.d: Microscopic anatomy (histology) studies thin (3–8 micrometer) tissue sections fixed in formalin, embedded in paraffin, and stained with dyes such as hematoxylin (basic dye staining acidic DNA/RNA blue-purple) and eosin (acidic dye staining basic cytoplasmic proteins and collagen pink), complemented by three-dimensional micro-anatomical reconstructions.
parts.f: Links two-dimensional stained light and electron micrographs with three-dimensional cellular polarity, basal lamina architecture, and microvascular relationships.
parts.c: Correlating three-dimensional micro-anatomical models with routine H&E biopsy sections, immunohistochemistry, and ultrastructural electron microscopy forms the cornerstone of diagnostic surgical pathology.

parts.bld: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
parts.nrv: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
parts.d: Flattened cell head contains compact haploid paternal DNA and an anterior cap; the picture is enlarged, not to biological scale.
parts.f: Delivers genetic material at fertilization.
parts.c: Shape alone on this teaching image cannot establish fertility.

parts.reg: Spermatozoa mature from seminiferous tubules through the epididymis
parts.bld: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries

faqs.q: How many chambers does the heart have?
faqs.a: The heart has two upper receiving chambers, the right and left atria, and two lower pumping chambers, the right and left ventricles. The right ventricle sends blood to the lungs; the left sends it to the body. The pulmonary trunk (Truncus pulmonalis) leaves the right ventricle and divides into right and left pulmonary arteries. Uniquely, it carries deoxygenated blood. Physiologically, the pulmonary trunk carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation.

faqs.q: What route does blood take through the heart?
faqs.a: Blood returns from the body to the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, then crosses the pulmonary valve to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium, passes the mitral valve to the left ventricle and leaves through the aortic valve. The left atrium (Atrium sinistrum) is the most posterior chamber, receiving the four pulmonary veins. Physiologically, the left atrium passes oxygenated blood to the left ventricle through the mitral valve.

faqs.q: Why is the left ventricular wall thicker?
faqs.a: The left ventricle must generate greater pressure to move blood through the systemic circulation. Its myocardium is therefore thicker than that of the right ventricle, which pumps into the lower-pressure pulmonary circulation. The right ventricle (Ventriculus dexter) is crescent-shaped chamber with a thinner wall than the left, lined by trabeculae carneae and containing the moderator band. Physiologically, the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.

faqs.q: Do coronary arteries carry blood through the heart chambers?
faqs.a: No. Coronary arteries branch near the aortic root and supply the heart muscle itself. The blood passing through the chambers does not directly nourish the full thickness of the myocardium. Structurally, the coronary arteries (Arteriae coronariae) comprises right and left coronary arteries arising from the aortic sinuses. The left divides into the anterior interventricular (LAD) and circumflex branches. Physiologically, the coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself — the heart fills during diastole but perfuses itself only then.

faqs.q: How do heart valves keep blood moving forward?
faqs.a: Tricuspid and mitral valves guard the atrioventricular openings; pulmonary and aortic valves guard ventricular outflow. They open and close in response to pressure changes, limiting backward flow rather than actively pumping blood. The myocardium is the thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of branching, interlinked cardiac muscle fibres joined by intercalated discs. Physiologically, the myocardium contracts to generate the pressure that ejects blood.

faqs.q: What are the lobes of the right and left lungs?
faqs.a: The right lung usually has superior, middle and inferior lobes; the left has superior and inferior lobes with a cardiac notch. Fissures divide the lobes, though normal anatomy can vary. Physiologically, the right lung — three lobes governs gas exchange across ~150 million alveoli. Clinically, regarding the right lung — three lobes, the right middle lobe is prone to collapse (middle-lobe syndrome) because its bronchus is narrow and surrounded by nodes.

faqs.q: Where does air go after the bronchi?
faqs.a: Air passes from progressively smaller bronchi to bronchioles, then through the respiratory zone toward alveoli. Exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide occurs across the very thin alveolar–capillary barrier. The alveoli & capillary bed (Alveoli pulmonis) is thin-walled sacs of type I pneumocytes wrapped in capillaries; type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant and alveolar macrophages patrol the surface. Together they present ~70 m² of membrane only 0.5 µm thick. Physiologically, the alveoli & capillary bed governs diffusion of O₂ into blood and CO₂ out of it.

faqs.q: What is a Type I pneumocyte?
faqs.a: A Type I pneumocyte is a very thin squamous cell forming much of the alveolar gas-exchange surface. It can be recognized on the separate microscopic-scale teaching illustration, not on the whole-lung image. Structurally, the type I pneumocyte (Pneumocytus typus I) comprises very thin squamous alveolar epithelial cell covering most alveolar surface. Physiologically, the type I pneumocyte governs minimizes gas diffusion distance.

faqs.q: What does a Type II pneumocyte do?
faqs.a: A Type II pneumocyte is a plumper alveolar cell that secretes pulmonary surfactant, which helps reduce surface tension. It also contributes to maintenance and repair of the alveolar lining. Structurally, the type II pneumocyte (Pneumocytus typus II) comprises cuboidal cell with lamellar bodies, commonly at alveolar corners. Physiologically, the type II pneumocyte secretes surfactant and contributes to epithelial renewal.

faqs.q: Is the enlarged alveolar image an actual microscope slide?
faqs.a: No. It is a digital educational illustration that shows the thin Type I lining next to a plumper Type II cell. It is not histology or a literal magnification of the macroscopic lung image. Structurally, the bronchioles (Bronchioli) comprises airways under 1 mm with no cartilage and relatively more smooth muscle, ending in terminal then respiratory bronchioles. Physiologically, the bronchioles regulate airflow resistance and deliver air to the alveolar ducts.

faqs.q: What are the main parts of the brain?
faqs.a: The cerebrum supports complex thought, sensation and voluntary movement; the cerebellum coordinates movement; and the brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord and helps regulate essential functions. The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain: two hemispheres of folded cortex over deep white matter, basal ganglia and the lateral ventricles. Physiologically, the cerebrum governs voluntary movement, sensation, language, memory, personality and conscious thought.

faqs.q: What protects the brain inside the skull?
faqs.a: The skull, three meningeal layers and cerebrospinal fluid provide physical protection. Blood vessels supply its metabolically active tissue. The corpus callosum is the great C-shaped commissure of ~200 million myelinated fibres: rostrum, genu, body and splenium. Physiologically, the corpus callosum connects matching regions of the two hemispheres so they work as one brain.

faqs.q: What is the frontal lobe?
faqs.a: Anterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. Contains the primary motor cortex, Broca's area (usually left) and the prefrontal cortex. Functionally, it governs planning, judgement, personality, voluntary movement and expressive speech. In clinical pathology involving the frontal lobe, prefrontal damage (classically Phineas Gage) changes personality and impulse control while sparing memory and IQ.

faqs.q: Where is the thalamus located?
faqs.a: Two ovals of grey matter flanking the third ventricle, subdivided into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups.
