Functionally, it serves as the relay station: nearly all sensory information (except smell) is edited and sent on to the cortex. Also involved in arousal. Medical evaluation of the thalamus also notes that a thalamic stroke can produce severe contralateral sensory loss and thalamic pain syndrome.

faqs.q: What is the function of the cerebellum?
faqs.a: Functionally, it compares intended movement with actual movement and corrects it: coordination, precision, timing, posture and motor learning. Two hemispheres and a midline vermis, with a densely folded cortex, deep nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial) and branching white matter — the arbor vitae. Clinically, regarding the cerebellum, damage causes ipsilateral ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia and a broad-based gait. Alcohol affects it first.

faqs.q: What do the kidneys do?
faqs.a: Kidneys filter blood, return most water and useful solutes to circulation, and excrete wastes in urine. They also help regulate electrolytes, blood pressure and acid-base balance. The glomerulus & Bowman's capsule (Corpusculum renale) is a tuft of fenestrated capillaries invaginating a double-walled capsule. Between them, the filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, fused basement membrane and podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms. Physiologically, the glomerulus & Bowman's capsule governs ultrafiltration of plasma — water and small solutes pass; cells and proteins do not.

faqs.q: How does urine travel from the kidney to the bladder?
faqs.a: Filtrate passes through nephron tubules into collecting ducts, then through calyces and the renal pelvis. A ureter carries the resulting urine to the bladder. The renal pyramid (Pyramides renales) is 8–18 cone-shaped regions of medulla, striped by the straight loops of Henle, vasa recta and collecting ducts that run through them. Physiologically, the renal pyramid governs create and exploit the osmotic gradient that concentrates urine.

faqs.q: What is the renal cortex?
faqs.a: The outer 1 cm, containing all the renal corpuscles, the proximal and distal convoluted tubules, and cortical tissue dipping between pyramids as the renal columns. Functionally, it governs site of blood filtration and most solute reabsorption. In clinical pathology involving the renal cortex, thinning or scarring of the cortex on ultrasound indicates chronic kidney disease.

faqs.q: Where is the glomerulus & Bowman's capsule located?
faqs.a: A tuft of fenestrated capillaries invaginating a double-walled capsule. Between them, the filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, fused basement membrane and podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms. Functionally, it governs ultrafiltration of plasma — water and small solutes pass; cells and proteins do not. Structurally, the glomerular capillaries (Glomerulus) comprises fenestrated capillary loops between afferent and efferent arterioles. Physiologically, the glomerular capillaries pass plasma water and small solutes toward Bowman space.

faqs.q: What is the function of the loop of Henle?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs countercurrent multiplication builds the medullary osmotic gradient that allows urine to be concentrated. A hairpin with a thin descending limb (water-permeable) and a thick ascending limb (actively pumps out NaCl but is water-impermeable), dipping into the medulla. Clinically, regarding the loop of Henle, loop diuretics such as furosemide block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter here and are the most powerful diuretics.

faqs.q: What are the main functions of the liver?
faqs.a: The liver processes nutrients, makes bile and many blood proteins, stores glycogen and participates in drug and toxin metabolism. Its blood arrives from both the portal vein and hepatic artery. Structurally, the hepatic lobule & sinusoids (Lobulus hepaticus) comprises hexagonal units ~1 mm across: plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, separated by sinusoids lined with endothelium and Kupffer macrophages; portal triads (artery, vein, bile duct) sit at the corners. Physiologically, the hepatic lobule & sinusoids governs blood flows from triad to central vein while bile flows the opposite way, from canaliculi to the triad bile duct.

faqs.q: Where is the liver located?
faqs.a: Most of the liver lies beneath the diaphragm in the right upper abdomen, with a smaller part extending across the midline. Structurally, the left lobe (Lobus sinister) comprises thinner and flatter, lying in the epigastrium and reaching across to the left. Separated from the right lobe on the diaphragmatic surface by the falciform ligament. Physiologically, the left lobe supplies the left half of the functional liver.

faqs.q: What is the gallbladder?
faqs.a: A 7–10 cm pear-shaped sac on the visceral surface of the right lobe, with fundus, body and neck. Its wall concentrates bile up to tenfold. Functionally, it stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum when fat arrives (CCK-mediated). In clinical pathology involving the gallbladder, gallstones (cholelithiasis) cause biliary colic; a stone impacted in the neck gives acute cholecystitis with Murphy's sign.

faqs.q: Where is the hepatic portal vein located?
faqs.a: Formed behind the pancreatic neck by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins; carries nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood from gut, spleen and pancreas. Functionally, it delivers 75% of hepatic blood and everything absorbed from the gut for first-pass processing. Medical evaluation of the hepatic portal vein also notes that portal hypertension (cirrhosis) causes oesophageal varices, splenomegaly and ascites.

faqs.q: What is the function of the hepatic lobule & sinusoids?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs blood flows from triad to central vein while bile flows the opposite way, from canaliculi to the triad bile duct. Hexagonal units ~1 mm across: plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, separated by sinusoids lined with endothelium and Kupffer macrophages; portal triads (artery, vein, bile duct) sit at the corners. Structurally, the hepatic sinusoid (Sinusoideum hepaticum) comprises wide, discontinuous capillary channel between plates of hepatocytes. Physiologically, the hepatic sinusoid allows blood–hepatocyte exchange en route to central vein.

faqs.q: What happens to food in the stomach and intestines?
faqs.a: The stomach stores and mixes food with acid and enzymes. The small intestine completes much digestion and absorbs nutrients; the large intestine absorbs water and forms stool. The body of stomach (Corpus ventriculi) is the main reservoir between fundus and antrum, lined by acid- and pepsin-secreting mucosa with rugae. Clinically, regarding the body of stomach, loss of parietal cells (autoimmune gastritis) causes pernicious anaemia through B12 malabsorption.

faqs.q: How long is the route through the digestive tract?
faqs.a: Food moves from oesophagus to stomach, small intestine and large intestine before leaving through the rectum and anal canal. Length varies between people and measurement methods. The oesophagus is a 25 cm muscular tube from pharynx to stomach, passing through the diaphragm at T10. Physiologically, the oesophagus propels the bolus by peristalsis; the lower sphincter prevents reflux.

faqs.q: What is the oesophagus?
faqs.a: A 25 cm muscular tube from pharynx to stomach, passing through the diaphragm at T10. Functionally, it propels the bolus by peristalsis; the lower sphincter prevents reflux. The fundus of stomach (Fundus ventriculi) is the dome above the oesophageal opening, usually filled with a gas bubble on erect films. Physiologically, the fundus of stomach stores swallowed air and gives the stomach its reservoir.

faqs.q: Where is the body of stomach located?
faqs.a: The main reservoir between fundus and antrum, lined by acid- and pepsin-secreting mucosa with rugae. Functionally, it mixes food with acid and pepsin; intrinsic factor for B12 absorption is made here. The pyloric antrum & pylorus (Antrum pyloricum) is the distal funnel ending in the thick pyloric sphincter. Physiologically, the pyloric antrum & pylorus governs grinds food and meters chyme into the duodenum; G cells here secrete gastrin.

faqs.q: What is the function of the rugae?
faqs.a: Functionally, it allow expansion and channel the flow of chyme. Longitudinal folds of gastric mucosa that flatten as the stomach distends. Clinically, regarding the rugae, thickened rugae (Ménétrier disease) cause protein-losing gastropathy.

faqs.q: How does the eye focus light on the retina?
faqs.a: The cornea provides much of the eye's focusing power, while the lens changes shape for near and far vision. Light is converted into neural signals by retinal photoreceptors. Structurally, the cornea comprises transparent, avascular, five-layered dome at the front of the eye. Provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power. Physiologically, the cornea bends and transmits light; its endothelium pumps water out to stay clear.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the retina and the optic nerve?
faqs.a: The retina is the light-sensitive neural tissue lining the back of the eye. Its ganglion-cell axons bundle together to form the optic nerve. The retina is ten-layered neural film: photoreceptors outermost (light must pass through the inner layers first), then bipolar and ganglion cells. Physiologically, the retina transduces light into nerve impulses.

faqs.q: What is the cornea?
faqs.a: Transparent, avascular, five-layered dome at the front of the eye. Provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power. Functionally, it bends and transmits light; its endothelium pumps water out to stay clear. The iris is the coloured diaphragm of smooth muscle (sphincter and dilator pupillae) in front of the lens. Physiologically, the iris controls pupil diameter and therefore light entry and depth of focus.

faqs.q: Where is the retina located?
faqs.a: Ten-layered neural film: photoreceptors outermost (light must pass through the inner layers first), then bipolar and ganglion cells. Functionally, it transduces light into nerve impulses. Structurally, the optic disc (Discus opticus) comprises where ganglion axons and the central retinal vessels pierce the sclera. It has no photoreceptors. Physiologically, the optic disc governs exit point of the optic nerve and entry of the central retinal artery.

faqs.q: What is the function of the macula & fovea?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs high-acuity central vision for reading and faces. A 5.5 mm yellow-pigmented area at the posterior pole; its centre, the fovea, contains cones only and no vessels. Clinically, regarding the macula & fovea, age-related macular degeneration destroys the fovea and central vision while sparing peripheral sight.

faqs.q: How do the outer, middle and inner ear work together?
faqs.a: The outer ear collects sound, the eardrum and three middle-ear bones transmit vibration, and the cochlea in the inner ear converts movement into nerve signals. The external acoustic meatus (Meatus acusticus externus) is a 2.5 cm S-shaped canal, cartilaginous outer third and bony inner two-thirds, lined by skin with ceruminous glands. Physiologically, the external acoustic meatus conducts sound to the eardrum; cerumen traps dust and insects.

faqs.q: Which part of the ear helps with balance?
faqs.a: The vestibular organs of the inner ear, including the semicircular canals and otolith organs, detect head rotation and linear movement. The vestibule (utricle & saccule) (Vestibulum) is two otolith organs whose hair cells carry crystals of calcium carbonate. Physiologically, the vestibule (utricle & saccule) governs sense linear acceleration and head tilt — gravity sensing.

faqs.q: What is the tympanic membrane?
faqs.a: A 9 × 10 mm cone of three layers, tilted so its umbo points medially; pars tensa below, pars flaccida above. Functionally, it converts sound pressure into mechanical vibration of the malleus. In clinical pathology involving the tympanic membrane, a red bulging drum means otitis media; a pearly white mass behind it suggests cholesteatoma.

faqs.q: Where is the stapes located?
faqs.a: The stirrup: the smallest bone in the body (~3 mm), its footplate closing the oval window. Functionally, it delivers amplified vibration into the cochlear fluid.

faqs.q: What is the function of the vestibule (utricle & saccule)?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs sense linear acceleration and head tilt — gravity sensing. Two otolith organs whose hair cells carry crystals of calcium carbonate. Structurally, the macula of utricle comprises otolith-bearing sensory patch in utricle oriented mainly for horizontal acceleration. Physiologically, the macula of utricle detects linear head acceleration and gravity component.

faqs.q: What does the pancreas do?
faqs.a: Its exocrine tissue releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine. Endocrine islets release hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the blood. Structurally, the islets of Langerhans (Insulae pancreaticae) comprises 1–1.5 million microscopic clusters of alpha (glucagon), beta (insulin, amylin), delta (somatostatin) and PP cells, richly capillarised. Physiologically, the islets of Langerhans governs minute-to-minute control of blood glucose, plus intermediary metabolism.

faqs.q: Where is the pancreas located?
faqs.a: It lies behind the stomach across the upper abdomen. Its head sits near the duodenum, while its tail reaches toward the spleen. The head (Caput pancreatis) is the broad end nestled in the C-loop of the duodenum, with the uncinate process hooking behind the superior mesenteric vessels. Physiologically, the head houses much of the exocrine tissue and the terminal duct.

faqs.q: Where is the head of the pancreas?
faqs.a: The broad end nestled in the C-loop of the duodenum, with the uncinate process hooking behind the superior mesenteric vessels. Functionally, it houses much of the exocrine tissue and the terminal duct. Structurally, the uncinate process comprises hook-shaped pancreatic head extension passing posterior to superior mesenteric vessels. Physiologically, the uncinate process governs completes deep head contour around the mesenteric root.

faqs.q: Where is the main pancreatic duct located?
faqs.a: Runs the length of the gland from tail to head, joining the common bile duct at the ampulla in the second part of duodenum. Functionally, it delivers ~1.5 L of enzyme- and bicarbonate-rich juice daily. Medical evaluation of the main pancreatic duct also notes that a "double duct sign" (dilated pancreatic and bile ducts) on imaging suggests a head tumour.

faqs.q: What is the function of the acinar cells & ductules?
faqs.a: Functionally, it secrete the pro-enzymes for digesting protein, fat and carbohydrate. Grape-like clusters of enzyme-packed cells draining into centroacinar cells and ductules. Clinically, regarding the acinar cells & ductules, premature activation of trypsin inside acinar cells is the initiating event of acute pancreatitis.

faqs.q: What is the spleen's function?
faqs.a: The spleen filters blood, removes aging red blood cells and helps immune cells respond to blood-borne material. Its red and white pulp perform different tasks. Structurally, the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath comprises t-cell-rich white-pulp cylinder surrounding a central arteriole. Physiologically, the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath governs samples blood-borne antigens with nearby immune cells.

faqs.q: Can you feel a normal spleen?
faqs.a: A normal adult spleen is usually protected beneath the left lower ribs and is not readily felt on examination; enlargement is a medical finding, not something this atlas can diagnose. The splenic vein (Vena lienalis) drains the spleen and joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein. Physiologically, the splenic vein returns filtered blood to the portal system.

faqs.q: What is the capsule & trabeculae?
faqs.a: A fibroelastic capsule sending trabeculae into the pulp, carrying the vessels. Functionally, it governs structural framework and conduit for vessels. In clinical pathology involving the capsule & trabeculae, the capsule is thin and the pulp fragile — the spleen tears easily in blunt abdominal trauma and bleeds briskly.

faqs.q: Where is the white pulp located?
faqs.a: Periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (T cells), follicles (B cells) and a marginal zone rich in macrophages. Functionally, it governs immune surveillance of blood: antibody and opsonin production, especially against capsules. Medical evaluation of the white pulp also notes that its loss explains why asplenic patients are vulnerable to pneumococcus, meningococcus and H. influenzae.

faqs.q: What is the function of the hilum?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs vascular gateway; also the site of accessory spleens in ~15% of people. The notched medial border where splenic vessels enter and the tail of pancreas and stomach fundus relate. Clinically, regarding the hilum, a missed accessory spleen can cause relapse of disease after splenectomy for ITP.

faqs.q: Where is the thyroid gland located?
faqs.a: The thyroid has two lateral lobes joined by an isthmus in the front of the neck, close to the larynx and upper trachea. The berry ligament is dense posteromedial attachment of thyroid to cricoid and upper trachea. Physiologically, the berry ligament anchors gland during swallowing.

faqs.q: What do thyroid follicles make?
faqs.a: Follicular cells use iodine and stored thyroglobulin in colloid to produce thyroid hormones. Nearby parafollicular cells produce calcitonin. Structurally, the follicle & colloid (Folliculi thyroidei) comprises spheres of follicular cells enclosing colloid (iodinated thyroglobulin). TSH stimulates iodide trapping, organification, coupling, and endocytosis of colloid to release T3/T4. Physiologically, the follicle & colloid governs synthesis and storage of thyroid hormone — the only endocrine gland that stores its product extracellularly.

faqs.q: What is the isthmus?
faqs.a: The bridge crossing the 2nd–4th tracheal rings, joining the two lobes. Functionally, it connects the lobes into a single gland. In clinical pathology involving the isthmus, it is the landmark for emergency tracheostomy and cricothyroidotomy is performed above it.

faqs.q: Where is the trachea & larynx located?
faqs.a: The gland wraps the airway; the cricoid cartilage and thyroid cartilage lie above. Functionally, it governs anatomical landmark and the reason goitres cause compressive symptoms. Medical evaluation of the trachea & larynx also notes that retrosternal extension of a goitre can be read on CT and may require sternotomy to remove.

faqs.q: What is the function of the follicle & colloid?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs synthesis and storage of thyroid hormone — the only endocrine gland that stores its product extracellularly. Spheres of follicular cells enclosing colloid (iodinated thyroglobulin). TSH stimulates iodide trapping, organification, coupling, and endocytosis of colloid to release T3/T4. Structurally, the thyroglobulin-rich colloid comprises extracellular storage material in follicular lumen. Physiologically, the thyroglobulin-rich colloid stores iodinated precursor for thyroid hormones.

faqs.q: How does the urinary bladder store and release urine?
faqs.a: A stretchable urothelial lining and detrusor muscle allow filling. During urination, coordinated detrusor contraction and sphincter relaxation empty the bladder. The detrusor muscle (Musculus detrusor) is three layers of interlacing smooth muscle with the wall thickened into trabeculae when obstructed. Physiologically, the detrusor muscle governs contraction empties the bladder; relaxation allows storage at low pressure.

faqs.q: What is the trigone of the bladder?
faqs.a: The trigone is a triangular region on the internal bladder floor between the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral opening. The trigone (Trigonum vesicae) is the smooth triangle bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; mucosa firmly bound to muscle. Physiologically, the trigone governs funnel for emptying; its stretch receptors trigger the micturition reflex.

faqs.q: What is the detrusor muscle?
faqs.a: Three layers of interlacing smooth muscle with the wall thickened into trabeculae when obstructed. Functionally, it governs contraction empties the bladder; relaxation allows storage at low pressure. The internal & external sphincters (Sphincteres urethrae) is the internal sphincter is smooth muscle of the bladder neck (sympathetic); the external is skeletal muscle in the urogenital diaphragm (pudendal, voluntary). Physiologically, the internal & external sphincters governs maintain continence; the external sphincter is under conscious control.

faqs.q: Where is the urothelium located?
faqs.a: Stratified transitional epithelium with umbrella cells whose plaques make it impermeable to urine. Functionally, it serves as a stretch-tolerant, urine-proof lining. Medical evaluation of the urothelium also notes that its instability to carcinogens (smoking, aniline dyes) makes transitional-cell carcinoma the classic bladder cancer.

faqs.q: What is the function of the trigone?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs funnel for emptying; its stretch receptors trigger the micturition reflex. The smooth triangle bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; mucosa firmly bound to muscle. The internal urethral orifice (Ostium urethrae internum) is the inferior angle of the trigone where the bladder neck meets the urethra. Physiologically, the internal urethral orifice governs outlet guarded by the internal sphincter.

faqs.q: What are the main layers of the skin?
faqs.a: The epidermis is the outer epithelial barrier; the vascular dermis contains connective tissue, vessels and nerves. Subcutaneous tissue lies beneath the skin and varies by region. Structurally, the hypodermis (subcutis) (Tela subcutanea) comprises loose connective tissue and fat, with larger vessels and nerves and, in places, panniculus carnosus. Physiologically, the hypodermis (subcutis) governs insulation, energy store, shock absorption and skin mobility.

faqs.q: How does skin help protect the body?
faqs.a: The keratinized epidermal surface limits water loss and helps block external injury and microbes, while deeper tissue supports sensation, repair and temperature regulation. Structurally, the stratum granulosum comprises flattened keratinocytes with keratohyalin granules and lipid-releasing lamellar bodies. Physiologically, the stratum granulosum governs builds the water-permeability barrier.

faqs.q: What is the stratum corneum?
faqs.a: 15–20 layers of dead, flattened, keratin-filled corneocytes held by lipids — the "brick and mortar" barrier. Functionally, it governs waterproofing and the main barrier to microbes and chemicals. In clinical pathology involving the stratum corneum, its thickness defines palms and soles; loss in burns allows catastrophic fluid and heat loss.

faqs.q: Where is the dermis (papillary & reticular) located?
faqs.a: Papillary layer of loose connective tissue forming dermal papillae; reticular layer of dense irregular collagen and elastin. Functionally, it governs strength, elasticity, sensation and the vascular supply of the epidermis. Clinically, the dermis (papillary & reticular) split-thickness grafts take from the dermal remnants left in the wound bed; keloids are dermal over-scarring.

faqs.q: What is the function of the hair shaft & follicle?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs protection, sensation and (in other mammals) insulation. A keratinised shaft growing from a follicle that dips into dermis or fat, with a bulb around a dermal papilla and a bulge of stem cells. Clinically, regarding the hair shaft & follicle, follicular stem cells re-epithelialise partial-thickness wounds; follicles are the target of alopecias.

faqs.q: Where does the spinal cord end in adults?
faqs.a: The spinal cord usually tapers to the conus medullaris near the L1-L2 vertebral level in adults; nerve roots continue below it as the cauda equina. Structurally, the conus medullaris comprises tapered end of adult spinal cord, usually near L1–L2 vertebral level. Physiologically, the conus medullaris contains terminal sacral cord segments.

faqs.q: What is the difference between gray and white matter in the spinal cord?
faqs.a: Central gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies and local circuits; surrounding white matter carries ascending sensory and descending motor pathways. Structurally, the dorsal root & ganglion (Radix dorsalis) comprises sensory rootlets converging on the oval dorsal root ganglion of pseudo-unipolar cell bodies. Physiologically, the dorsal root & ganglion carries all afferent input from one dermatome.

faqs.q: What is the posterior (dorsal) horn?
faqs.a: The slender upper horns receiving sensory afferents; laminae I–VI including the substantia gelatinosa. Functionally, it governs first synapse for pain, temperature and touch; gate control of nociception happens here. In clinical pathology involving the posterior (dorsal) horn, loss of the spinothalamic decussation at a segment causes a segmental band of lost pain and temperature (syringomyelia).

faqs.q: Where is the lateral horn located?
faqs.a: Present only in T1–L2, holding preganglionic sympathetic neurons (and S2–S4 parasympathetic equivalents). Functionally, it governs origin of the sympathetic outflow. Medical evaluation of the lateral horn also notes that horner syndrome follows interruption of the T1 lateral horn or its pathway (e.g. Pancoast tumour).

faqs.q: What is the function of the white funiculi & tracts?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs highways for sensation upward and motor commands downward. Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis & cuneatus), lateral spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts. Clinically, regarding the white funiculi & tracts, b12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) damages dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts together.

faqs.q: How is sperm produced and transported?
faqs.a: Sperm develop in seminiferous tubules of the testes, mature in the epididymis and pass through the vas deferens and ejaculatory ducts into the urethra. The vas deferens (Ductus deferens) is a thick-walled 45 cm muscular duct from the epididymal tail, through the inguinal canal into the pelvis. Physiologically, the vas deferens propels sperm by powerful peristalsis at emission.

faqs.q: What do the prostate and seminal vesicles contribute?
faqs.a: The seminal vesicles and prostate add fluids to semen. Their ducts join the sperm outflow route near the prostate before ejaculation. The seminal vesicle (Vesicula seminalis) is a coiled sac behind the bladder whose duct joins the vas to form the ejaculatory duct. Physiologically, the seminal vesicle governs adds ~60% of semen volume: fructose, prostaglandins and clotting proteins.

faqs.q: What is the testis & seminiferous tubules?
faqs.a: 250–300 lobules of coiled seminiferous tubules (total ~250 m) with Sertoli cells and developing germ cells, wrapped in tunica albuginea. Functionally, it governs spermatogenesis and testosterone production. In clinical pathology involving the testis & seminiferous tubules, undescended testis (cryptorchidism) raises infertility and germ-cell tumour risk; torsion is a 6-hour surgical emergency.

faqs.q: Where is the vas deferens located?
faqs.a: A thick-walled 45 cm muscular duct from the epididymal tail, through the inguinal canal into the pelvis. Functionally, it propels sperm by powerful peristalsis at emission. The epididymis is a 6 m coiled duct (head, body, tail) applied to the posterior border of the testis. Physiologically, the epididymis governs sperm maturation, motility acquisition and storage (up to weeks).

faqs.q: What is the function of the prostate?
faqs.a: Functionally, it secretes citrate, zinc and PSA that liquefy the seminal coagulum. A walnut-sized fibromuscular gland around the urethra below the bladder, with peripheral, central and transition zones. Clinically, regarding the prostate, benign hyperplasia of the transition zone obstructs voiding; most cancers arise in the peripheral zone (felt on DRE).

faqs.q: What organs are included in the female reproductive system?
faqs.a: The system includes ovaries, uterine tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina and external genital structures. Each has distinct roles in cycles, reproduction and pelvic support. Structurally, the broad & suspensory ligaments (Ligamentum latum) comprises peritoneal folds (broad, round, ovarian, suspensory) carrying the tubes, vessels and ureters. Physiologically, the broad & suspensory ligaments governs suspend the uterus and convey its vessels.

faqs.q: Where does fertilization usually occur?
faqs.a: Fertilization most often occurs in the ampulla of a uterine tube. The resulting early embryo travels toward the uterine cavity. The uterine tube (Tuba uterina) is a 10 cm ciliated duct with interstitial, isthmic, ampullary and infundibular parts. Physiologically, the uterine tube governs captures the oocyte, is the site of fertilisation (ampulla) and transports the embryo by ciliary beat and peristalsis.

faqs.q: What is the fundus & body?
faqs.a: The domed fundus above the tubal openings and the tapering body, of smooth muscle (myometrium) lined by endometrium. Functionally, it houses and nourishes a pregnancy; the myometrium generates labour. In clinical pathology involving the fundus & body, fibroids (leiomyomas) arise in the myometrium and cause heavy bleeding and pressure symptoms.

faqs.q: Where is the cervix located?
faqs.a: The fibrous neck projecting into the vagina, with an endocervical canal of mucus-secreting columnar epithelium and a squamous ectocervix. Functionally, it keeps pregnancy in and microbes out; dilates 10 cm in labour. Medical evaluation of the cervix also notes that the squamocolumnar junction is where cervical cancer begins — the target of smear tests and HPV vaccination.

faqs.q: What is the function of the uterine tube?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs captures the oocyte, is the site of fertilisation (ampulla) and transports the embryo by ciliary beat and peristalsis. A 10 cm ciliated duct with interstitial, isthmic, ampullary and infundibular parts. The uterine cornua (Cornua uteri) is upper lateral junctions where uterine tubes enter. Physiologically, the uterine cornua governs communicate with intramural tube segments.

faqs.q: Where are the main organs in the male body?
faqs.a: The brain is in the skull; lungs and heart occupy the chest; liver, stomach, intestines and kidneys occupy the abdomen; and pelvic organs include bladder and reproductive structures. The lungs (Pulmones) is paired thoracic organs flanking the heart. Physiologically, the lungs governs gas exchange across ~300 million alveoli.

faqs.q: Does a male body map show every deep structure?
faqs.a: No. The overview is an orientation map; its chapter links provide deeper tissue, vascular, skeletal and nerve details not separately visible on one full-body plate. Structurally, the penis comprises external organ of urination and copulation. Physiologically, the penis governs erectile tissue engorges; delivers semen.

faqs.q: Where is the brain shown on the male body map?
faqs.a: Control centre housed in the skull, glowing through the translucent scalp. Functionally, it integrates sensation, movement, thought, memory and autonomic drive. In clinical pathology involving the brain, stroke risk rises with age — remember FAST: face, arms, speech, time.

faqs.q: Where are the lungs in the male body map?
faqs.a: Paired thoracic organs flanking the heart. Functionally, it governs gas exchange across ~300 million alveoli. The kidneys is paired retroperitoneal organs on either side of the upper lumbar spine. Physiologically, the kidneys filter plasma and regulate fluid, electrolytes and blood pressure.

faqs.q: What does the liver do in the male body?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs metabolism, detoxification, bile, plasma proteins. Largest internal organ, right upper quadrant. Clinically, regarding the liver, cirrhosis scars the parenchyma (alcohol, hepatitis).

faqs.q: Where are the main organs in the female body?
faqs.a: The brain lies in the skull; lungs and heart in the chest; digestive and urinary organs in the abdomen; and uterus, tubes and ovaries in the pelvis. The lungs (Pulmones) is paired thoracic organs flanking the heart. Physiologically, the lungs governs gas exchange across ~300 million alveoli.

faqs.q: Does a female body map show every deep structure?
faqs.a: No. It is a regional orientation view. Detailed chapters explain deeper pelvic supports, breast tissue, nerves and microscopic layers that a single image cannot resolve. Structurally, the adrenal glands comprises endocrine glands positioned on the superior aspects of the kidneys. Physiologically, the adrenal glands governs release corticosteroids and catecholamines.

faqs.q: Where is the brain shown on the female body map?
faqs.a: Control centre housed in the skull, glowing through the translucent scalp. Functionally, it integrates sensation, movement, thought, memory and autonomic drive. In clinical pathology involving the brain, stroke risk rises with age — remember FAST: face, arms, speech, time.

faqs.q: Where are the lungs in the female body map?
faqs.a: Paired thoracic organs flanking the heart. Functionally, it governs gas exchange across ~300 million alveoli. The kidneys is paired retroperitoneal organs beside the upper lumbar spine. Physiologically, the kidneys filter plasma and regulate fluid, electrolytes and blood pressure.

faqs.q: What does the liver do in the female body?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs metabolism, detoxification, bile, plasma proteins. Largest internal organ, right upper quadrant. Clinically, regarding the liver, cirrhosis scars the parenchyma (alcohol, hepatitis).

faqs.q: What are the main divisions of the nervous system?
faqs.a: The central nervous system consists of brain and spinal cord. Peripheral nerves and ganglia connect it to the rest of the body; autonomic circuits regulate many involuntary functions. Structurally, the spinal cord (Medulla spinalis) comprises 31-segment cord from foramen magnum to L1–L2. Physiologically, the spinal cord governs two-way tracts plus segmental reflex circuits.

faqs.q: How do nerves carry information between the body and brain?
faqs.a: Sensory pathways bring information toward the central nervous system, and motor pathways send commands outward. Spinal and cranial nerves also support reflexes and organ control. Structurally, the brain (Encephalon) comprises cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem inside the cranial vault. Physiologically, the brain governs integration, consciousness, motor planning and autonomic control.

faqs.q: What is the brain?
faqs.a: Cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem inside the cranial vault. Functionally, it governs integration, consciousness, motor planning and autonomic control. Structurally, the cerebellum comprises hindbrain structure behind the brainstem. Physiologically, the cerebellum governs coordination, balance and motor learning.

faqs.q: Where is the brainstem located?
faqs.a: Midbrain, pons and medulla connecting cord to brain. Functionally, it governs vital centres: respiration, heart rate, consciousness. Medical evaluation of the brainstem also notes that brainstem death is legal death in most jurisdictions.

faqs.q: What is the function of the cervical plexus?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs neck muscles and skin; phrenic nerve to diaphragm. Nerve network in the posterior triangle of the neck. Clinically, regarding the cervical plexus, c3-4-5 keeps the diaphragm alive — injury above C4 stops breathing.

faqs.q: Is the male nervous system built differently from the female nervous system?
faqs.a: The main brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerve plan is shared. A male-focused pelvic view highlights branches serving the prostate, penis and scrotum rather than implying separate male brain or spinal pathways. The pudendal nerve is paired somatic S2–S4 nerve passes through the pudendal canal toward the perineum. Physiologically, the pudendal nerve supplies external genital and perineal sensation plus motor branches to sphincters.

faqs.q: Which nerves contribute to penile erection?
faqs.a: Autonomic cavernous nerves arising from the prostatic plexus influence penile smooth muscle and blood flow. Somatic sensation from the penis is carried largely through the dorsal nerve of the penis, a pudendal branch. The cavernous nerves of penis is small autonomic branches run from the prostatic plexus toward penile erectile tissue. Physiologically, the cavernous nerves of penis regulate erectile smooth muscle and arterial inflow.

faqs.q: What is the pudendal nerve in the male pelvis?
faqs.a: The pudendal nerve derives from sacral segments S2–S4 and supplies much of the perineum. Its branches include the inferior rectal, perineal and dorsal penile nerves; these are distinct from pelvic autonomic nerves. Structurally, the pelvic splanchnic nerves comprises parasympathetic fibers from sacral levels S2–S4 travel to pelvic autonomic plexuses. Physiologically, the pelvic splanchnic nerves governs reach bladder, rectal and reproductive pelvic organ targets.

faqs.q: How do pelvic splanchnic nerves differ from hypogastric nerves?
faqs.a: Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry sacral parasympathetic fibers from S2–S4 into pelvic plexuses. Hypogastric nerves convey predominantly sympathetic pathways from higher plexuses; both contribute to pelvic organ innervation. The inferior hypogastric plexus is paired networks on the lateral walls of the rectum combine sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers. Physiologically, the inferior hypogastric plexus governs distribute autonomic pathways to pelvic organs.

faqs.q: Can the full-body male nerve picture show individual cavernous nerves?
faqs.a: No. It is an orientation image for major nervous-system routes. Cavernous and prostatic plexus branches are described as unpinned study structures rather than falsely marked on a whole-body plate. Structurally, the prostatic plexus comprises autonomic branches of the inferior hypogastric plexus course along the prostate. Physiologically, the prostatic plexus governs distribute fibers to the prostate and continue toward penile erectile tissue.

faqs.q: Is the female nervous system built differently from the male nervous system?
faqs.a: The central and most peripheral pathways share the same basic organization. A female-focused pelvic view discusses branches serving the uterus, vagina, clitoris and vulva without implying a separate female brain or spinal cord. Structurally, the uterovaginal plexus comprises pelvic autonomic network associated with the cervix and upper vagina. Physiologically, the uterovaginal plexus distributes fibers toward the uterus, cervix and upper vagina.

faqs.q: What carries sensation from the clitoral glans?
faqs.a: The dorsal nerve of the clitoris, a terminal branch of the pudendal nerve, conveys much of the somatic sensation. Autonomic nerves influence erectile tissues but should not be confused with that sensory pathway. Structurally, the dorsal nerve of clitoris comprises terminal sensory branch of the pudendal nerve runs toward the clitoral glans. Physiologically, the dorsal nerve of clitoris governs conveys much of the clitoral somatic sensation.

faqs.q: Which nerves supply the vulva and lower vagina?
faqs.a: Pudendal branches supply much of the posterior vulva and lower vaginal region. The anterior labia also receive contributions from ilioinguinal and genitofemoral branches, so a single nerve label cannot cover the entire area. Structurally, the posterior labial nerves comprises cutaneous branches of the pudendal perineal nerve enter the posterior labial region. Physiologically, the posterior labial nerves supply sensation to posterior vulvar skin.

faqs.q: What is the uterovaginal plexus?
faqs.a: It is an autonomic network associated with the cervix and upper vagina that carries branches toward the uterus and upper vagina. It is anatomically distinct from the superficial pudendal branches of the perineum. The vaginal autonomic branches branches from the pelvic plexus reach the upper vaginal wall. Physiologically, the vaginal autonomic branches carry autonomic innervation and visceral sensory pathways.

faqs.q: Does the full-body female nerve plate identify tiny pelvic branches?
faqs.a: No. The full-body plate is for orientation to larger pathways. The pudendal nerve is paired somatic S2–S4 nerve passes through the pudendal canal toward the perineum. Physiologically, the pudendal nerve supplies external genital and perineal sensation plus motor branches to sphincters.

faqs.q: How many cranial nerves are there?
faqs.a: There are 12 paired cranial nerves, numbered I through XII. Their functions include smell, vision, eye movement, facial sensation, hearing, swallowing and tongue movement. Structurally, the internal acoustic meatus (Meatus acusticus internus) comprises temporal-bone canal shared by CN VII, CN VIII and labyrinthine artery. Physiologically, the internal acoustic meatus governs conveys nerve toward facial canal.

faqs.q: Which cranial nerve controls facial expression?
faqs.a: The facial nerve, cranial nerve VII, supplies most muscles of facial expression. The trigeminal nerve, cranial nerve V, carries most facial skin sensation. The v · Trigeminal nerve (N. trigeminus) is three divisions: ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular. Physiologically, the v · Trigeminal nerve governs face sensation + muscles of mastication.

faqs.q: What is the olfactory nerve (CN I)?
faqs.a: Sensory filaments from nasal epithelium to bulb. Functionally, it governs smell. In clinical pathology involving the i · Olfactory nerve, lesion: anosmia — test each nostril with coffee.

faqs.q: Where does the oculomotor nerve (CN III) originate?
faqs.a: Midbrain nerve to four eye muscles + lid + pupil. Functionally, it governs eye elevation/adduction, lid lift, pupil constriction. Medical evaluation of the III · Oculomotor nerve also notes that first sign of uncal herniation: a blown pupil.

faqs.q: What does the trigeminal nerve (CN V) do?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs face sensation + muscles of mastication. Three divisions: ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular. Structurally, the VII · Facial nerve (N. facialis) comprises motor to face, taste anterior 2/3, lacrimal/salivary. Physiologically, the VII · Facial nerve governs facial expression.

faqs.q: What is the difference between sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves?
faqs.a: Both are autonomic pathways. Sympathetic activity often prepares organs for exertion; parasympathetic pathways support many resting functions. Their effects depend on the organ and receptor. The inferior hypogastric plexus is paired pelvic autonomic networks lateral to rectum, bladder and reproductive organs. Physiologically, the inferior hypogastric plexus governs distribute sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers to pelvic organs.

faqs.q: Where are autonomic ganglia located?
faqs.a: Sympathetic ganglia lie in chains beside the spine or in prevertebral groups; many parasympathetic ganglia lie near or within their target organs. The sympathetic trunk (Truncus sympathicus) is paired chain from neck to sacrum beside vertebrae. Physiologically, the sympathetic trunk governs mass fight-or-flight discharge.

faqs.q: What is the sympathetic trunk?
faqs.a: Paired chain from neck to sacrum beside vertebrae. Functionally, it governs mass fight-or-flight discharge. Structurally, the adrenal medulla (Medulla glandulae suprarenalis) comprises modified sympathetic ganglion releasing adrenaline. Physiologically, the adrenal medulla governs hormonal fight-or-flight broadcast.

faqs.q: Where is the coeliac ganglion & plexus located?
faqs.a: Largest prevertebral relay at T12/L1, around coeliac trunk. Functionally, it governs foregut sympathetic supply. Medical evaluation of the coeliac ganglion & plexus also notes that coeliac plexus block for pancreatic cancer pain.

faqs.q: What is the function of the inferior mesenteric ganglion?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs hindgut and pelvic sympathetic supply. Relay at IMA origin. Clinically, regarding the inferior mesenteric ganglion, involved in post-ejaculatory pain syndromes.

faqs.q: What structures make up breast tissue?
faqs.a: Breast tissue includes glandular lobules, a branching duct network, connective-tissue support, fat, vessels and nerves. Ducts open at the nipple. Structurally, the lobules (glandular) (Lobuli glandulae) comprises secretory alveolar clusters at duct ends. Physiologically, the lobules (glandular) governs milk production under prolactin.

faqs.q: Are breast lobules and milk ducts the same thing?
faqs.a: No. Lobules contain milk-producing units; ducts transport secretions toward the nipple. Both are embedded in supporting connective and fatty tissue. The subareolar lactiferous ducts (Ductus lactiferi) is branching ducts converge near the nipple; classic large lactiferous sinuses are not consistently seen on ultrasound. Physiologically, the subareolar lactiferous ducts carry milk from alveoli and lobules toward nipple openings, rather than acting as a major storage reservoir.

faqs.q: What are the lobules (glandular)?
faqs.a: Secretory alveolar clusters at duct ends. Functionally, it governs milk production under prolactin. The terminal duct lobular unit is small duct and associated glandular acini forming a functional breast unit. Physiologically, the terminal duct lobular unit produces milk in lactation and drains into larger duct tree.

faqs.q: Where is the lactiferous ducts located?
faqs.a: 15–20 branching channels to the nipple. Functionally, it transport milk. Medical evaluation of the lactiferous ducts also notes that ductal carcinoma in situ stays inside this lining.

faqs.q: What is the function of the axillary lymph nodes?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs immune surveillance of the breast. 75% of breast lymph drains here. Clinically, regarding the axillary lymph nodes, sentinel node biopsy stages cancer spread.

faqs.q: Why is the adult human skeleton usually counted as 206 bones?
faqs.a: The conventional adult count includes bones that have fused during development and six middle-ear ossicles. Individual counts can differ because accessory bones, variable sesamoids and fusion patterns vary among people. Structurally, the skull (Cranium) comprises fuses 8 cranial + 14 facial bones; houses brain and senses. Physiologically, the skull governs protection and mastication anchor.

faqs.q: What belongs to the axial skeleton?
faqs.a: The axial skeleton contains the skull, vertebral column and thoracic cage. It supports the head and trunk and helps protect the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs. Structurally, the vertebral column (Columna vertebralis) comprises 7C-12T-5L-sacrum-coccyx with four curves. Physiologically, the vertebral column governs axial support and cord protection.

faqs.q: What belongs to the appendicular skeleton?
faqs.a: The shoulder and pelvic girdles, arms and legs form the appendicular skeleton. These bones provide attachment and leverage for movement and connect the limbs to the axial framework. Structurally, the clavicle (Clavicula) comprises s-strut between sternum and scapula. Physiologically, the clavicle holds the shoulder off the chest.

faqs.q: What is the difference between compact and spongy bone?
faqs.a: Compact bone forms a dense outer layer; spongy bone contains a lattice of trabeculae inside many bones. Both are living tissues, and marrow occupies spaces within bones. Structurally, the sternum comprises manubrium, body and xiphoid in the midline. Physiologically, the sternum governs rib anchor; marrow biopsy site.

faqs.q: Where is blood cell production found in adult bones?
faqs.a: Red marrow produces blood cell precursors in selected adult bones, especially axial bones and the proximal ends of some long bones. Yellow marrow is richer in fat and has different activity. Structurally, the scapula comprises triangular shoulder blade with glenoid fossa. Physiologically, the scapula governs mobile socket for the arm.

faqs.q: How do skeletal muscles move joints?
faqs.a: Skeletal muscle fibers contract and transmit force through tendons or other attachments. When a muscle crosses a joint, its contraction can pull the attached bones; opposing muscles help control the movement. Structurally, the diaphragm central tendon comprises strong aponeurotic center receiving diaphragm muscle fibers. Physiologically, the diaphragm central tendon transmits inspiratory muscle force and supports pericardium.

faqs.q: Are all human muscles listed among the overview cards?
faqs.a: No. The overview cards introduce major regions, while the linked full-body muscle and tendon atlas contains hundreds of named records. A single fixed count of muscles varies with naming and counting conventions. Structurally, the rotator cuff muscle group comprises supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis surround shoulder joint. Physiologically, the rotator cuff muscle group governs center humeral head during motion.

faqs.q: Where can I find posterior muscles such as the triceps and hamstrings?
faqs.a: The full-body muscle atlas groups them by arm and thigh region, including deeper layers and sex-specific pelvic floor views. The front-oriented overview image alone cannot identify posterior fibers. Structurally, the pelvic diaphragm comprises levator ani and coccygeus form muscular pelvic-floor support. Physiologically, the pelvic diaphragm supports pelvic viscera and continence.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a tendon and a ligament?
faqs.a: A tendon transfers muscular force to an attachment, commonly a bone; a ligament connects bones across a joint. Both consist largely of dense collagenous connective tissue but have different mechanical roles. Structurally, the biceps brachii (M. biceps brachii) comprises scapula to radial tuberosity. Physiologically, the biceps brachii governs elbow flexion + supination.

faqs.q: Is the diaphragm a skeletal muscle?
faqs.a: Yes. The diaphragm is a dome-shaped skeletal muscle separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities and is the primary muscle used during quiet inspiration. Its central tendon is an attachment region, not a separate muscle. The transversus abdominis is deep horizontal-fiber abdominal wall muscle beneath obliques. Physiologically, the transversus abdominis compresses abdominal contents and stabilizes trunk.

faqs.q: What does the lymphatic system do?
faqs.a: It returns excess interstitial fluid to the bloodstream, transports absorbed fats from the intestine and supports immune surveillance through nodes and lymphoid organs. Structurally, the lymphatic vessels (Vasa lymphatica) comprises blind-start capillaries to trunks. Physiologically, the lymphatic vessels returns 3 L of interstitial fluid daily.

faqs.q: Where does lymph drain back into the blood?
faqs.a: Large lymphatic ducts empty near the junctions of the internal jugular and subclavian veins. The thoracic duct drains most of the body. Structurally, the thoracic duct (Ductus thoracicus) comprises largest lymph channel, cisterna chyli to left venous angle. Physiologically, the thoracic duct returns 3/4 of body lymph.

faqs.q: What is the cervical nodes?
faqs.a: Chains along jugular and spine. Functionally, it drain head and neck. In clinical pathology involving the cervical nodes, rubbery vs hard-fixed distinguishes infection from malignancy.

faqs.q: Where is the inguinal nodes located?
faqs.a: Horizontal + vertical groups in the groin. Functionally, it drain leg, perineum and lower abdominal wall. Medical evaluation of the inguinal nodes also notes that enlarge in leg infections and STIs.

faqs.q: What is the function of the thymus?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs t-cell maturation in childhood. Bilobed school for T cells, behind sternum. Clinically, regarding the thymus, thymic hyperplasia accompanies myasthenia gravis.

faqs.q: What is the difference between arteries and veins?
faqs.a: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it. The distinction is direction of flow, not oxygen level: pulmonary arteries carry less-oxygenated blood. The superior vena cava (V. cava superior) is short trunk from brachiocephalic veins. Physiologically, the superior vena cava governs upper-body return to right atrium.

faqs.q: What is the aorta's role in circulation?
faqs.a: The aorta receives blood from the left ventricle and supplies the systemic arterial tree through branches serving the head, trunk and limbs. Structurally, the aortic arch (Arcus aortae) comprises curve giving brachiocephalic, left carotid, left subclavian. Physiologically, the aortic arch distributes to head and arms.

faqs.q: What is the aortic arch?
faqs.a: Curve giving brachiocephalic, left carotid, left subclavian. Functionally, it distributes to head and arms. Structurally, the common carotid artery (A. carotis communis) comprises neck artery bifurcating at C4. Physiologically, the common carotid artery governs brain and face supply.

faqs.q: Where is the subclavian artery located?
faqs.a: Under clavicle to axillary artery. Functionally, it governs arm supply; gives vertebral to brain. Medical evaluation of the subclavian artery also notes that subclavian steal reverses vertebral flow on exertion.

faqs.q: What is the function of the descending aorta?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs segmental branches to wall and viscera. Thoracic then abdominal aorta. Clinically, regarding the descending aorta, aneurysm screening in male smokers over 65.

faqs.q: What organs make up the endocrine system?
faqs.a: The endocrine system includes hormone-producing structures such as the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals and pancreatic islets, with other organs also contributing hormones. Structurally, the pancreatic beta cells comprises insulin-producing cells of endocrine pancreatic islets. Physiologically, the pancreatic beta cells lower circulating glucose by promoting uptake/storage.

faqs.q: How do endocrine glands differ from exocrine glands?
faqs.a: Endocrine tissue releases hormones into the blood. Exocrine glands deliver products through ducts to a surface or lumen, as pancreatic acini do for digestion. The parathyroid chief cells is small endocrine cells of parathyroid glands. Physiologically, the parathyroid chief cells secrete PTH in response to falling ionized calcium.

faqs.q: What is the pituitary gland?
faqs.a: Pea-sized master gland in the sella turcica. Functionally, it releases ACTH, TSH, GH, LH/FSH, prolactin, ADH/oxytocin store. In clinical pathology involving the pituitary gland, pituitary adenoma → visual field loss (optic chiasm above).

faqs.q: Where in the neck is the thyroid gland located?
faqs.a: Butterfly gland on the trachea. Functionally, it governs t3/T4 metabolic rate; calcitonin. Medical evaluation of the thyroid gland also notes that goitre and thyrotoxicosis are common presentations.

faqs.q: What is the function of the adrenal glands?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs cortisol, aldosterone, adrenaline. Caps on each kidney: cortex + medulla. Clinically, regarding the adrenal glands, addison's: hypotension, pigmentation, fatigue.

faqs.q: What holds a joint together?
faqs.a: A joint may be supported by a capsule, ligaments, tendons and nearby muscles. Exact stabilizers vary between joints; the knee also has menisci and cruciate ligaments. Structurally, the menisci (medial & lateral) (Menisci) comprises fibrocartilage crescents on the tibial plateau. Physiologically, the menisci (medial & lateral) governs load sharing, shock absorption, joint lubrication.

faqs.q: What do the ACL and PCL do in the knee?
faqs.a: The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments resist different directions of tibial translation and help stabilize the knee during movement. Structurally, the anterior cruciate ligament (Lig. cruciatum anterius) comprises from lateral femoral condyle to anterior tibial plateau. Physiologically, the anterior cruciate ligament governs blocks anterior tibial translation; pivots in rotation.

faqs.q: What is the anterior cruciate ligament?
faqs.a: From lateral femoral condyle to anterior tibial plateau. Functionally, it governs blocks anterior tibial translation; pivots in rotation. The posterior cruciate ligament (Lig. cruciatum posterius) is medial femoral condyle to posterior tibia. Physiologically, the posterior cruciate ligament governs blocks posterior tibial slide (dashboard injury).

faqs.q: Where is the posterior cruciate ligament located?
faqs.a: Medial femoral condyle to posterior tibia. Functionally, it governs blocks posterior tibial slide (dashboard injury). Structurally, the medial collateral ligament (Lig. collaterale tibiale) comprises femoral epicondyle to tibial shaft, fused with meniscus. Physiologically, the medial collateral ligament governs resists valgus stress.

faqs.q: What is the function of the menisci (medial & lateral)?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs load sharing, shock absorption, joint lubrication. Fibrocartilage crescents on the tibial plateau. The articular cartilage (Cartilago articularis) is hyaline cartilage 2–4 mm on joint surfaces. Physiologically, the articular cartilage governs near-frictionless load bearing.

faqs.q: Why can the shoulder move so freely?
faqs.a: The shallow glenoid cavity permits a wide range of movement. The labrum, capsule, rotator cuff and surrounding muscles help stabilize the humeral head. Structurally, the glenoid fossa comprises shallow scapular socket deepened by its labrum. Physiologically, the glenoid fossa receives humeral head in shoulder joint.

faqs.q: Which muscles form the rotator cuff?
faqs.a: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis form the rotator cuff around the glenohumeral joint. Anatomically, the teres minor tendon (Tendo m. teretis minoris) lies below infraspinatus. Physiologically, the teres minor tendon governs external rotation + capsule tension.

faqs.q: What is the supraspinatus tendon?
faqs.a: Over the top of the humeral head. Functionally, it initiates abduction (first 15°). In clinical pathology involving the supraspinatus tendon, most torn cuff tendon — painful arc 60–120°.

faqs.q: Where is the teres minor tendon located?
faqs.a: Below infraspinatus. Functionally, it governs external rotation + capsule tension. The infraspinatus tendon (Tendo m. infraspinati) is posterior to the head. Medical evaluation of the infraspinatus tendon also notes that tear → weak external rotation.

faqs.q: What is the function of the glenoid labrum?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs adds ~50% of glenoid depth. Fibrocartilage rim deepening the socket. Clinically, regarding the glenoid labrum, SLAP lesions in throwers; Bankart in dislocation.

faqs.q: What is the path of air through the upper airway?
faqs.a: Air enters the nose or mouth, passes through the pharynx and larynx, then moves down the trachea toward the bronchi. The epiglottis is elastic leaf above the larynx. Physiologically, the epiglottis governs flips to cover the larynx during swallowing.

faqs.q: What does the epiglottis do during swallowing?
faqs.a: The epiglottis is one structure involved in protecting the laryngeal entrance during swallowing; coordinated movement of the larynx and vocal folds also matters. Structurally, the vocal folds (Plicae vocales) comprises ligament + muscle under mucosa, glottis between. Physiologically, the vocal folds governs vibrate to phonate; close to protect lungs.

faqs.q: What is the nasal cavity & conchae?
faqs.a: Three conchae turbo-charge the surface area. Functionally, it warms, humidifies and filters inspired air. In clinical pathology involving the nasal cavity & conchae, deviated septum + turbinate hypertrophy = blocked nose.

faqs.q: Where is the nasopharynx & adenoid located?
faqs.a: Posterior nasal chamber with lymphoid adenoid. Functionally, it governs air passage; immune sampling in childhood. Medical evaluation of the nasopharynx & adenoid also notes that adenoid hypertrophy causes snoring and glue ear in kids.

faqs.q: What is the function of the epiglottis?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs flips to cover the larynx during swallowing. Elastic leaf above the larynx. Anatomically, the oropharynx lies behind the mouth, tonsils at its sides. Physiologically, the oropharynx governs shared food–air corridor; speech resonance.

faqs.q: What is the difference between red and yellow bone marrow?
faqs.a: Red marrow supports blood-cell production. Yellow marrow contains more fat; distribution changes with age and differs across skeletal sites. The red marrow (Medulla ossium rubra) is spongy bone of vertebrae, pelvis, sternum, epiphyses. Physiologically, the red marrow governs haematopoiesis: all blood cell lines.

faqs.q: Where are blood cells made in adults?
faqs.a: Most adult blood-cell production occurs in red marrow of axial bones and selected proximal long-bone regions. The sinusoidal endothelium is specialized discontinuous lining of marrow venous sinuses. Physiologically, the sinusoidal endothelium allows mature blood cells to enter bloodstream.

faqs.q: What is the red marrow?
faqs.a: Spongy bone of vertebrae, pelvis, sternum, epiphyses. Functionally, it governs haematopoiesis: all blood cell lines. Structurally, the trabecular (spongy) bone (Os spongiosum) comprises latticework of struts along stress lines. Physiologically, the trabecular (spongy) bone governs strength at low weight; houses red marrow.

faqs.q: Where is the trabecular (spongy) bone located?
faqs.a: Latticework of struts along stress lines. Functionally, it governs strength at low weight; houses red marrow. The haversian canal is central canal of compact-bone osteon containing vessels and nerves. Physiologically, the haversian canal supplies concentric lamellae.

faqs.q: What is the function of the endosteum & osteoblasts?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs remodelling: osteoblasts build, osteoclasts eat. Cellular lining of all internal bone surfaces. Clinically, regarding the endosteum & osteoblasts, paget's disease is remodelling gone chaotic.

faqs.q: Which organs are located in the male pelvis?
faqs.a: The male pelvis contains bladder, prostate and rectum, along with parts of the urethra, reproductive ducts, pelvic vessels and nerves. Structurally, the ejaculatory ducts (Ductus ejaculatorii) comprises vas + seminal vesicle ducts through prostate. Physiologically, the ejaculatory ducts deliver sperm into prostatic urethra.

faqs.q: What is the pelvic floor's role in men?
faqs.a: Pelvic-floor muscles support pelvic organs and contribute to continence. Their relationship to the urethra and perineal structures is important in regional anatomy. Structurally, the perineal body (Centrum perineale) comprises fibromuscular node between anus and bulb. Physiologically, the perineal body anchor for nine perineal muscles.

faqs.q: Where is the urinary bladder in the male pelvis?
faqs.a: Reservoir behind the pubis. Functionally, it stores urine; trigone is its smooth base. In clinical pathology involving the urinary bladder, outlet obstruction in men is usually prostatic.

faqs.q: Where is the prostatic & membranous urethra located?
faqs.a: Urethra traversing prostate and perineum. Functionally, it governs conduit for urine and semen; sphincters here. Medical evaluation of the prostatic & membranous urethra also notes that catheterisation respects the puboprostatic curve.

faqs.q: What is the function of the rectum?
faqs.a: Functionally, it stores stool before defecation. Terminal 12–15 cm with three valves. Clinically, regarding the rectum, rectal exam reaches prostate anteriorly, rectum all round.

faqs.q: Which organs are located in the female pelvis?
faqs.a: The female pelvis contains bladder, uterus, cervix, vagina and rectum, with ovaries and uterine tubes toward the lateral pelvic regions. The vagina is muscular canal from cervix to vestibule. Physiologically, the vagina governs intercourse, menstrual flow, birth canal.

faqs.q: What supports the uterus and pelvic organs?
faqs.a: Pelvic-floor muscles and connective-tissue attachments provide key support. The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold, not the sole load-bearing support. The broad ligament (Ligamentum latum uteri) is double peritoneal sheet draped over uterus, tubes and associated structures. Physiologically, the broad ligament supports relationships but is not the main mechanical uterine support.

faqs.q: Where is the urinary bladder in the female pelvis?
faqs.a: Reservoir behind the pubic symphysis. Functionally, it stores urine. In clinical pathology involving the urinary bladder, stress incontinence follows pelvic-floor weakness.

faqs.q: Where is the vagina located?
faqs.a: Muscular canal from cervix to vestibule. Functionally, it governs intercourse, menstrual flow, birth canal. Structurally, the cardinal & uterosacral ligaments (Ligg. cardinalia) comprises condensed endopelvic fascia at cervix sides. Physiologically, the cardinal & uterosacral ligaments governs suspend cervix and upper vagina.

faqs.q: What is the function of the vesico- & recto-uterine pouches?
faqs.a: Functionally, it allow organ movement; collect free fluid. Peritoneal recesses front and back of uterus. Clinically, regarding the vesico- & recto-uterine pouches, the recto-uterine pouch is the most dependent — pus collects there.

faqs.q: What are the layers of the uterine wall?
faqs.a: The uterus has an inner endometrium, muscular myometrium and outer serosal or connective covering depending on the region. The endometrial–myometrial junction (Zona junctionalis) is inner myometrial zone adjacent to the endometrium. Physiologically, the endometrial–myometrial junction governs interface for cyclical uterine peristalsis and implantation.

faqs.q: What happens to the endometrium during the menstrual cycle?
faqs.a: The endometrium responds to changing ovarian hormones. Its functional layer grows and changes during the cycle and is shed if pregnancy does not occur. The endometrial glands is simple tubular glands extending through uterine mucosa into stroma. Physiologically, the endometrial glands governs change secretion and shape during menstrual cycle.

faqs.q: What is the fundus?
faqs.a: Dome above the two tubal openings. Functionally, it expands in pregnancy; fundal position is an obstetric landmark. In clinical pathology involving the fundus, fundal height is a rough gestational growth marker.

faqs.q: Where are the uterine cornua located?
faqs.a: Upper lateral junctions where uterine tubes enter. Functionally, it governs communicate with intramural tube segments. Medical evaluation of the uterine cornua also notes that interstitial ectopic pregnancy arises near the cornu.

faqs.q: What is the function of the endometrium — functionalis?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs proliferates under estrogen and becomes secretory under progesterone. Superficial cyclic glandular layer; sheds with menses. Clinically, regarding the endometrium — functionalis, abnormal bleeding can arise from altered endometrial architecture.

faqs.q: What is the cervical transformation zone?
faqs.a: It is the region where squamous epithelium of the ectocervix and columnar epithelium of the endocervix meet and change over time. Structurally, the transformation zone (Zona transformationis) comprises region of squamous metaplasia between original and current SCJ. Physiologically, the transformation zone governs physiologic remodeling of exposed columnar epithelium.

faqs.q: Why is the transformation zone important in cervical screening?
faqs.a: Many cervical precancerous changes arise near the squamocolumnar junction. Screening samples this region, but this atlas does not interpret individual test results. Structurally, the ectocervical squamous epithelium (Epithelium squamosum) comprises nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium continuous with vaginal mucosa. Physiologically, the ectocervical squamous epithelium protects exposed cervical surface.

faqs.q: What is the ectocervix?
faqs.a: Part of cervix visible at the vaginal vault. Functionally, it governs covered by nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. In clinical pathology involving the ectocervix, visual examination and directed biopsy sample this surface.

faqs.q: Where is the endocervical columnar epithelium located?
faqs.a: Mucus-secreting simple columnar lining of the canal. Functionally, it produces cervical mucus under hormonal regulation. Medical evaluation of the endocervical columnar epithelium also notes that glandular lesions need distinct cytologic evaluation.

faqs.q: What is the function of the squamocolumnar junction?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs migrates with age, hormones and pregnancy. Border where glandular and squamous epithelia meet. Clinically, regarding the squamocolumnar junction, colposcopy assesses whether the entire junction is visible.

faqs.q: Where does an egg go after ovulation?
faqs.a: After release from an ovarian follicle, the oocyte is taken up near the fimbriae and usually enters the uterine tube before moving toward the uterus. Structurally, the fimbriae (Fimbriae tubae) comprises fringed distal projections adjacent to ovary. Physiologically, the fimbriae governs sweep oocyte toward tubal abdominal ostium.

faqs.q: Which part of the fallopian tube is the usual site of fertilization?
faqs.a: The ampulla, a wider segment of the uterine tube, is the most common site of fertilization. Structurally, the ampulla (Ampulla tubae) comprises wide, folded lateral tubal segment. Physiologically, the ampulla governs usual site of fertilization.

faqs.q: What is the ovarian cortex?
faqs.a: Outer ovarian zone with follicles at several stages. Functionally, it houses the oocyte reserve. In clinical pathology involving the ovarian cortex, cortical tissue is considered in fertility-preserving surgery.

faqs.q: Where are the primordial follicles located?
faqs.a: Small oocyte with flat granulosa cells in outer cortex. Functionally, it governs dormant ovarian reserve pool. Medical evaluation of the primordial follicles also notes that reserve declines with age and treatment exposure.

faqs.q: What is the function of the dominant antral follicle?
faqs.a: Functionally, it releases a secondary oocyte after the LH surge. Large fluid-filled preovulatory follicle. Clinically, regarding the dominant antral follicle, functional cysts may arise from follicular persistence.

faqs.q: What are the layers of the vaginal wall?
faqs.a: The vaginal wall contains a mucosal lining, a muscular layer and outer connective tissue. Its folds and tissue properties vary with age and hormonal state. The adventitia & paravaginal fascia (Tunica adventitia) is outer connective tissue joining vaginal walls to pelvic sidewall. Physiologically, the adventitia & paravaginal fascia contains neurovascular routes and supports the canal.

faqs.q: Where are the vaginal fornices?
faqs.a: Fornices are recesses around the cervix at the upper end of the vagina; the posterior fornix lies behind the cervix. The lateral fornices (Fornices laterales) is paired recesses to either side of cervix. Physiologically, the lateral fornices governs anatomic route near cervical attachments.

faqs.q: What is the vaginal lumen?
faqs.a: Potential space whose walls normally lie against one another. Functionally, it governs passage for menstrual flow, intercourse and birth.

faqs.q: Where is the posterior vaginal wall located?
faqs.a: Wall lying anterior to rectum, longer near posterior fornix. Functionally, it supports the posterior compartment. Medical evaluation of the posterior vaginal wall also notes that posterior wall defects may accompany rectocele.

faqs.q: What is the function of the vaginal muscularis?
faqs.a: Functionally, it allows distension and elastic return. Circular and longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles. Clinically, regarding the vaginal muscularis, at the introitus skeletal pelvic floor muscles contribute support.

faqs.q: What structures are included in the vulva?
faqs.a: The vulva is the external genital region: mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoral structures and the vestibule with urethral and vaginal openings. Some deeper glands, vessels and nerves are described separately. Structurally, the vulvar vestibule (Vestibulum vaginae) comprises space between labia minora containing urethral and vaginal openings. Physiologically, the vulvar vestibule governs shared surface region for urinary and genital outlets.

faqs.q: Are the vulva and vagina the same structure?
faqs.a: No. The vulva refers to external genital anatomy; the vagina is an internal muscular canal extending from the cervix to the vaginal opening. The opening lies within the vulvar vestibule. Structurally, the external urethral meatus (Ostium urethrae externum) comprises urinary opening anterior to vaginal introitus. Physiologically, the external urethral meatus governs urine exits here, not through the vagina.

faqs.q: How are the urethral and vaginal openings positioned?
faqs.a: The external urethral opening is typically inferior to the clitoral glans and superior to the vaginal opening within the vestibule. Their appearance varies normally, so a teaching illustration is not a diagnostic reference. The greater vestibular gland ducts is paired ducts open near the posterior part of the vestibule, lateral to the vaginal opening. Physiologically, the greater vestibular gland ducts governs convey gland secretions to the vestibular surface.

faqs.q: What do the labia minora do?
faqs.a: The labia minora are inner hairless folds that border the vestibule and join anteriorly near the clitoral hood. Their size, color and asymmetry vary normally between people. The labia minora (Labia minora pudendi) is inner hairless folds, highly variable in size and pigmentation.

faqs.q: Can the surface image show Bartholin glands or the clitoral crura?
faqs.a: No. The greater vestibular glands and most clitoral erectile structures lie below the surface. Their locations are described as deep study notes, not marked as visible on the external surface illustration. The clitoral body & crura (Corpus et crura clitoridis) is paired erectile corpora extend along pubic rami. Physiologically, the clitoral body & crura governs erectile engorgement.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the broad ligament and pelvic support ligaments?
faqs.a: The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold. Cardinal and uterosacral connective tissues, together with pelvic-floor muscles, contribute substantially to uterine support. Structurally, the cardinal ligament (Ligamentum cardinale) comprises transverse cervical connective tissue to pelvic sidewall. Physiologically, the cardinal ligament governs important apical support with uterine artery/vein.

faqs.q: Why is the ureter important in pelvic surgery anatomy?
faqs.a: The ureter travels near the uterine artery and cervix. Understanding their relationship helps explain why surgical planes require careful identification. The distal ureter (Ureter) runs along pelvic sidewall then beneath uterine artery near cervix. Physiologically, the distal ureter delivers urine to bladder.

faqs.q: What is the broad ligament?
faqs.a: Double peritoneal sheet draped over uterus, tubes and associated structures. Functionally, it supports relationships but is not the main mechanical uterine support. In clinical pathology involving the broad ligament, ureter and uterine vessels course at its base.

faqs.q: Where is the mesosalpinx located?
faqs.a: Broad ligament portion related to uterine tube. Functionally, it supports tube and its vessels. Medical evaluation of the mesosalpinx also notes that tubal surgery separates this vascular fold.

faqs.q: What is the function of the round ligament?
faqs.a: Functionally, it helps maintain anteversion; not principal apical support. Band from uterine cornu through inguinal canal to labium majus. Clinically, regarding the round ligament, relevant to round-ligament pain and inguinal surgery.

faqs.q: Where are sperm made in the testis?
faqs.a: Sperm develop within seminiferous tubules. Supporting Sertoli cells and hormone-producing interstitial Leydig cells occupy different microscopic compartments. The rete testis channels within mediastinum draining straight tubules. Physiologically, the rete testis collect sperm from seminiferous system.

faqs.q: How do sperm leave the testis?
faqs.a: They move from seminiferous tubules through a collecting network and efferent ductules into the epididymis, where maturation and storage continue. Structurally, the epididymal head (Caput epididymidis) comprises enlarged superior epididymis receiving efferent ductules. Physiologically, the epididymal head governs starts sperm maturation.

faqs.q: What is the tunica vaginalis?
faqs.a: Serous covering with visceral and parietal layers. Functionally, it allows mobile testis within scrotum. In clinical pathology involving the tunica vaginalis, fluid accumulation in the cavity forms a hydrocele.

faqs.q: Where is the mediastinum testis located?
faqs.a: Posterior thickening of albuginea containing rete testis. Functionally, it governs organizes lobules and duct outflow. Medical evaluation of the mediastinum testis also notes that important landmark in testicular ultrasound.

faqs.q: What is the function of the seminiferous tubules?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs spermatogenesis. Coiled tubules lined by developing germ cells and Sertoli cells. Clinically, regarding the seminiferous tubules, tubular atrophy reduces fertility.

faqs.q: Where is the prostate located?
faqs.a: The prostate sits below the bladder and surrounds the first part of the urethra. Ducts from the reproductive tract open into the prostatic urethra. Structurally, the prostatic urethra (Pars prostatica urethrae) comprises urethra through prostate from bladder neck to membrane. Physiologically, the prostatic urethra conducts urine and semen in separate phases.

faqs.q: What are the main anatomical zones of the prostate?
faqs.a: The transition, central and peripheral zones differ in location and surrounding structures. The peripheral zone occupies much of the posterior gland. Structurally, the anterior fibromuscular stroma comprises non-glandular anterior component of prostate rich in muscle and connective tissue. Physiologically, the anterior fibromuscular stroma provides structural support to prostatic urethra.

faqs.q: What is the bladder neck / internal sphincter?
faqs.a: Smooth-muscle outlet superior to prostate. Functionally, it closes during emission to limit retrograde ejaculation. In clinical pathology involving the bladder neck / internal sphincter, bladder-neck dysfunction may affect voiding.

faqs.q: Where is the prostatic peripheral zone located?
faqs.a: Posterior-lateral zone palpable through rectum. Functionally, it produces prostatic secretions. Medical evaluation of the prostatic peripheral zone also notes that most prostatic cancers arise in this zone.

faqs.q: What is the function of the prostatic urethra?
faqs.a: Functionally, it conducts urine and semen in separate phases. Urethra through prostate from bladder neck to membrane. Structurally, the prostatic venous plexus comprises veins around capsule, communicating with deep dorsal penile and vesical veins. Physiologically, the prostatic venous plexus drain gland and adjacent bladder neck.

faqs.q: Is the clitoris only the visible glans?
