faqs.a: No. The visible glans is part of a larger erectile complex that includes a body, paired crura and associated vestibular bulbs. Structurally, the clitoral body (Corpus clitoridis) comprises midline body formed by apposition of the paired corpora cavernosa, deep to the external glans. Physiologically, the clitoral body governs engorges via cavernous vascular spaces.

faqs.q: Where are the clitoral crura located?
faqs.a: The crura extend along the ischiopubic rami beneath the vulvar surface and join the midline erectile body. The crura of clitoris (Crura clitoridis) is two proximal cavernous limbs fixed to the inferior pubic and ischial rami. Physiologically, the crura of clitoris anchor the erectile body to pelvic bone.

faqs.q: What is the clitoral glans?
faqs.a: External distal part beneath or exposed by the hood; dense sensory innervation and distinct histology from cavernous bodies. Functionally, it governs conveys fine sensation.

faqs.q: Where is the clitoral body located?
faqs.a: Midline body formed by apposition of the paired corpora cavernosa, deep to the external glans. Functionally, it governs engorges via cavernous vascular spaces. Structurally, the crural cavernous sinusoids comprises endothelium-lined vascular spaces within paired proximal clitoral corpora. Physiologically, the crural cavernous sinusoids governs expand as smooth muscle relaxes.

faqs.q: What is the function of the left corpus cavernosum?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs contributes to body rigidity and expansion. Contralateral cavernous cylinder joining the body along the midline. Clinically, regarding the left corpus cavernosum, paired anatomy can be traced into the crura.

faqs.q: What are the three erectile bodies of the penis?
faqs.a: Two paired corpora cavernosa form the main dorsal erectile cylinders. A single corpus spongiosum surrounds the urethra and expands into the glans. The paired corpora cavernosa (Corpora cavernosa penis) is two dorsal longitudinal erectile cylinders that unite in shaft and separate proximally as crura. Physiologically, the paired corpora cavernosa governs primary rigid erectile compartment.

faqs.q: What does the tunica albuginea do in erectile tissue?
faqs.a: It is a dense connective-tissue covering around erectile compartments, particularly strong around the corpora cavernosa. Structurally, the tunica albuginea comprises strong fibrous sheath encasing cavernosa, with distinct collagen layers. Physiologically, the tunica albuginea governs resists expansion and aids venous occlusion.

faqs.q: What are the paired corpora cavernosa?
faqs.a: Two dorsal longitudinal erectile cylinders that unite in shaft and separate proximally as crura. Functionally, it governs primary rigid erectile compartment. The cavernosal septum is fibrous partition between right and left corpora cavernosa, incomplete distally in places. Physiologically, the cavernosal septum connects paired erectile bodies.

faqs.q: Where is the tunica albuginea located?
faqs.a: Strong fibrous sheath encasing cavernosa, with distinct collagen layers. Functionally, it governs resists expansion and aids venous occlusion. Structurally, the glans penis comprises distal expansion of corpus spongiosum over tips of corpora cavernosa. Physiologically, the glans penis contains terminal urethral opening and sensory receptors.

faqs.q: What is the function of the deep penile arteries?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs feed cavernosal tissue. Internal pudendal branches traveling within each corpus cavernosum.

faqs.q: What are the five epidermal layers in thick skin?
faqs.a: From deep to superficial they are stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum and corneum. Thin skin does not have a distinct lucidum. The stratum lucidum is thin translucent transition zone most apparent in glabrous palms and soles. Physiologically, the stratum lucidum governs adds specialized layer in thick skin.

faqs.q: Does the epidermis have its own blood vessels?
faqs.a: No. The epidermis receives nutrients by diffusion from capillaries in the underlying dermis. The papillary dermis (Stratum papillare dermis) is superficial loose connective tissue with capillaries and fine collagen. Physiologically, the papillary dermis nourishes avascular epidermis by diffusion.

faqs.q: What is the stratum basale?
faqs.a: Deep single proliferative keratinocyte layer adjoining basement membrane. Functionally, it governs renews overlying epidermis. In clinical pathology involving the stratum basale, basal-cell carcinoma derives from basal-type cells.

faqs.q: Where is the stratum granulosum located?
faqs.a: Flattened keratinocytes with keratohyalin granules and lipid-releasing lamellar bodies. Functionally, it governs builds the water-permeability barrier. Medical evaluation of the stratum granulosum also notes that barrier injury increases transepidermal water loss.

faqs.q: What is the function of the stratum corneum?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs principal external permeability barrier. Anucleate flattened corneocytes surrounded by intercellular lipid lamellae. Clinically, regarding the stratum corneum, loss in large burns causes fluid and heat loss.

faqs.q: What does the facial nerve control?
faqs.a: Cranial nerve VII supplies muscles of facial expression and also carries taste and parasympathetic fibers through specific branches. The parotid plexus (Plexus intraparotideus) is branching motor network within parotid gland. Physiologically, the parotid plexus distributes facial expression motor fibers.

faqs.q: Does the facial nerve provide most facial skin sensation?
faqs.a: No. Most facial skin sensation travels in branches of the trigeminal nerve; the facial nerve is mainly known for its motor supply to facial expression. Structurally, the facial sensation · CN V (Nervus trigeminus) comprises v1/V2/V3 provide most cutaneous sensory input from face, unlike VII expression branches. Physiologically, the facial sensation · CN V separates sensory testing from facial movement testing.

faqs.q: What is the facial motor nucleus?
faqs.a: Motor cell bodies in pons send axons looping around abducens nucleus before exit. Functionally, it controls muscles of facial expression. In clinical pathology involving the facial motor nucleus, upper face often retains bilateral cortical input in supranuclear lesions.

faqs.q: Where is the internal acoustic meatus located?
faqs.a: Temporal-bone canal shared by CN VII, CN VIII and labyrinthine artery. Functionally, it governs conveys nerve toward facial canal. Medical evaluation of the internal acoustic meatus also notes that lesions here may affect facial movement and hearing/balance.

faqs.q: What is the function of the greater petrosal nerve?
faqs.a: Functionally, it supports lacrimal and nasal/palatine gland secretion. Carries preganglionic fibers toward pterygopalatine ganglion. Clinically, regarding the greater petrosal nerve, a lesion proximal to branch can impair lacrimation.

faqs.q: What are the three branches of the trigeminal nerve?
faqs.a: Ophthalmic V1, maxillary V2 and mandibular V3 supply different facial territories. V3 also carries motor fibers to muscles of mastication. Structurally, the mandibular V3 (Nervus mandibularis) comprises sensory and motor roots unite at foramen ovale. Physiologically, the mandibular V3 governs sensation lower face and motor to mastication.

faqs.q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the cornea?
faqs.a: The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, especially through the nasociliary pathway, carries most corneal sensation. Structurally, the nasociliary nerve (Nervus nasociliaris) comprises orbital V1 branch giving long ciliary, ethmoidal and infratrochlear fibers. Physiologically, the nasociliary nerve carries corneal sensation through long ciliary nerves.

faqs.q: What is the trigeminal sensory root?
faqs.a: Large sensory root emerges from lateral pons into trigeminal cistern. Functionally, it governs conveys facial somatic sensation centrally. In clinical pathology involving the trigeminal sensory root, brainstem lesions can combine facial and body sensory findings.

faqs.q: Where is the ophthalmic V1 located?
faqs.a: Passes superior orbital fissure into orbit; gives frontal, lacrimal and nasociliary branches. Functionally, it governs sensation from forehead, upper lid and cornea. Medical evaluation of the ophthalmic V1 also notes that afferent limb of corneal reflex.

faqs.q: What is the function of the nasociliary nerve?
faqs.a: Functionally, it carries corneal sensation through long ciliary nerves. Orbital V1 branch giving long ciliary, ethmoidal and infratrochlear fibers. The frontal nerve (Nervus frontalis) is superior orbital branch dividing into supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves. Physiologically, the frontal nerve governs sensation over forehead and anterior scalp.

faqs.q: What are the three main coats of the eyeball?
faqs.a: The outer fibrous coat is cornea and sclera; the middle vascular coat is the uvea; the inner neural coat includes the retina. Structurally, the choroid (Choroidea) comprises pigmented vascular layer between retina and sclera. Physiologically, the choroid supplies outer retina, especially photoreceptors.

faqs.q: Which layers make up the cornea?
faqs.a: Corneal epithelium, stroma and endothelium are major components, with Bowman and Descemet layers between them in standard descriptions. Structurally, the corneal epithelium (Epithelium anterius corneae) comprises surface stratified nonkeratinizing epithelial layer. Physiologically, the corneal epithelium governs barrier and smooth refractive surface.

faqs.q: What is the corneal epithelium?
faqs.a: Surface stratified nonkeratinizing epithelial layer. Functionally, it governs barrier and smooth refractive surface. Structurally, the Bowman layer (Lamina limitans anterior) comprises acellular anterior limiting layer beneath epithelium. Physiologically, the Bowman layer governs adds anterior structural support.

faqs.q: Where is the corneal stroma located?
faqs.a: Organized collagen lamellae form most of corneal thickness. Functionally, it governs precise collagen arrangement maintains transparency. Medical evaluation of the corneal stroma also notes that edema disrupts transparency.

faqs.q: What is the function of the corneal endothelium?
faqs.a: Functionally, it pumps fluid from stroma to maintain optical clarity. Single posterior cell layer lining anterior chamber. Clinically, regarding the corneal endothelium, cell loss may cause persistent edema.

faqs.q: Where are rods and cones located in the retina?
faqs.a: Photoreceptors lie in the outer neural retina next to retinal pigment epithelium, even though incoming light first passes through more internal layers. Structurally, the retinal pigment epithelium (Epithelium pigmentosum retinae) comprises pigmented monolayer adjacent to photoreceptors and Bruch membrane. Physiologically, the retinal pigment epithelium governs recycles visual pigment, phagocytoses shed discs and forms outer blood–retinal barrier.

faqs.q: What is the difference between rods and cones?
faqs.a: Rods are especially sensitive in low light; cones support high-acuity and color vision, particularly near the fovea. Structurally, the cones (Coni) comprises color- and acuity-sensitive photoreceptors concentrated at fovea. Physiologically, the cones governs high-resolution daylight and color vision.

faqs.q: What are the photoreceptor segments?
faqs.a: Rod and cone inner/outer segments facing RPE. Functionally, it governs capture photons and start phototransduction. In clinical pathology involving the photoreceptor segments, outer-segment injury impairs vision despite intact inner retina.

faqs.q: Where is the retinal pigment epithelium located?
faqs.a: Pigmented monolayer adjacent to photoreceptors and Bruch membrane. Functionally, it governs recycles visual pigment, phagocytoses shed discs and forms outer blood–retinal barrier. Structurally, the external limiting membrane (Membrana limitans externa) comprises adherens junction belt between Müller cells and photoreceptors. Physiologically, the external limiting membrane provides organized retinal scaffold.

faqs.q: What is the function of the fovea centralis?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs peak spatial acuity. Small central pit with closely spaced cones and displaced inner layers. Clinically, regarding the fovea centralis, foveal injury causes major central visual impairment.

faqs.q: What are the main parts of a nephron?
faqs.a: A renal corpuscle filters plasma; proximal tubule, loop of Henle and distal tubule modify filtrate. Collecting ducts receive fluid from multiple nephrons. The collecting duct (Ductus colligens) receives distal connecting tubules from multiple nephrons and descends through medulla. Physiologically, the collecting duct governs ADH-sensitive water reabsorption and acid/base regulation.

faqs.q: Where does filtration occur in the kidney?
faqs.a: Filtration occurs across the glomerular capillary barrier into Bowman space in the renal corpuscle, mainly in the kidney cortex. Structurally, the glomerular capillaries (Glomerulus) comprises fenestrated capillary loops between afferent and efferent arterioles. Physiologically, the glomerular capillaries pass plasma water and small solutes toward Bowman space.

faqs.q: What is the bowman capsule?
faqs.a: Parietal squamous layer and visceral podocyte layer enclosing Bowman space. Functionally, it collects primary filtrate from glomerulus. In clinical pathology involving the Bowman capsule, filtrate flows from urinary pole to proximal tubule.

faqs.q: Where are the podocyte foot processes located?
faqs.a: Interdigitating podocyte extensions with slit diaphragms over glomerular capillaries. Functionally, it governs final cellular component of filtration barrier. Medical evaluation of the podocyte foot processes also notes that effacement accompanies proteinuric disease.

faqs.q: What is the function of the collecting duct?
faqs.a: Functionally, it governs ADH-sensitive water reabsorption and acid/base regulation. Receives distal connecting tubules from multiple nephrons and descends through medulla. Structurally, the intercalated cells (Cellulae intercalatae) comprises acid/base-specialized collecting duct cells with subtype-dependent transport. Physiologically, the intercalated cells secrete hydrogen or bicarbonate as appropriate.

faqs.q: Which spinal nerves form the brachial plexus?
faqs.a: Its main roots usually arise from ventral rami C5 through T1. They organize into trunks, divisions, cords and terminal branches. The c5–T1 ventral rami (Rami anteriores C5–T1) is five spinal nerve ventral rami build the typical plexus; not the intrathecal dorsal/ventral rootlets. Physiologically, the c5–T1 ventral rami provide segmental motor and sensory fibers to upper limb.

faqs.q: What are the five major terminal branches of the brachial plexus?
faqs.a: Musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves are the five commonly taught terminal branches. Structurally, the medial cord (Fasciculus medialis) comprises continuation of lower trunk anterior division, medial to axillary artery. Physiologically, the medial cord gives ulnar and medial root of median nerve.

faqs.q: What is the C5–T1 ventral rami?
faqs.a: Five spinal nerve ventral rami build the typical plexus; not the intrathecal dorsal/ventral rootlets. Functionally, it provide segmental motor and sensory fibers to upper limb. Structurally, the upper trunk (Truncus superior) comprises formed by union of C5 and C6 ventral rami. Physiologically, the upper trunk governs redistributes upper-root fibers into divisions.

faqs.q: Where is the upper trunk located?
faqs.a: Formed by union of C5 and C6 ventral rami. Functionally, it governs redistributes upper-root fibers into divisions. Structurally, the lower trunk (Truncus inferior) comprises formed by C8 and T1 ventral rami. Physiologically, the lower trunk carries lower-root fibers toward hand pathways.

faqs.q: What is the function of the lower trunk?
faqs.a: Functionally, it carries lower-root fibers toward hand pathways. Formed by C8 and T1 ventral rami. The posterior divisions (Divisiones posteriores) is one posterior division from each trunk converges on posterior cord. Physiologically, the posterior divisions governs feed extensor-compartment pathways.

faqs.q: What lies beneath the cerebral cortex?
faqs.a: Deep white-matter pathways connect cortical regions with each other and with subcortical structures, while deep gray nuclei and ventricles occupy related spaces. Structurally, the subcortical white matter (Substantia alba cerebri) comprises myelinated association, commissural and projection fibers beneath cortex. Physiologically, the subcortical white matter connects distributed gray-matter networks.

faqs.q: Does every part of the cerebral cortex have six layers?
faqs.a: Most neocortex has six layers, but cortical regions vary, and older cortical areas such as hippocampal cortex have a different laminar organization. The hippocampal formation (Formatio hippocampi) is medial temporal folded cortex with fewer layers than typical neocortex. Physiologically, the hippocampal formation governs participates in memory encoding and spatial processing.

faqs.q: What is the cortical gray matter?
faqs.a: Neuronal cell-body sheet folded into gyri and sulci. Functionally, it integrates sensory, motor and association information. In clinical pathology involving the cortical gray matter, regional cortical lesions give different deficits.

faqs.q: Where is the layer II · external granular located?
faqs.a: Small pyramidal and granule-cell zone. Functionally, it governs contributes intracortical signaling. Medical evaluation of the layer II · external granular also notes that cell density varies across sensory and motor cortex.

faqs.q: What is the function of the layer IV · internal granular?
faqs.a: Functionally, it receives major thalamocortical afferents. Prominent thalamic input layer, particularly in primary sensory cortex. Clinically, regarding the layer IV · internal granular, relatively thin in primary motor cortex.

faqs.q: What are the three meninges around the brain?
faqs.a: From outside inward they are dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater. Cerebrospinal fluid occupies the subarachnoid space. The arachnoid mater (Arachnoidea mater) is thin membrane deep to dura spanning over sulci; trabeculae bridge to pia. Physiologically, the arachnoid mater governs bounds CSF-filled subarachnoid space.

faqs.q: Where does cerebrospinal fluid flow?
faqs.a: CSF circulates through the ventricles and subarachnoid spaces before being returned to venous or lymphatic drainage pathways. Structurally, the choroid plexus (Plexus choroideus) comprises vascular core with specialized epithelial covering in ventricles. Physiologically, the choroid plexus secretes much of cerebrospinal fluid and forms blood–CSF barrier.

faqs.q: What is the periosteal cranial dura?
faqs.a: Outer cranial dural layer adherent to inner skull. Functionally, it forms tough outer covering and part of sinus walls. In clinical pathology involving the periosteal cranial dura, spinal epidural space differs from cranial periosteal interface.

faqs.q: Where is the falx cerebri located?
faqs.a: Vertical sickle-shaped dural sheet between hemispheres. Functionally, it supports superior and inferior sagittal sinuses. Medical evaluation of the falx cerebri also notes that bridging veins cross toward its superior sinus.

faqs.q: What is the function of the superior sagittal sinus?
faqs.a: Functionally, it receives superficial cerebral veins and arachnoid granulation drainage. Midline dural channel at upper attached edge of falx. Clinically, regarding the superior sagittal sinus, sinus thrombosis impairs venous outflow.

faqs.q: What are the three parts of the brainstem?
faqs.a: The brainstem consists of midbrain, pons and medulla. It carries major pathways and houses many cranial-nerve nuclei. Structurally, the midbrain (Mesencephalon) comprises rostral brainstem around cerebral aqueduct between diencephalon and pons. Physiologically, the midbrain governs hosts III/IV-related nuclei and visual/auditory orienting circuits.

faqs.q: What does the cerebellum do?
faqs.a: The cerebellum helps coordinate movement, timing and balance by integrating sensory and motor information; it is not the same structure as the brainstem. Structurally, the medulla oblongata comprises caudal brainstem continuous with spinal cord. Physiologically, the medulla oblongata contains autonomic, swallowing and motor/sensory pathways.

faqs.q: What is the midbrain?
faqs.a: Rostral brainstem around cerebral aqueduct between diencephalon and pons. Functionally, it governs hosts III/IV-related nuclei and visual/auditory orienting circuits. Structurally, the superior colliculus (Colliculus superior) comprises dorsal midbrain paired structure. Physiologically, the superior colliculus coordinates orienting eye/head movements to visual stimuli.

faqs.q: Where is the inferior colliculus located?
faqs.a: Dorsal caudal midbrain auditory relay structure. Functionally, it integrates auditory pathway toward thalamus. Medical evaluation of the inferior colliculus also notes that auditory pathways are largely bilateral centrally.

faqs.q: What is the function of the cerebral peduncles?
faqs.a: Functionally, it transmit corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine signals. Ventral midbrain bundles carrying major descending cortical fibers. Clinically, regarding the cerebral peduncles, ventral lesion may cause contralateral weakness.

faqs.q: What is a pulmonary acinus?
faqs.a: An acinus is the lung region distal to a terminal bronchiole where respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli participate in gas exchange. It is a microanatomical unit, not a whole lung lobe. Structurally, the respiratory bronchiole (Bronchiolus respiratorius) comprises first airway segment with alveoli interrupting its wall. Physiologically, the respiratory bronchiole governs combines air conduction and some gas exchange.

faqs.q: How do Type I and Type II alveolar cells differ?
faqs.a: Type I pneumocytes are thin squamous lining cells specialized for gas exchange. Type II pneumocytes are plumper cells that make surfactant and help replenish the alveolar lining. Structurally, the type I pneumocyte (Pneumocytus typus I) comprises very thin squamous alveolar epithelial cell covering most alveolar surface. Physiologically, the type I pneumocyte governs minimizes gas diffusion distance.

faqs.q: What is the alveolar–capillary barrier?
faqs.a: It is the thin interface separating air in an alveolus from blood in a nearby capillary, involving alveolar epithelium, shared basement membranes and capillary endothelium. Its short diffusion distance supports gas exchange. The pulmonary interstitium is thin connective compartment between epithelium and capillary endothelium. Physiologically, the pulmonary interstitium supports cells, matrix and diffusion interface.

faqs.q: Are alveolar macrophages attached to the wall?
faqs.a: Alveolar macrophages can move on the air-facing surface of alveoli and engulf inhaled particles and debris. They are not the same as Type I or Type II epithelial cells. Structurally, the alveolar epithelial tight junctions comprises sealing contacts between adjacent alveolar epithelial cells. Physiologically, the alveolar epithelial tight junctions governs maintain fluid barrier despite thin gas-exchange surface.

faqs.q: Is the Type I cell image a histology photograph?
faqs.a: No. The separate alveolar cell view is a digital teaching illustration. The thin lining and plumper Type II cell are depicted for learning, not presented as a clinical slide or a literal lung-image zoom. Structurally, the type II pneumocyte (Pneumocytus typus II) comprises cuboidal cell with lamellar bodies, commonly at alveolar corners. Physiologically, the type II pneumocyte secretes surfactant and contributes to epithelial renewal.

faqs.q: How does blood flow through a hepatic lobule?
faqs.a: Branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery feed sinusoids near portal tracts; blood then drains toward the central vein. Structurally, the central vein (Vena centralis) comprises terminal hepatic venule at center of classical lobule. Physiologically, the central vein collects sinusoidal blood toward hepatic veins.

faqs.q: Does bile flow in the same direction as blood in a liver lobule?
faqs.a: No. Hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi that move toward bile ducts in portal tracts, generally opposite the sinusoidal blood flow. The bile canaliculi (Canaliculi biliferi) is tiny sealed channels formed between adjacent hepatocyte apical surfaces. Physiologically, the bile canaliculi move bile toward portal ductules opposite blood flow.

faqs.q: What is the portal venule?
faqs.a: Small portal vein branch delivering nutrient-rich splanchnic blood to sinusoids. Functionally, it feeds liver parenchyma. In clinical pathology involving the portal venule, portal obstruction can raise portal pressure.

faqs.q: Where is the interlobular bile duct located?
faqs.a: Cholangiocyte-lined duct traveling with arterial and portal venous branches. Functionally, it receives bile from canalicular/ductular route. Medical evaluation of the interlobular bile duct also notes that duct injury causes cholestatic patterns.

faqs.q: What is the function of the central vein?
faqs.a: Functionally, it collects sinusoidal blood toward hepatic veins. Terminal hepatic venule at center of classical lobule. Structurally, the hepatic sinusoid (Sinusoideum hepaticum) comprises wide, discontinuous capillary channel between plates of hepatocytes. Physiologically, the hepatic sinusoid allows blood–hepatocyte exchange en route to central vein.

faqs.q: What are the layers of the small intestinal wall?
faqs.a: From lumen outward they include mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa and serosa or adventitia depending on the segment. Structurally, the villus (Villus intestinalis) comprises fingerlike projection of small-intestinal mucosa with epithelial cover and lamina propria core. Physiologically, the villus expands absorptive surface.

faqs.q: What do intestinal villi and crypts do?
faqs.a: Villi expand the absorptive surface. Crypts contain renewing epithelial cells and other specialized cells that help maintain the mucosa. Structurally, the crypt stem cells (Cellulae stipitales cryptarum) comprises progenitor population near crypt base continuously renewing epithelium. Physiologically, the crypt stem cells governs replaces short-lived epithelial lineages.

faqs.q: What is the villus?
faqs.a: Fingerlike projection of small-intestinal mucosa with epithelial cover and lamina propria core. Functionally, it expands absorptive surface. Structurally, the enterocyte (Enterocytus) comprises absorptive columnar epithelial cell with apical microvilli. Physiologically, the enterocyte governs takes up digested nutrients.

faqs.q: Where is the enterocyte located?
faqs.a: Absorptive columnar epithelial cell with apical microvilli. Functionally, it governs takes up digested nutrients. Structurally, the enteroendocrine cell (Cellula enteroendocrina) comprises scattered hormone-secreting epithelial cells. Physiologically, the enteroendocrine cell governs sense nutrients and release regulatory peptides.

faqs.q: What is the function of the goblet cell?
faqs.a: Functionally, it lubricates and helps protect mucosal surface. Mucin-producing epithelial cell scattered among enterocytes. Clinically, regarding the goblet cell, cell proportions vary along intestine.

faqs.q: How many facial bones are in an adult human skull?
faqs.a: Fourteen: paired maxillae, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine and inferior nasal concha bones, plus the single vomer and mandible. The adult skull also has eight cranial bones, for 22 skull bones in total. The mandible (Mandibula) is single adult lower jaw consisting of a body and paired ascending rami. Physiologically, the mandible houses lower teeth and moves at the temporomandibular joints for chewing and speech.

faqs.q: Which facial bones are easiest to identify from the front?
faqs.a: The maxillae form the upper jaw, the zygomatic bones form the cheeks, the nasal bones form the bony bridge of the nose, and the single mandible forms the lower jaw. Small lacrimal and deep palatine bones cannot reliably be isolated on a simple anterior photograph. The right nasal bone (Os nasale dextrum) is small right bone at the bony bridge of the nose, above the nasal opening. Physiologically, the right nasal bone forms the upper nasal bridge, not the flexible nose tip.

faqs.q: Is the inferior nasal concha part of the ethmoid bone?
faqs.a: No. Right and left inferior nasal conchae are independent facial bones. The middle and superior conchae are parts of the ethmoid, which is counted as a cranial bone. Anatomically, the ethmoid bone (Os ethmoidale) lies between the orbits; forms the upper nasal septum, parts of the orbit and nasal roof. Physiologically, the ethmoid bone supports the olfactory region and separates the upper nasal cavity from the cranial cavity.

faqs.q: Does the 22-bone skull count include ear ossicles or the hyoid?
faqs.a: No. The six middle-ear ossicles and the single hyoid bone are additional bones associated with the head and neck; they are included separately in the conventional 206-bone adult skeleton count. Structurally, the right parietal bone (Os parietale dextrum) comprises right upper side of the cranial vault; meets the frontal, opposite parietal, occipital and temporal bones. Physiologically, the right parietal bone protects the superior and lateral cerebrum.

faqs.q: Which nerve moves the facial-expression muscles around the skull?
faqs.a: Facial nerve CN VII drives most muscles of facial expression after passing through the temporal bone and parotid region. Trigeminal CN V carries most facial skin sensation, and its V3 division supplies the major jaw-closing muscles. Bones and nerves are different structures. Structurally, the right temporal bone (Os temporale dextrum) comprises right lower side and base of the skull, surrounding the external acoustic opening and internal ear spaces. Physiologically, the right temporal bone houses hearing and balance structures; helps form the jaw joint.

faqs.q: What are the main layers of a tooth crown and root?
faqs.a: Crown dentin is covered by enamel; root dentin is covered by cementum. Pulp occupies the central chamber and canals, while the periodontal ligament connects the root to its alveolar socket. These are distinct tissues, not interchangeable layers. Structurally, the tooth root (Radix dentis) comprises portion anchored below the crown in an alveolar socket; molar roots may be multiple but number and canal shape vary. Physiologically, the tooth root anchors the tooth through periodontal ligament and cementum.

faqs.q: Which nerves carry sensation from upper and lower teeth?
faqs.a: Upper tooth sensory fibers generally travel through superior alveolar branches of maxillary trigeminal CN V2; lower tooth fibers travel through the inferior alveolar branch of mandibular CN V3. Facial CN VII supplies facial-expression muscles, not dental pulp sensation. Structurally, the inferior alveolar nerve (V3) (Nervus alveolaris inferior) comprises mandibular division branch entering the mandibular foramen and canal; dental branches serve lower teeth. Physiologically, the inferior alveolar nerve (V3) carries sensory fibers from mandibular teeth; its terminal mental branch supplies chin and lower lip.

faqs.q: How are permanent and primary teeth numbered?
faqs.a: The Universal system labels 32 conventional permanent positions 1–32 and 20 primary positions A–T. The two-digit FDI system uses quadrants 1–4 for permanent teeth and 5–8 for primary teeth, with a second digit for position within each quadrant. Structurally, the universal and FDI tooth designation (Numeratio dentium) comprises universal 1–32 names permanent teeth and A–T primary teeth in US practice; two-digit FDI identifies quadrant and position internationally. Physiologically, the universal and FDI tooth designation governs lets students locate a tooth unambiguously before describing its anatomy.

faqs.q: Do adults always have 32 teeth and do primary teeth have premolars?
faqs.a: Thirty-two is the full conventional permanent set including third molars, but actual adult counts vary because third molars may be absent, unerupted or removed. Primary dentition typically has 20 teeth and no premolars; primary molars are succeeded by permanent premolars. The primary and permanent dentitions (Dentes decidui et permanentes) is the usual primary dentition has 20 teeth; the conventional full permanent dentition has 32 including third molars. Physiologically, the primary and permanent dentitions governs primary teeth support chewing, speech and the developing dental arches.

faqs.q: Can one molar cutaway show the exact canal and root shape of every tooth?
faqs.a: No. Root number, canal configuration and cusp morphology vary between tooth classes and individuals. The illustration is a representative digital teaching model; each chart position has a name and class, but is not a patient scan or an individually rendered tooth. Structurally, the permanent maxillary right third molar · #1 (FDI 18) comprises right maxillary third molar, Universal #1 (FDI 18). Most posterior permanent molar; development, eruption, presence and root configuration are highly variable. This position is a dental-arch location, not a pin on the representative molar section. Physiologically, the permanent maxillary right third molar · #1 governs has a broad cusp-bearing crown for grinding food. It is anchored in the maxilla.

faqs.q: What is the standard anatomical position?
faqs.a: The subject stands upright facing forward, with arms at the sides and palms facing anteriorly; thumbs point laterally. Right and left always belong to the subject, even when a patient is lying down. Structurally, the standard anatomical position comprises upright, face forward, upper limbs at sides with palms anterior and thumbs lateral; feet directed forward. Directions use the subject’s body, not the viewer’s. Physiologically, the standard anatomical position provides a consistent reference for locations and movements.

faqs.q: How do sagittal, coronal and transverse planes differ?
faqs.a: A sagittal plane separates right from left, a coronal plane separates anterior from posterior, and a transverse plane separates superior from inferior. The median sagittal plane passes through the midline. Structurally, the median sagittal plane comprises vertical plane through the midline dividing the body into equal right and left halves. The translucent sheet is a conceptual aid. Physiologically, the median sagittal plane governs defines exact midline relationships.

faqs.q: What is the difference between proximal and distal?
faqs.a: Proximal means closer to the point where a limb joins the trunk; distal means farther from that attachment. The elbow is proximal to the wrist in the upper limb. Structurally, the proximal and distal comprises proximal is nearer a limb’s attachment to the trunk; distal farther away along the limb. Physiologically, the proximal and distal governs describes relative position along a limb.

faqs.q: Why does patient right appear on the left side of a front-facing illustration?
faqs.a: An anterior image faces the patient. Their right side is therefore on the observer’s left. Anatomical descriptions use the patient’s own side, not the screen’s left or right. Structurally, the patient right and left comprises right and left always refer to the subject; on an anterior image, patient right usually appears on the viewer’s left. Physiologically, the patient right and left prevents reversal when describing a structure or reading a map.

faqs.q: Are the colored planes in this atlas real body membranes?
faqs.a: No. The translucent sheets are computer-generated reference planes used to explain sections. They are not physical tissues, and the chapter does not place false anatomical pins on them. Structurally, the frontal (coronal) plane comprises vertical plane dividing anterior and posterior portions; shown by a translucent sheet, not a real tissue boundary. Physiologically, the frontal (coronal) plane governs organizes front-to-back relationships.

faqs.q: What are the dorsal and ventral body cavities?
faqs.a: The dorsal compartment includes cranial and vertebral cavities containing the central nervous system. The ventral compartment is commonly divided by the diaphragm into thoracic and abdominopelvic regions. The dorsal body cavity is posterior continuous compartment composed of cranial and vertebral cavities, with brain and spinal cord inside. Physiologically, the dorsal body cavity protects central nervous tissue.

faqs.q: Which body cavity contains the heart?
faqs.a: The heart is in the thorax, in the middle mediastinum. It is enclosed by a pericardial sac; the pericardial cavity is the thin potential space between the serous pericardial layers. Structurally, the pericardial cavity comprises potential space between visceral and parietal serous pericardium around the heart. Physiologically, the pericardial cavity governs reduces friction as the heart beats.

faqs.q: Where are the kidneys in relation to the peritoneum?
faqs.a: The kidneys lie retroperitoneally, posterior to the parietal peritoneum. They are not floating inside the potential peritoneal cavity. The abdominal cavity is upper portion of abdominopelvic compartment below the diaphragm, containing much of the digestive tract and associated organs. Physiologically, the abdominal cavity governs accommodates abdominal organs and their motion.

faqs.q: What are the four abdominal quadrants?
faqs.a: A vertical and a horizontal line crossing at the umbilicus form the patient's right upper, left upper, right lower and left lower quadrants. These are surface-location guides, not exact organ outlines. The right hypochondriac region is upper right of the nine abdominal regions, beneath the right costal margin. Physiologically, the right hypochondriac region governs refines location compared with four broad quadrants.

faqs.q: How do the nine abdominal regions differ from quadrants?
faqs.a: The nine-region system uses a three-by-three arrangement: hypochondriac, epigastric; lumbar, umbilical; and iliac, hypogastric positions. Right and left always refer to the patient, not the person viewing the image. The epigastric region is central upper abdomen between right and left hypochondriac regions. Physiologically, the epigastric region governs names a midline upper-abdominal surface region.

faqs.q: What are the four basic types of tissue?
faqs.a: The broad categories are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue. Most organs contain multiple types; the images show specific teaching examples, not all subtypes. Physiologically, the four fundamental tissue categories provides a framework for reading tissue architecture. Clinically, regarding the four fundamental tissue categories, an organ usually contains more than one tissue type.

faqs.q: What makes epithelial tissue different from connective tissue?
faqs.a: Epithelia form close-packed sheets with apical and basal surfaces and little extracellular space. Connective-tissue cells are often dispersed in extracellular matrix. Epithelium is generally avascular and nourished from underlying tissues. The epithelial tissue close-packed cell sheets cover body surfaces, line passages and form much glandular tissue; the image depicts one simple columnar example. Physiologically, the epithelial tissue provides selective barrier, absorption, transport and secretion.

faqs.q: Are these four pictures actual microscope slides?
faqs.a: No. They are digitally generated microscopic-scale educational cutaways rather than histology specimens, patient images, measured magnifications or diagnostic evidence. Structurally, the histology versus digital cutaway comprises histology examines prepared tissue sections with microscopy; these four generated images are stylized educational cutaways.
